NRE_note: The tool automates pre-print engineering review and suggests materials, print parameters and geometries, claiming over 99% of preparation time and cost saved, but engineering effort is an activity it performs and is not shown as an input to its recommendations (Voxelmatters 2020; 3D Printing Industry 2020).
Production_note: Coverage says the tool generates a price from 'customizable rate settings' after STL upload, but no rate, material, machine-time or labour input is itemised, so it outputs a quote with undocumented inputs (Additive Manufacturing Media; 3Dnatives directory).
QA_Qual_note: Launch coverage frames meeting regulations in aerospace and defense as the problem the tool addresses, motivation only, and no qualification step or gate is described; the company site can no longer be checked (Voxelmatters 2020).
QA_Insp_note: The 'AI inspection engine' cited earlier was on the company site, which now redirects to a parked domain; reachable coverage describes only printability verdicts and predicted failure points before printing, not inspection of printed parts (Additive Manufacturing Media; Fabbaloo).
Storage_note: The documented scope is pre-print part analysis, printability verdicts and quoting, which plainly excludes spare-part inventory (Additive Manufacturing Media; Voxelmatters 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: Settings reflect the machines a company owns and the dashboard is said to help users judge the capital investment needed, a claimed benefit; whether machine capital enters the tool's recommendations cannot be confirmed (Additive Manufacturing Media).
Shared_Capacity_note: As a per-part pre-print analysis and quoting tool for one organisation's machines, its documented scope does not extend to capacity pooled across sites or users (Additive Manufacturing Media; 3DPrint.com 2020).
Speed_note: Shorter time to market, faster turnaround and days saved on trial and error are claimed, but no source shows print or lead time used in the tool's recommendations (3D Printing Industry 2020; 3DPrint.com 2020).

name: Replique digital inventory and on-demand manufacturing platform
year: 2021 (launched Apr 2021 from BASF's Chemovator); spun out Jun 2023
developer: Replique GmbH (BASF Chemovator venture; spun out Jun 2023)
description: OEMs store encrypted part designs in a digital inventory; orders are routed automatically to quality-approved print partners selected by capability, capacity and location. Replique also reviews spare-part inventories for AM suitability and reverse-engineers or converts 2D drawings.
NRE_note: Design, reverse engineering, process adaptation and part optimisation, including an FEM redesign of a hydraulic block, are offered as services when part documentation is missing; whether that effort enters the platform's quoting or routing decisions cannot be confirmed from public sources (Replique spare-parts page; Replique homepage).
Production_note: Engineers prepare free non-binding quotes and choose process by quantity, material and cost, and the platform lists a Quoting module, but no cost inputs or method are documented (Replique homepage; Replique platform page).
QA_Qual_note: Orders go only to partners vetted for capability to make repeatable fit-for-purpose parts, and series production includes first-article inspection with a documented process, but qualification is not modelled or costed (Replique homepage; ManufacturingTomorrow 2021; spare-parts page).
QA_Insp_note: Replique checks part quality against customer requirements, tracks print and process parameters at bureaus and holds quality documents in a quality module, but whether inspection results enter any platform decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Replique homepage; AWS blog; platform page).
Storage_note: OEM spare-part inventories are screened on material, height, demand frequency and supplier dependency, and parts are stored digitally to cut storage and disposal costs, but holding cost or stock levels are not computed (Replique spare-parts page; ManufacturingTomorrow 2021).
Shared_Capital_note: The company pages, AWS blog and CEO interview discuss avoided tooling and storage costs but never machine investment or utilisation, and no product documentation is public, so this cannot be established (ManufacturingTomorrow 2021; Replique homepage).
Shared_Capacity_note: Orders are routed automatically across a network of 450+ vetted partners chosen by capability, capacity and location, but no effect on lead time is modelled (AWS blog; Replique homepage).
Speed_note: The vendor quotes 3 weeks versus 16 weeks conventional and a 6-week MAN case, figures from cases; whether the platform uses lead time in its decisions cannot be confirmed from public sources (Replique homepage; spare-parts page).

name: SelectAM
year: 2022 (free software launched Oct 2022); AI ordering workflow added Sep 2023
developer: SelectAM Oy (Finland; co-founder and CEO Niklas Kretzschmar)
decision_levels: Part selection; Process/machine choice; Adopt or make-vs-buy
description: AI workflow from part selection to ordering: instant price and lead time, TCO comparison with conventional manufacturing and AM savings (free); custom machines/materials, nesting and slicing simulation, production cost/time and best-technology identification (premium).
NRE_note: The software shows redesign potential and SelectAM offers Leap3D 2D-to-3D conversion and TDP creation as services, but whether engineering effort or CAD availability enters the part-selection decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Metal AM 2023; SelectAM home page; product page).
Production_note: Premium calculates AM production and post-processing costs and times per part with user-configured machine and material parameters, nesting and slicing, and the free tier gives instant prices and CM/AM break-even (Metal AM 2023; product page; 3Dnatives DE 2025).
QA_Qual_note: 'Qualify' in SelectAM means technical and economic feasibility, and no source read says the platform tracks or costs material, process or part qualification (SelectAM home page; product page).
QA_Insp_note: The software checks surface roughness, tolerances and CAD file health for feasibility, but no source says whether part inspection or testing is costed (3DPI 2022; product page).
Storage_note: Top-down screening weighs remaining lifecycle, annual demand, available stock and MOQ to find parts where AM can cut inventory, but no holding cost or stock level is output (3Dnatives DE 2025).
Shared_Capital_note: Voxel-based nesting of many parts per build feeds the automated cost calculation with configurable machine profiles, but machine capital and its amortisation are not documented (product page; 3DPI 2022).
Shared_Capacity_note: Parts can be exported for in-house production or ordered through a Hoffmann Group-operated partner platform, but the software is not shown assigning or routing work across sites, which public sources cannot confirm (SelectAM product page; home page).
Speed_note: The software returns instant lead times for individual parts and assemblies alongside price quotes, and premium calculates production times, though the method is undocumented (Metal AM 2023).

name: aPriori (Additive Manufacturing process group)
developer: aPriori Technologies
description: Digital-factory should-cost software whose AM process group computes physics-based cycle time, orientation, supports, nesting, post-processing (secondary machining, heat treat, powder recycling) and downstream surface treatment, heat treatment, inspection and packaging. Breakeven reports compare AM with casting across volumes.
NRE_note: Build-job setup is costed (default load-file-and-splice time of 15 minutes, amortised over the batch at labour plus direct overhead rate), but no one-time redesign, reverse engineering or parameter-development cost appears in the AM formulas (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Metal Sintering Formulas).
Production_note: Per-part metal AM cost is built from cycle time (preparation, support, part, recoat, powder-removal and cool time shared across nested parts), material cost with supports, waste and powder-recycling mass, labour cost and direct overhead per part (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Metal Sintering and Accounting Formulas; Overhead Costs per Part).
QA_Qual_note: The AM chapter's documented scope is manufacturing times and costs for AM and subsequent processes, and its 13 formula sections (accounting, yield, printing, laser and metal sintering, curing, breakoff, base removal, cleaning, sieving, powder loading) contain no qualification element (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2).
QA_Insp_note: The AM process group estimates times and costs of subsequent inspection processes for the part, and the guide's secondary inspection operations compute per-part inspection time from part surface area and an inspection rate, which aPriori costs at labour and overhead rates (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, AM chapter intro; CT Scan; Inspecting Component-level Operation).
Storage_note: aPriori is a per-part should-cost engine whose documented AM scope is manufacturing times and costs, so inventory holding is outside it (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, AM chapter).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine capital is amortised with utilisation and multi-part-build assumptions: the direct overhead rate is annual depreciation, maintenance, energy, supplies and imputed interest divided by work-centre hours times machine uptime, charged per part through cycle time, and build preparation and cooling are divided across the parts nested on the plate (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Overhead Rates and Metal Sintering Formulas; 2021 R1 Annual Direct Overhead).
Shared_Capacity_note: Work-centre capacity appears only as the denominator that turns annual machine cost into an hourly rate; the per-part should-cost scope has no sites, queues or capacity contention (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Overhead Rates; AM chapter).
Speed_note: Per-part cycle time is computed from preparation, support, part, recoat, powder-removal and cool times, a partial time model; no lead time or availability output is documented (Cost Model Guide 2019 R2, Metal Sintering Formulas).

name: AMFG (Auto-Quoting, Geometric Estimating Engine, Planning & Scheduling, Quality Tracking)
developer: AMFG (London)
description: Quoting, order management and production workflow software for high-mix manufacturers, with an estimating engine using adjustable machine/labor rates and post-processing, plus scheduling, job tracking, traceability and a reorder 'digital warehouse'.
NRE_note: The AM pricing-formula help article shows no setup, engineering or file-preparation term and formulas are shop-defined 'pricing scripts', so whether NRE is costed for AM cannot be settled (AMFG help: AM pricing formulas; AMFG AM page).
Production_note: Per-part AM prices are computed from shop-defined formulas on part volume x material rate per technology, surface area and bounding-box coefficients plus per-service post-processing formulas; machine time and labour terms are not documented (AMFG help: AM pricing formulas).
QA_Qual_note: The AS9100 and AM pages offer compliance control, QA task tracking and traceability, but no public page mentions first-article, process or part qualification (AMFG AM and ISO/AS9100 pages).
QA_Insp_note: Quality Tracking records non-conformances and quality reports and the AS9100 page tracks QA tasks, data the software stores; no source shows inspection scope or results changing or gating its outputs (AMFG quality pages; Digital Engineering 24/7).
Storage_note: A 'digital warehouse' keeps standing-order parts so customers can reorder without new quotes, a feature whose stock effect enters no documented decision (AMFG Technology Applied case).
Shared_Capital_note: The AM and scheduling pages describe production slots and machine monitoring but do not say whether machine cost, utilisation or amortisation enters quotes, and the pricing article has no machine term (AMFG AM, planning pages; pricing article).
Shared_Capacity_note: Planning & Scheduling automatically assigns jobs to 'the best available machines and operators' and uses a timeline to plan capacity within a shop, with no documented effect on lead time and no multi-site pooling (AMFG planning-scheduling page).
Speed_note: The scheduling page says a timeline view helps teams 'plan capacity and delivery dates' and the AM page promises orders 'on time', but no lead-time or due-date input or calculation is documented, so whether the scheduler acts on lead time cannot be confirmed (AMFG planning-scheduling and AM pages).

name: Authentise Flows (FlowsAM, RFQ Responder, Design Warehouse)
year: Launch year of Flows not confirmed; Authentise software integrated Prosper3D quoting in Oct 2018 and Elements was acquired in Feb 2022
developer: Authentise Inc. (acquired Elements, Feb 2022; integrated Prosper3D quoting engines, Oct 2018)
description: AM workflow/MES suite with RFQ and quoting (pricing rules, templates, automated calculations, swappable quoting algorithms such as Prosper3D), production planning/scheduling, subcontractor management and digital traceability.
NRE_note: Reusable workflows are offered to cut duplicate prep work and a Boeing case claims build-preparation time fell by more than 95%, but whether the software uses NRE in its quoting or routing decisions cannot be confirmed from public sources (RFQ Responder page; 3DPrint.com Boeing interview).
Production_note: Quotes come from configurable pricing rules, templates and automated calculations, with internal quoting tools 'based on data drawn from AM machines', but no cost inputs or formula are documented (RFQ Responder page; Metal AM 2018).
QA_Qual_note: FlowsAM lists 'qualification-aware routing' as a feature, so qualification status gates where work is routed, with no qualification cost or effort (FlowsAM page).
QA_Insp_note: FlowsAM captures part-level QA data and automated reports and powder tracking records testing actions with genealogy, but these are records, and whether inspection enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (FlowsAM page; Design World powder tracking).
Storage_note: Design Warehouse is pitched as storing spares digitally with 'lower storage and transport costs' as a benefit, but whether the software uses stock in any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Authentise digital design warehousing blog).
Shared_Capital_note: FlowsAM shows live machine status and claims per-part savings of about $0.35 to $48, and Boeing time studies claim 3x software ROI, but no page says whether machine cost, utilisation or amortisation enters quoting (FlowsAM page; Metal AM Dec 2022).
Shared_Capacity_note: FlowsAM claims capacity-aware scheduling and routing of jobs across internal sites and external partners, but no capacity model or lead-time effect is documented (FlowsAM page).
Speed_note: Digital design warehousing is claimed to give 'reduced lead times and downtime', but whether the software estimates or uses lead time in its decisions cannot be confirmed from public sources (Authentise digital design warehousing blog; FlowsAM page).

name: Materialise CO-AM software platform
year: Unknown start year for CO-AM (current in 2026; DigiFabster quoting integration Nov 2023)
developer: Materialise NV (Belgium)
earlier_versions: Materialise Streamics (date not found): Materialise AM production-management system used at Avio Aero; the entry treats it as the predecessor of CO-AM's AM MES, which the sources read do not confirm.
description: Production software stack: Magics build preparation (nesting, metal supports, pre-print checks), AM MES for work orders, capacity and throughput, quality data with NCR/CAPA, and multi-site visibility and secure data delivery. Cost estimation is not described natively.
NRE_note: CO-AM automates build preparation (metal supports, nesting, labelling) to cut repetitive prep work, a feature whose effort does not enter any decision in the sources read (Materialise CO-AM page).
Production_note: Quotes come from the separate DigiFabster portal integrated with CO-AM order management and the CO-AM, MES and planning pages describe no cost calculation of their own, so whether the platform itself uses per-part cost in its decisions cannot be confirmed from public sources (PR Newswire 2023; Materialise MES and CO-AM pages).
QA_Qual_note: CO-AM records nonconformances, CAPA reports and traceability for regulatory compliance, but no source shows a qualification gate or qualification entering any decision (Materialise CO-AM page).
QA_Insp_note: Quality questionnaires record which parts meet quality standards and shop-floor, sensor and image data are collected for quality assurance, but no source shows inspection results gating parts or entering a decision (Materialise MES and CO-AM pages).
Storage_note: The CO-AM, MES and planning pages do not mention parts inventory or digital inventory, and no product documentation was found, so whether stock is addressed cannot be settled (Materialise product pages).
Shared_Capital_note: The planner nests multiple work orders into builds to optimise material and machine usage, so shared machine use drives its build decisions, but machine cost is never calculated and the 'analyze ROI' view has no documented inputs (Materialise planning page).
Shared_Capacity_note: A central planning tool assigns jobs to build capacity and schedules them by due date on Gantt charts, with data viewed across connected facilities, but no source shows capacity contention setting lead time or cross-site pooling (Materialise MES, planning and CO-AM pages).
Speed_note: Magics, part of CO-AM, estimates build time per machine with a self-learning method, a partial time model; lead time is not computed and lead-time reduction is only claimed (Materialise Magics build-time tutorial; CO-AM page).

name: Oqton MOS (Manufacturing OS) with 3DXpert add-on
year: Start year not confirmed; MOS current in 2026
developer: Oqton (Ghent, Belgium); acquisition by 3D Systems announced Sep 2021 ($180M); on 1 Oct 2025 3D Systems agreed to sell Oqton MOS and 3DXpert to Hubb Global Holdings (closing expected Q4 2025)
description: Cloud manufacturing operating system linking ERP/MES/PLM with AI-automated nesting, print prep, build monitoring, KPI reporting and traceability for regulated production.
NRE_note: 3DXpert prepares builds (orient, nest, support, slice, DfAM, distortion pre-compensation) and MOS claims to automate manual tasks, features whose effort does not enter any decision in public sources (oqton.com 3DXpert and MOS pages).
Production_note: 3DXpert print estimation computes material cost from system-calculated volumes (per cm3) plus machine-time cost (hourly rate x print time from build rates and recoating), but only as Parts, Supports, Lattices and Total rows summed over all bodies on the build, with no per-part allocation and no labour or post-processing terms; MOS itself only automates quoting (3DXpert print-estimation tutorial; oqton.com MOS page).
QA_Qual_note: MOS claims to help 'gain certifications and qualify quicker', captures data needed for certification and is said to manage qualification steps, but no source shows qualification gating production or entering a decision (oqton.com MOS pages).
QA_Insp_note: MOS links production steps to quality inspection results and 3DXpert offers inspect-and-report functions, recorded data and features that no source shows entering a decision (oqton.com MOS MES and 3DXpert pages).
Storage_note: The Digital Warehouse replaces physical stock with a digital catalogue and claims to minimise capital tied up in inventory, a feature and claim with no stock or holding cost used in any decision (oqton.com/manufacturing-os).
Shared_Capital_note: 3DXpert costs machine time at a flat hourly rate times estimated print time, and MOS claims better machine utilisation through job allocation, but no utilisation, volume or per-part allocation of nested builds is documented (3DXpert print-estimation tutorial; oqton.com MOS MES page).
Shared_Capacity_note: MOS is said to 'balance workloads across sites' and the Digital Warehouse can send files to a qualified facility anywhere, so the tool routes work across sites, but no capacity or queue model is described (oqton.com MOS pages).
Speed_note: 3DXpert estimates print time from user-set build rates plus per-layer recoating time (print time only), while MOS scheduling weighs delivery deadlines and claims shorter lead times without computing them (3DXpert print-estimation tutorial; oqton.com MOS MES page).

name: Autodesk Fusion with Netfabb
year: Origin year not confirmed; Netfabb 2019 release Nov 2018; sold as Fusion with Netfabb (2025 features page)
developer: Autodesk
earlier_versions: Autodesk Netfabb 2019 (Nov 2018): standalone Netfabb release whose simulation supported parameter (PRM) file development; the product is now sold as Fusion with Netfabb.
description: Build preparation (repair, 2D/3D packing, supports), quoting/manufacturing reports and thermo-mechanical simulation of metal PBF/DED builds to predict distortion. Dedicated cost estimation is not listed on the current features page.
NRE_note: Simulation-based PRM file generation, distortion compensation and support design are offered to cut trial builds, but this one-time engineering effort is a feature the software performs and does not enter its quoting or any decision (Autodesk features page).
Production_note: The report generator outputs part volume, support volume, part count and, for selected engines, a build-time estimate in a format meant 'for estimates, quotations', but no documented report field gives a cost or price (Netfabb 2024 help, report generator and report field reference).
QA_Qual_note: The edition capability lists cover build files, toolpaths, supports, latticing, optimisation and thermo-mechanical simulation, and qualification is absent from this documented scope (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb; Autodesk features page).
QA_Insp_note: The documentation names no inspection or testing function; simulation predicts hot spots and lack of fusion before the build but does not set or cost inspection (Autodesk features page; Netfabb 2024 help).
Storage_note: The documented scope is build preparation, toolpaths and process simulation, which plainly excludes inventory (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb).
Shared_Capital_note: Automatic 2D/3D packing places many parts in one build and the report counts parts, but no machine cost is entered or spread across parts, so capital sharing enters no decision (Autodesk features page; Netfabb 2024 report field reference).
Shared_Capacity_note: Netfabb prepares and simulates builds for one machine workspace and documents no capacity shared across machines, sites or users (Netfabb 2024 help, About Netfabb; Autodesk features page).
Speed_note: A build-time estimate ('Build time in current machine workspace') is reported for selected machine engines, a build-time-only output with no lead time or availability (Netfabb 2024 help, report field reference).

name: Etteplan AMOTool
developer: Etteplan (Finland), AMO team; Business Finland support
description: Quick metal AM cost estimator from part height and volume covering material, printing and post-processing; compares with conventional manufacturing, gives ROI, recommends orientation to maximize parts per plate and indicates if redesign would pay off.
NRE_note: The tool indicates whether redesign is profitable and how much material must be removed for a viable printed part, but it does not estimate redesign or other one-time engineering cost (3Dnatives 2020; Etteplan release).
Production_note: From entered part height and volume (and the chosen material) the tool computes a per-part metal AM cost covering material, the printing process and post-processing and compares it with conventional manufacturing, though the algorithm itself is unpublished and the tool is withdrawn (3Dnatives 2020; Etteplan release).
QA_Qual_note: The launch articles list material, printing and post-processing costs and redesign advice but never mention qualification, and the tool page is withdrawn, so this cannot be settled (Etteplan release; 3Dnatives 2020).
QA_Insp_note: Only 'post-processing steps' are named and no launch article says whether inspection is part of them, and the tool can no longer be checked (3Dnatives 2020).
Storage_note: AMOTool estimates a single part's cost from its height and volume, a documented scope that excludes inventory (3Dnatives 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: It recommends the orientation that maximises the number of parts on the build plate, so multi-part builds drive its recommendation, but how machine cost is spread over those parts is not described (3Dnatives 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: AMOTool estimates single-part cost from two geometric inputs and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (3Dnatives 2020).
Speed_note: None of the launch articles mentions print, build or lead time as an input or output, and the withdrawn tool cannot be checked (3Dnatives 2020; Etteplan release; Metal AM 2020).

name: ExOne Production Metal Cost Calculator
developer: The ExOne Company (later ownership changes not verified in this session)
description: Online per-part cost estimator for binder-jetted metal parts on ExOne's four Pro-series printers, from material, machine, part dimensions and volume, including capital investment, throughput, material, binder and printhead replacement.
NRE_note: The release lists capital, throughput, material, binder and printhead costs 'and more' and the gated access page shows only dimension and nesting fields, so whether setup or engineering effort is included is not shown (BusinessWire release; calculator access page).
Production_note: The calculator computes a per-part binder-jet cost from material, machine, part dimensions and volume inputs, covering capital investment, throughput, material, binder and printhead replacement (BusinessWire Jan 2021 release; 3DPI 2021).
QA_Qual_note: The documented scope is a per-part printing cost based on buying one Pro-series printer, and material qualification is referred to an ExOne representative outside the calculator (calculator access page; BusinessWire release).
QA_Insp_note: Neither the release, the 3DPI article nor the access page mentions inspection or post-processing, and the cost list ends with 'and more', so inspection cannot be ruled in or out (BusinessWire release; calculator access page).
Storage_note: The only stated output is a per-part binder-jet printing cost, a scope that excludes inventory (BusinessWire release).
Shared_Capital_note: Initial capital investment of the chosen printer is a cost element of the per-part estimate, together with throughput and a 'Nesting' (parts per build) input, so capital is allocated per part with a multi-part-build assumption; whether the 'volume' input means part volume or quantity is not stated (BusinessWire release; calculator access page).
Shared_Capacity_note: The estimate assumes the purchase of one ExOne Pro-series printer and does not address capacity shared across sites or users (3DPI 2021; BusinessWire release).
Speed_note: Throughput speed is a cost factor and printer build rates are quoted as specifications, but no source shows whether print time or lead time is output, and the calculator is form-gated (3DPI 2021; BusinessWire release).

name: DigiFabster (AM quoting and e-commerce)
year: Unknown (active by Nov 2021; integrated with Materialise CO-AM Nov 2023)
developer: DigiFabster (US-based)
description: ML-assisted instant quoting and e-commerce for AM service providers, using one-off per-build costs (e.g., recoat time driven by part height in powder bed) and per-part material and machine time; order data flows into Materialise CO-AM.
NRE_note: Cost-based pricing includes setup and programming costs and time-based pricing includes programming time, but redesign, digitisation and parameter development are not covered (DigiFabster Instant Quoting page).
Production_note: Per-part quotes are computed from geometry analysis with machine, operator and programming time or operation, material, setup and programming costs, with material consumption and per-piece and per-batch fields (Instant Quoting page; help: shared print time).
QA_Qual_note: The quoting, features, settings and post-production pages and the 2021 guest post mention no qualification or certification beyond ITAR data handling, and no full user manual is public, so this cannot be settled (DigiFabster features list).
QA_Insp_note: User-defined post-production options can be priced per part or with other pricing parameters, but no source shows inspection set up as one, so it can be neither confirmed nor ruled out (DigiFabster help: post productions).
Storage_note: The documented scope is quoting, ordering, payment and order tracking for manufacturers, which excludes inventory holding (DigiFabster features list).
Shared_Capital_note: For powder-bed builds a user-entered machine price per hour is charged per batch and split across the copies in the build (e.g. EUR 25.40 batch, 10 copies at EUR 2.54), but no machine purchase cost, depreciation or utilisation is entered or amortised (DigiFabster help: shared print time).
Shared_Capacity_note: DigiFabster quotes and manages orders for one shop, and 'printer capacity' appears only as build-volume fill that restarts batch pricing, with no shared capacity or lead-time effect (features list; help: shared print time).
Speed_note: Print time is computed internally for pricing, but the quoting, features and settings pages mention only quote turnaround and do not show whether build time, lead time or delivery dates are reported (Instant Quoting page; help: settings page).

name: Rickenbacher integrated SLM cost model
developer: L. Rickenbacher, A. Spierings, K. Wegener (ETH Zurich / inspire AG)
description: Adapts Alexander et al.'s generic cost model to SLM, covering pre- and post-processing steps plus a regression-based build-time estimate for mixed build jobs. It allocates build cost to parts by volume and build height so that parts of different size and complexity sharing one build each get a fair cost. Building parts simultaneously gave a 41% average cost reduction in the case study.
NRE_note: Geometry-data preparation (orientation, supports) and build-job assembly are costed per job and allocated to its parts, which is recurring build prep with no redesign, reverse engineering or parameter development (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).
Production_note: Cost per part sums geometry preparation, job assembly, set-up, build (machine rate x regression build time plus material), removal, substrate separation and post-processing (Costabile et al. 2017; Emerald abstract).
QA_Qual_note: The full cost equation reproduced in two reviews consists of seven SLM process-step terms, so qualification lies outside the model's documented scope (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).
QA_Insp_note: The reproduced equation has only a generic post-processing term; Costabile et al.'s conclusions group the model with two others that 'consider post-processing activities like surface treatments and quality controls', but their own Rickenbacher section and Dogea et al.'s reproduction never mention inspection, and the paywalled paper was not read (Costabile et al. 2017; Dogea et al. 2023).
Storage_note: The model allocates SLM process-step costs to parts sharing build jobs, a scope that plainly excludes inventory (Emerald abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine-time build cost is allocated among parts from different projects sharing a build job by cross-section or height, so filling the build space cuts unit cost by 41% on average, though the machine rate is given rather than derived from capital (Emerald abstract; Costabile et al. 2017).
Shared_Capacity_note: Pooling happens only within one machine's build jobs as a cost-allocation effect, and the documented model has no lead-time, queue or multi-site capacity element (Emerald abstract; Costabile et al. 2017).
Speed_note: Build time per job is estimated by a linear regression on 24 builds and allocated to parts, but only for cost; lead time is not reported (Costabile et al. 2017; Rudolph and Emmelmann 2018).

name: Lindemann et al. (2013) DMRC lifecycle-cost model with TD-ABC
developer: C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, M. Moi, R. Koch (Paderborn University, Direct Manufacturing Research Center)
earlier_versions: Lindemann, Jahnke, Moi, Koch (2012), 'Analyzing Product Lifecycle Costs for a Better Understanding of Cost Drivers in Additive Manufacturing', SFF Symposium 2012: earlier DMRC cost-driver analysis whose results the 2013 lifecycle-cost paper builds on.
description: Lifecycle cost model following the DIN/IEC 60300-3-3 phases: concept, design and development, production, installation, usage/maintenance, and disposal. Production is costed with time-driven activity-based costing across build-job preparation, build, part and support removal, and post-processing. Build rate, machine cost, material cost and utilization come out as the dominant drivers.
NRE_note: Build-job preparation is a costed TD-ABC process (complexity factor times engineer labour), but the design-and-development phase only lists the costs it would cover (drawings, component design, QM planning, prototype and test) with no inputs, method or values, and the 2012 version leaves design cost to future work (SFF 2013; SFF 2012).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is computed by TD-ABC over build-job preparation, build (machine hourly rate x build time), part and support removal and post-processing, with material, personnel, energy and consumables (SFF 2013; SFF 2012).
QA_Qual_note: A prototype and test phase and QM planning are named as design-and-development cost categories, but the model gives them no inputs or figures and qualification cost does not enter its output (SFF 2013).
QA_Insp_note: Quality control is one of the manual post-processing steps costed as average processing time x labour rate, bundled with support removal and polishing, with no separate NDI, CT or coupon-test line (SFF 2012; SFF 2013).
Storage_note: Usage-phase logistics include spare-part storage at 22% of acquisition value per year as a fixed lifecycle element, but AM's effect on stock levels is only discussed, not modelled (SFF 2013).
Shared_Capital_note: The machine hourly rate comes from a EUR 500,000 investment, 5-year depreciation and 4,500 h/yr utilisation (with a 7,800 h/yr optimised case), and the 2013 paper assumes 75% utilisation (673 parts/yr per machine) (SFF 2012; SFF 2013).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read; capacity appears only as an illustrative parts-per-year figure and forecast build rates, with no pooling, contention or service effect (SFF 2013).
Speed_note: Build time is estimated and each process is timed only as a cost driver; lead time is not modelled, and the EUR 100,000/day aircraft-on-ground cost is cited only as motivation (SFF 2013; SFF 2012).

name: Atzeni & Salmi DMLS vs. die-casting break-even model
developer: E. Atzeni, A. Salmi (Politecnico di Torino)
description: Builds cost models for DMLS and high-pressure die casting of the same DfAM-redesigned aerospace part to find the volume at which AM becomes competitive. It concludes AM can compete for small-to-medium batches.
NRE_note: Pre-processing is costed per build as setup time times operator rate, but the DfAM redesign credited for the savings is not shown as a one-time engineering cost (Khanna et al. 2024 review; IRIS abstract).
Production_note: Per-part DMLS cost is built from material (volume x unit price), pre-processing, processing (machine cost over parts per build) and post-processing (operator rate, heat treatment), against a die-casting cost model (Khanna et al. 2024 review; Baumers et al. 2017, Table 5).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract and the two reviews that describe the model do not mention qualification or certification, and no open full text exists (IRIS record has no file), so presence cannot be established (IRIS; Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017).
QA_Insp_note: The reviews list material, pre-processing, processing and post-processing (operator, heat treatment) terms without inspection, but absence cannot be confirmed without the full text (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017).
Storage_note: The documented scope is a per-part production cost comparison by batch size against die casting, which plainly excludes inventory (IRIS abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost (5-year straight-line depreciation, about 90% of AM part cost) is divided by the number of parts in a multi-part build that assumes the build space is used efficiently, the rubric's multi-part-build assumption (Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017, Table 5 and Conclusions).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model costs one part on one DMLS route at different batch sizes, so pooling capacity across sites or users is plainly outside its documented scope (IRIS abstract; reviews).
Speed_note: Neither the abstract nor the two reviews say whether build time is reported or only drives cost, and tooling lead time for die casting is not mentioned; the full text could not be reached (IRIS; Khanna et al. 2024; Baumers et al. 2017).

name: Baumers et al. (2017) total-cost and capacity-utilisation model (IJPR)
developer: M. Baumers, P. Dickens, C. Tuck, R. Hague (University of Nottingham), with L. Beltrametti and A. Gasparre on the 2017 paper
earlier_versions: Baumers, Dickens, Tuck, Hague (2016), Technol. Forecast. Soc. Change 102:193-201: production-cost model for EBM and DMLS (about GBP 2.39 vs. 6.18 per cm3 deposited) showing machine productivity drives cost; the 2017 model adds total cost with build-failure risk, filling build volume with other geometries, and the value of design adaptation.
description: Activity-based production cost models that combine direct costs with time-allocated indirect (machine and overhead) costs, voxel-based build-time estimates, and computational packing of the build volume. The 2017 version adds per-layer build-failure risk and the discounted value of design adaptation. It shows single-geometry builds overstate unit cost by 157% on average compared with full mixed builds.
NRE_note: Only per-build machine setup and unloading labour (180 min, EUR 72.04 per build) is costed, and the cost of re-design is explicitly ignored, so one-time engineering is missing (arXiv full text, Table 2).
Production_note: Unit cost is built from material, energy, build-time-allocated indirect cost, setup labour and 37 min/part post-processing labour, inflated for per-layer build-failure risk (arXiv full text, Table 2, Table 4).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper explicitly omits the cost of component re-validation and has no qualification term (arXiv full text, Discussion).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is only folded into the 37 min/part post-processing labour bundle with support removal, finishing and washing, with no separate inspection cost (arXiv full text).
Storage_note: In-process inventory, warehousing and logistics are explicitly excluded from scope (arXiv full text, Discussion).
Shared_Capital_note: Indirect machine cost is allocated by build time and apportioned to each part by its volume fraction of the build, and filling unused build volume with other geometries cuts unit cost, an explicit multi-part-build assumption (arXiv full text, Eq. 2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Build-volume utilisation is modelled by packing other parts into the same build on one machine, but with no effect on lead time; machine scheduling is left to future work (arXiv full text).
Speed_note: The voxel-based tool computes and reports build time per configuration (8.86 h for one blower to 23.00 h for 20; 53.38 to 41.41 h in mixed builds), a partial time model, but lead time is excluded from scope (arXiv full text, Table 4).

name: Laureijs/Fuchs (CMU) process-based cost model: metal AM vs. forging
developer: R. E. Laureijs, J. Bonnín Roca, S. P. Narra, C. Montgomery, J. L. Beuth, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University; E. R. H. Fuchs lab, Engineering & Public Policy)
description: Process-based cost model built on data from 14 anonymous firms (AM producers, powder and equipment suppliers, a university lab) and the Forging Industry Association. The AM route is modelled from the build step through stress relief (DMLS only), wire EDM, HIP, shot peening and destructive testing. At 1,000/yr the AM bracket costs about $3,200 vs. about $400 forged. With a 10-year fuel-saving NPV ($1,300 base, up to $3,000 per bracket), AM is competitive at 2,000-12,000/yr. Powder price and batch size (set by build orientation) are the top sensitivities. Cutting destructive testing from 1 part in 8 to 1 in 100 saves about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr, and about $410 when combined with vertical builds. FAA configuration control is modelled as 'one machine, one part' dedication of the AM machines.
NRE_note: The model starts at the build step with the design already optimised and converted to STL, so redesign enters only as the lighter geometry and its fuel saving (ASME full text as read in the earlier pass; ScienceGate abstract).
Production_note: Per-bracket cost for DMLS, EBM and forging is built up process step by step from 14 firms' data, with reject rates and best/base/worst ranges across 1,000-12,000 brackets/yr (ASME full text, Figs. 4-7; ScienceGate abstract).
QA_Qual_note: FAA configuration control is modelled only as a 'one machine, one part' dedication rule that raises AM machine cost per part at low volume; certification activities themselves are not costed (ASME full text as read in the earlier pass).
QA_Insp_note: Destructive testing is modelled as a sampled yield loss (1 part in 8, swept to 1 in 100, worth about $150/bracket at 10,000/yr), but test labour, equipment and NDI are not costed (ASME full text, Fig. 8; ScienceGate abstract).
Storage_note: Inventory and spares are outside the model, which compares production cost plus fuel-saving NPV only (ASME full text as read in the earlier pass; ScienceGate abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost per part depends on annual volume and on batch size per build set by vertical vs horizontal orientation, with AM machines dedicated to the bracket (ASME full text, Fig. 9; ScienceGate abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production is modelled at a single dedicated facility with no pooling of capacity across sites or users and no lead-time effect (ASME full text as read in the earlier pass).
Speed_note: Time value is not modelled; the lifecycle benefit is fuel saving from weight reduction, with lead time only in the introduction and a footnote (ASME full text; ScienceGate abstract).

name: Bonnín Roca (CMU) process-based cost model + facility-location model for decentralized metal AM
developer: J. Bonnín Roca, P. Vaishnav, R. E. Laureijs, J. Mendonça, E. R. H. Fuchs (Carnegie Mellon University EPP; Universidade de Lisboa / IN+ via CMU Portugal; Bonnín Roca now at TU Eindhoven). M. G. Morgan is not a co-author of this paper; he co-authored the team's regulation papers.
description: A location-dependent process-based cost model (local labour and land costs) feeds an uncapacitated facility-location MILP. The MILP picks the cost-minimising number and location of AM sites, trading production scale economies against transport and inventory costs. The optimal number of sites barely changes across technology-improvement scenarios, and as demand grows the factory moves toward the highest-demand airports. Decentralisation pays only for non-critical parts that can share the same equipment with minimal certification requirements, at combined volumes in the tens of thousands per year. At lower volumes it pays only for parts that need no HIP. Expensive post-processing equipment is what favours centralisation.
NRE_note: The abstract, keywords and section snippets do not say whether design, reverse-engineering or build-preparation cost is in the process-based cost model, and neither the paper nor the CMU dissertation full text could be reached (ScienceDirect abstract page).
Production_note: A location-dependent process-based cost model of the metal AM process, with HIP post-processing driving results, computes the production cost fed into the location optimisation (ScienceDirect abstract and introduction; IN+ seminar abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Minimal certification requirements appear only in the authors' conclusion that decentralisation pays for non-critical parts on shared equipment; whether the model uses qualification cost or criteria cannot be confirmed from the abstracts (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection or testing is not mentioned in the abstract, snippets or press, and the full text could not be reached to check for testing costs or yields (ScienceDirect abstract page).
Storage_note: The abstract states the optimisation trades off production, transportation and inventory costs when choosing the number and location of AM sites, so inventory cost varies with configuration; the inventory formulation itself is not visible (ScienceDirect abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The number of AM sites is traded off against production economies of scale, and parts sharing the same equipment or avoiding costly HIP equipment favour decentralisation (ScienceDirect abstract; IN+ seminar abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The number and location of AM sites serving airports are optimised, but the model is an uncapacitated facility-location MILP, so capacity contention does not set lead time or service (ScienceDirect introduction snippet).
Speed_note: Lead-time reduction appears only as general AM motivation in the introduction, and whether lead time or service enters the cost terms cannot be seen without the full text (ScienceDirect introduction snippet).

name: Paderborn DMRC Trade-off Methodology (TOM), 2017 version (Kruse, Reiher & Koch)
developer: C. Lindemann, T. Reiher, U. Jahnke, R. Koch; A. Kruse (Paderborn University, DMRC)
earlier_versions: Lindemann, Jahnke, Reiher & Koch (2014), SFF Symposium paper 'Towards a sustainable and economic selection of part candidates for AM': original workshop-based part-selection matrix with an early cost-estimation module. | Lindemann, Reiher, Jahnke & Koch (2015), Rapid Prototyping Journal 21(2):216-227 (doi:10.1108/RPJ-12-2014-0179): journal version reporting 90% overlap with independent expert selections in an ESA project; the 2017 version adds knock-out gates, four value categories, company and product questionnaires, and an Excel implementation.
description: Three-phase workshop (information, assessment, decision) in which non-experts and AM experts score candidate parts in a trade-off matrix. Criteria cover size limits, part class, assembly suppression, post-processing need, material applicability, design rules, property improvement and processing time, then material change, buy-to-fly, lead time and an AM-vs-milling cost ratio. Redesign and economic evaluation follow, and the 2017 revision adds knock-out gates and four value categories.
NRE_note: The 2014 paper compares four redesign approaches by workload and CAD data quality and recommends one for the later redesign step, but this is the authors' advice and the 2017 selection matrix has no redesign-effort, CAD-data or reverse-engineering criterion (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Production_note: A cost calculation module gives a first AM-vs-milling cost ratio from production quantities, current production cost, dimensions and raw-material and part volumes, without a documented cost build-up; full costing is planned (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
QA_Qual_note: Material applicability is a matrix criterion that favours materials already used in industry because fatigue and similar tests would be costly for others, and printable material is a knock-out gate, with no certification step (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
QA_Insp_note: Both full papers were read; post-processing need and achievable surface quality and accuracy are scored as feasibility items, but quality inspection is not a criterion (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Storage_note: Avoiding tooling and tool warehousing is mentioned in the economic discussion and the 2017 questionnaire asks about spare-part and tool management only 'to get a complete company overview', with no inventory criterion in the matrix (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: A cost analysis starting from material and machine hourly rates is listed under Development Opportunities and future work, and high machine prices are cited only as a barrier, so machine capital does not enter the methodology's decision (SFF 2017).
Shared_Capacity_note: Both full papers were read; equipment availability in-house or at service providers is checked only for build-chamber size, and capacity sharing is not addressed (SFF 2014; SFF 2017).
Speed_note: Experts estimate lead, process (scaled to one piece) and post-processing times for milling and AM and these values are compared to produce part scores, so entered times drive the ranking but no lead time is computed or valued (SFF 2014).

name: VTT/Aalto digital spare parts program (DIVA / DIVALIITO): screening, metal PBF cost tool, qualification workflow
developer: M. Salmi, J. Partanen, J. Tuomi, S. Chekurov, N. Kretzschmar et al. (Aalto University); S. Metsä-Kortelainen, A. Jussila et al. (VTT)
description: Four-phase spare-part classification adapted from Knofius et al.: technical (material, size), photo-based geometry review, ranking, then economic (price, resupply lead time, annual consumption, MOQ). Only ~2% of one firm's items were feasible. It adds an STL-based metal PBF cost tool and illustrative AM vs. conventional business cases that include downtime. Its cost tool was later released as AMDSP 2.0, which is listed separately.
NRE_note: 3D-model availability was meant as a screening consideration but was not applied for lack of data, and digitisation and redesign are never costed, so NRE does not enter the classification or cost tool (DIVA report pp. 12-13).
Production_note: The MATLAB tool takes an STL, places it with supports and splits per-part cost into machine amortisation (8-yr depreciation), work and material (74% powder packing, up to 95% recycling, 10% follow-up time), giving e.g. about EUR 55 per Inconel 718 pin (DIVA report pp. 14-16, Table 3).
QA_Qual_note: DIVALIITO sets out a qualification workflow on DNV GL CG-0197 (pMPS and test plan, notified-body review, qualification build with witness specimens tested to acceptance criteria, component and powder test lists), but gives no test counts, costs or part-class tiers (2020 report pp. 20-21).
QA_Insp_note: Hardness, porosity, Charpy, tensile and microstructure tests are reported for the qualification build and its witness specimens and same-run witness pieces are recommended, but no per-part or per-build inspection step is required to accept parts and inspection does not enter the screening or cost tool (DIVA report; 2020 report pp. 20-21, Table 4).
Storage_note: The enclosure business case computes total storage cost for each route from stock level and unit storage cost (average stock 10 vs 1 pcs, EUR 100 vs EUR 1, plus logistics to stock EUR 30 vs 0), and the cost tool accepts storage and transport costs as inputs; the stock levels themselves are assumed, not derived (DIVA report p. 14, Table 4 p. 37).
Shared_Capital_note: The DIVA cost tool includes machine amortisation from 8-year depreciation, but no machine price, utilisation, operating-hours or parts-per-build input is described, and the full-platform pricing assumption belongs to a separate, unnamed tool used only in the heated-cutter case (DIVA report pp. 14-16, 24).
Shared_Capacity_note: Five supply-chain models and networks of AM service providers are described, and providers are said to reach higher utilisation through a wider customer base, but these are concepts and capacity does not enter the screening or business cases (DIVA report pp. 41-42; 2020 report p. 5).
Speed_note: The enclosure business case enters delivery time (20 vs 19 days) and a downtime rate (EUR 1,000/h) and the cost tool estimates manufacturing time, but no lead time, availability or downtime total is computed; resupply lead time is also a screening criterion (DIVA report p. 14, Table 4 p. 37).

name: Klahn-Leutenecker-Meboldt (ETH Zurich) design-strategy and indicator method
developer: C. Klahn, B. Leutenecker, M. Meboldt (ETH Zurich; inspire AG)
description: Separates a manufacturing-driven strategy (substituting AM for an existing process, possibly later in the lifecycle) from a function-driven strategy (redesign for performance). It proposes indicators for parts that gain most from AM through process advantages vs. design advantages.
NRE_note: The two strategies differ in how much redesign they involve, but redesign or engineering effort is not an indicator and does not enter the choice of part or strategy (Procedia CIRP full text, Sec. 5; ICED 2015 full text).
Production_note: Cost acts as a screen, with parts that cannot be made additively for 'dimensions, costs or other restrictions' set aside and annual quantity a negative indicator, and the case compares supplier-quoted unit costs by lot size (SLS EUR 6.88 vs EUR 107.83 prototype moulding at 25 units), but the method computes no cost (ICED 2015 full text, Table 1; Procedia CIRP Fig. 4).
QA_Qual_note: Both full papers were read; qualification is not part of the strategies or indicators, and the cases mention only a customer test of 50 SLS parts and a sawdust benchmark (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).
QA_Insp_note: Both full papers were read and inspection is not addressed (Procedia CIRP and ICED 2015 full texts).
Storage_note: Both full papers were read; inventory, spares and obsolescence are not among the indicators or strategies and appear only in a cited Wohlers list of general AM benefits (ICED 2015 Sec. 2, 5.1; Procedia CIRP).
Shared_Capital_note: Both full papers were read; AM machine investment is not discussed, only avoided part-specific tooling investment (Procedia CIRP Sec. 5.1).
Shared_Capacity_note: Both full papers were read; capacity is not addressed beyond a remark that growing build chambers and build rates shift the screening limits (ICED 2015 Sec. 5.1).
Speed_note: Rapid availability for launch is given as a benefit of the manufacturing-driven strategy and the case quotes about 3 weeks for prototype moulds vs 3 months for a series tool, but the indicators are size, material, volume and design features and time does not enter the choice of part or strategy (Procedia CIRP Secs. 3, 6.1; ICED 2015 full text).

name: Purdue/Virginia Tech Decision Engine for AM in defense acquisition
developer: W. Tsutsui, Q. Shi, I. Walter, A. Wei, C. Williams, D. DeLaurentis, J. Panchal (Purdue University; Virginia Tech)
description: Expected-utility engine that ranks AM and conventional routes on total cost, total time and part mass, with a bounding-box go/no-go check. Cost comes from a Gibson et al.-style model (prorated machine purchase, operation, material, labour). Hybrid WAAM ranked highest in both scenarios.
NRE_note: Print set-up per batch is costed inside human time and labour, but the topology-optimised redesign (Fusion 360) enters only as lower mass, with no design, CAD or engineering cost (NPS paper SYM-AM-23-069, Table 3 footnotes).
Production_note: Cost per alternative is built from prorated machine purchase, machine operation, material and labour, with build time from scan length and process parameters, for each AM route and casting (NPS paper, cost model and Table 3).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper models no qualification or certification term; heat treatment of the hWAAM part is mentioned only as a post-processing need (NPS paper, full text).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper models no inspection or testing term; human time covers set-up, depowdering and machining only (NPS paper, full text).
Storage_note: Inventory reduction is named only as a general AM benefit in the introduction and is not an attribute of the decision engine (NPS paper, full text).
Shared_Capital_note: A prorated machine purchase cost is a cost term per route and parts per batch are listed, but the proration basis (life, utilisation or volume) is not stated and machine sharing is not modelled (NPS paper, cost model and Table 3).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper models no machine counts, utilisation or shared capacity; build volume is used only as a go/no-go check (NPS paper, full text).
Speed_note: Total time for the 100-part lot (machine build time from scan length plus human time) is computed and weighted 0.3-0.4 in the utility, a production-time model with no lead time, queueing or availability (NPS paper, Table 3).

name: Zaman et al. integrated material & AM process selection (Ashby + AHP)
developer: U. K. uz Zaman, M. Rivette, A. Siadat (Arts et Métiers ENSAM, LCFC Metz); S. M. Mousavi (Shahed University, Tehran)
description: Translates requirements, screens materials and processes with Ashby material indices, then ranks them with AHP (validated with SAW) on function, cost and environment. Criteria include machine cost, labour cost, build speed, accuracy and build volume.
NRE_note: The full paper was read; design or engineering effort is not a criterion or cost term in the method, with a longer design cycle mentioned only in the literature review (ENSAM author copy).
Production_note: Per-part material cost is computed with the Yim and Rosen model (support, recycling, count, volume, price, density), while machine and labour cost enter only as AHP criteria, so no full per-part cost is built up (ENSAM author copy, Eq. 1, Table 8, Table 11).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper was read and qualification or certification is not addressed in the Ashby screening or AHP hierarchy (ENSAM author copy).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper was read; inspection is not in the method, with metrology and quality control appearing only as challenges in the introduction (ENSAM author copy).
Storage_note: The full paper was read and inventory is not addressed (ENSAM author copy).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine purchase cost is a US$ field in the machine database and an AHP criterion (7.9% global priority, differing by machine), but it is not amortised and sharing or utilisation is not modelled (ENSAM author copy, Table 4, Table 11).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper was read; capacity is reflected only as machine build volume (a 12.1% AHP criterion), and throughput or shared capacity is not modelled (ENSAM author copy, Table 11).
Speed_note: Printing speed on a 50x50x20 mm reference part is the most heavily weighted machine criterion (26.9%) and a 24-hour time margin is noted as a requirement, but no build or lead time is computed for the part (ENSAM author copy, Table 4, Table 11).

name: Liu-Zhu-Ye design-integrated AM process & machine selection
developer: W. Liu (Aston University), Z. Zhu (University of Sheffield), S. Ye (University of Cambridge)
description: Four-stage method run alongside design: must-have screening (volume, lead time, accuracy, surface, durability), AHP technical ranking, feature-based re-evaluation after detailed design, and per-machine cost estimation. The cost step adapts Fera et al.'s model, adding print success rate, labour, energy and maintenance; an SLM280 was selected at $277/part.
NRE_note: The cost equation includes per-part geometry preparation (supports, orientation), build-job assembly and machine set-up, but one-time redesign or design effort is not costed (Aston accepted manuscript, Sec. 4.5, Eq. 1).
Production_note: Per-part cost is computed for each feasible machine from preparation, set-up, build (incl. material) and post-processing, divided by print success rate and grossed up for labour, energy and maintenance, giving e.g. $277.33/part for the SLM280 (Aston accepted manuscript, Eq. 1-2, Table 9).
QA_Qual_note: The full method (must-have screening, AHP ranking, feature re-evaluation, cost) was read and contains no qualification or certification element (Aston accepted manuscript).
QA_Insp_note: Post-processing (support removal, bead blasting) and a print success rate are costed, but no inspection or quality-check term appears anywhere in the method (Aston accepted manuscript, Eq. 1-2).
Storage_note: The full method was read and inventory is not addressed (Aston accepted manuscript).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine maintenance enters as a fixed technology rate (e.g. $20k/yr, $3.5/h), but machine purchase, utilisation and parts per build are not modelled, with packing left to future work (Aston accepted manuscript, Eq. 2).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full method was read; capacity appears only as machine build volume in the screening and sharing is not addressed (Aston accepted manuscript).
Speed_note: Required lead time (12 weeks in the case) is a must-have screening threshold against tabulated process lead times (4 weeks AM vs 8-12 weeks conventional), but lead time is not computed (Aston accepted manuscript, Sec. 4.2, Table 2).

name: Fera/Costabile/Lambiase (Salerno) MiProCAMAM mixed-build cost-allocation model
developer: M. Fera, F. Fruggiero, G. Costabile, A. Lambiase, D. T. Pham (University of Salerno and co-authors)
description: Step-wise cost model (data preparation, build-job assembly, setup, building, removal) with skill-specific labour rates and OEE-adjusted times. Mixed-build costs are allocated per geometry with a coating-time algorithm adapted from Rickenbacher. Outputs are cost per part, completion time and capacity-utilisation indicators.
NRE_note: Per-build data preparation (orientation, supports) and build-job assembly are costed from operator and workstation rates (Eqs. 18-19), but redesign is only cited from the literature and no one-time engineering term exists (UNISA preprint).
Production_note: Cost per part for each geometry sums preparation, build job, setup, building (machine, gas, energy, material with powder waste) and removal costs, validated on an 85-part build (UNISA preprint, Eqs. 17-23).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is not addressed anywhere in the full preprint's model or case (UNISA preprint).
QA_Insp_note: Quality control is named but explicitly neglected in the cost calculation, and production rejects enter only as a quality loss in the OEE time adjustment (UNISA preprint, Eqs. 7-8).
Storage_note: Inventory is not part of the model, which covers one build job in a job shop; fewer spares in stock is only a cited literature advantage (UNISA preprint).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine cost per hour is purchase cost over depreciation period and annual uptime (Eq. 21), and building cost is allocated across the geometries the machine builds concurrently, with chamber-utilisation indicators (UNISA preprint, Eqs. 9-15, 22, 25-26).
Shared_Capacity_note: Build-chamber capacity utilisation is computed for the mixed build (Eqs. 25-26), but on one machine with no queue, scheduling or cross-site pooling affecting completion time, which the authors leave to future work (UNISA preprint).
Speed_note: Eq. 16 outputs a completion time in days per geometry as the sum of build-job assembly, setup, OEE-adjusted build and removal times, i.e. production duration of one job, but it excludes post-processing, queueing and delivery and is never treated as lead time (UNISA preprint, Eq. 16).

name: Di & Yang DMLS cost model with dynamic process planning
developer: L. Di, Y. Yang (University of Texas at Arlington)
description: Production cost = energy + labour + material + overhead, where overhead covers machine amortisation, maintenance and administration by build time. It is coupled with a layer-wise process-parameter search that cut total cost 12.7%. Mixed-batch cost is allocated by mass × geometric complexity.
NRE_note: Labour cost includes per-build setup and pre-processing hours (Eq. 7), but one-time parameter development or design effort is not costed (MDPI full text).
Production_note: Total cost = energy + labour + material + overhead with unit cost per part; a single Ti part costs USD 119.98, falling to USD 104.70 with dynamic process planning (MDPI full text, Eqs. 1-10).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper has no qualification cost or time term and lists missing quality and mechanical-property constraints as a limitation (MDPI full text, Sect. 4).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper has no inspection, testing or reject term in Eqs. 1-10 (MDPI full text).
Storage_note: Inventory and storage do not appear in the full paper (MDPI full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment (USD 600,000 over a 3-year life) is charged by build time (Eq. 10) and a mixed 15-geometry build's cost is split across parts by mass x geometric complexity (Eq. 2), a multi-part-build assumption (MDPI full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper costs a single machine's builds; capacity, queues or multiple sites are not modelled and build-space utilisation is only future work (MDPI full text).
Speed_note: Scan time (Eqs. 5-6) and total production time t_build drive energy, gas and overhead cost, but the results, figures and validation report only costs and never a time value, and no lead time is computed (MDPI full text, Sect. 3).

name: Barclift et al. powder-reuse depreciation extension to PBF cost model
developer: M. Barclift, S. Joshi, T. Simpson, C. Dickman (Pennsylvania State University)
description: Extends an existing PBF cost model with sum-of-the-years'-digits depreciation of reused powder by build cycle. Fixed-material-cost models can undervalue high-value virgin-powder jobs by ~3-11% or 13-75%, depending on material and the allowed number of reuse cycles.
NRE_note: Per-part digital geometry preparation, build-tray assembly and machine setup are costed, but the paper states that re-design and engineering of a pre-existing component are not captured (SFF 2016, Eq. 12, Sec. 5.4).
Production_note: Total cost per part (Eq. 12) sums geometry preparation, tray assembly, setup, build (machine and gas rates x build time, material with reuse-cycle depreciation), removal, separation and support removal (SFF 2016, Sec. 3.2).
QA_Qual_note: Full paper read: reused-powder acceptance is left to supplier-purchaser agreement and no powder, material or part qualification is costed (SFF 2016, Sec. 3.1).
QA_Insp_note: Full paper read: CT scanning to validate part integrity is named only as an unmodelled possible post-processing step, and no inspection or testing is costed (SFF 2016, Sec. 5.4).
Storage_note: Full paper read: storage appears only as a labour activity within part removal, with no inventory or carrying cost (SFF 2016, Eq. 9).
Shared_Capital_note: Build time at a flat $60/h machine rate is split among the parts in a build and setup and removal are divided by part count, but machine purchase price, capital depreciation and utilisation are not modelled (SFF 2016, Table 1, Eqs. 2-5).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read: powder lots are reused on a single machine, sharing across machines or customers is not modelled, and supply-chain modelling is future work (SFF 2016, Secs. 3.1, 6).
Speed_note: Build time per part is estimated and reported (Eq. 3, overpredicting the actual by 6%), a print-time-only time model; lead time and delivery are not modelled (SFF 2016, Secs. 3.2, 5.1).

name: Kamps et al. integrated cost + LCA model for LBM gears
developer: T. Kamps, M. Lutter-Guenther, C. Seidel, T. Gutowski, G. Reinhart (Fraunhofer / TU Munich; MIT)
description: Cradle-to-gate integrated cost and life-cycle-assessment models covering full process sequences. Lightweight design is the most significant lever for both cost and energy.
NRE_note: The abstract names lightweight design as the most significant lever for cost and energy, an author finding, and whether the model includes one-time design effort cannot be confirmed because the full text could not be reached (BL catalogue abstract).
Production_note: The paper builds integrated cost models over complete process sequences (machining, hobbing, LBM) for low-volume, high-variant gears, and the author's slides plot cumulative unit cost through build, heat treatment and finishing (BL catalogue abstract; Fraunhofer slides).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract and keywords do not mention qualification, and the paywalled full paper could not be read (BL catalogue abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract covers complete process sequences but does not say whether gear inspection or testing is a cost step, and the full paper could not be read (BL catalogue abstract).
Storage_note: The models are scoped cradle-to-gate to manufacturing cost and energy of gear process sequences, which plainly excludes inventory (BL catalogue abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The abstract does not show how LBM machine cost is allocated or whether utilisation or build sharing is assumed, and the full paper could not be read (BL catalogue abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The cradle-to-gate comparison of single gear process sequences plainly excludes printer capacity pooled across sites or users (BL catalogue abstract).
Speed_note: The abstract has no time term and the slides show processing time only as a chart axis, so whether the paper reports build or lead time is not established; the full paper could not be read (BL catalogue abstract; Fraunhofer slides).

name: Dias et al. (2022) WAAM process-based cost model (Sustainability)
developer: M. Dias, J. P. M. Pragana, B. Ferreira, I. Ribeiro, C. M. A. Silva (Instituto Superior Técnico, University of Lisbon)
earlier_versions: Dias (2021) IST MSc thesis 'Economic and Environmental Potential of Wire Arc Additive Manufacturing' (July 2021): original Excel process-based cost model and cradle-to-gate LCA of a 316L part; the 2022 Sustainability paper publishes this work with co-authors.
description: Excel process-based cost model of setup, deposition and machining. Fixed costs cover equipment annualised and scaled by utilisation, building and overhead; variable costs cover wire, baseplate, gas, labour, energy and a scrap credit. WAAM beats machining from solid at all volumes studied and beats die casting up to ~2,000-2,300 parts, with buy-to-fly as the most sensitive parameter.
NRE_note: Per-part setup time, which covers inputting and compiling CNC programs, machine offsetting and clamping, is costed in labour (Eq. 11), but one-time pre-processing (3D modelling, parameter choice, deposition planning) is explicitly excluded (Sustainability full text, Sect. 2).
Production_note: Per-part cost vs annual volume is built from wire, baseplate, gas, labour, energy, equipment, tooling, building and overhead; WAAM costs EUR 39.34 per part, 34% below machining from solid (Sustainability full text, Eqs. 2-11).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper has no qualification or certification term in the cost model (Sustainability full text).
QA_Insp_note: Part inspection is explicitly excluded as post-processing, but a rejection rate inflates equipment utilisation and material use and yields scrap income, so quality loss enters only as a reject-rate factor (Sustainability full text, Eqs. 4, 8, 10, Sect. 2.1).
Storage_note: Inventory is not addressed in the full paper (Sustainability full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Machinery is annualised over its life and multiplied by a utilisation rate built from cycle time, annual production, rejection rate and uptime, and fixed costs scale with the number of machine sets (Sustainability full text, Eq. 4).
Shared_Capacity_note: The model adds WAAM-plus-machining sets when annual production would exceed available uptime, so capacity is modelled, but at one site and with no effect on lead time (Sustainability full text).
Speed_note: Deposition time from wire feed speed (Eq. 9), inter-layer cooling and machining time are computed and reported per part (t_WAAM 49 min, t_machining 30 min), a production-time partial model with no lead time (Sustainability full text, Eqs. 9, 12).

name: Cranfield WAAM early-stage cost estimation models (vs. CNC machining)
developer: Cranfield University: J. Guo (MSc by Research, supervisors J. Mehnen, Y. Xu) and Y. Zhai ('Early cost estimation for additive manufacture', MSc by Research, supervisor H. L. Lockett)
description: Feature-based cost (and GHG) models that let designers estimate WAAM cost from CAD features and compare it with machining. Wire cost and buy-to-fly ratio drive the WAAM advantage; in Zhai's Ti case, WAAM cost £1,800 vs. £2,150 for CNC, with setup 28%, wire 27% and welding labour 25%.
NRE_note: Setup cost from the process plan is reported as 28% of WAAM product cost in the titanium case, but no one-time design or reverse-engineering cost is shown and the review notes none of the approaches covers AM design activities (Busachi et al. 2017 review, Sect. 5).
Production_note: Per-part WAAM cost is built from process-plan times, wire, welding and setup costs and compared with CNC (GBP 1,800 vs 2,150 for the titanium case), and Guo's tool reads CAD features to compute cost (Busachi et al. 2017 review, Sect. 5; Guo thesis abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Neither thesis abstract nor the review mentions qualification, and the full theses are not retrievable from the Cranfield records, so whether it is costed cannot be established (Cranfield records; Busachi et al. 2017).
QA_Insp_note: The review names setup, wire and welding as cost elements and does not mention inspection, and the full theses are not retrievable (Busachi et al. 2017; Cranfield records).
Storage_note: Both models are design-stage per-part cost (and carbon) estimators for WAAM vs CNC, a scope that plainly excludes inventory (Guo and Zhai thesis abstracts).
Shared_Capital_note: No source shows machine capital, depreciation or a machine rate in Zhai's or Guo's model: the review's 'hourly rates of operators, machines and software' sentence is the reviewers' own general advice, its 'lower capital investment' remark is narrative, and the Zhai abstract mentions none of these (Busachi et al. 2017, Sect. 5, 7; Zhai thesis record).
Shared_Capacity_note: Both models are single-part design-stage cost estimators, a scope that plainly excludes pooled print capacity (Zhai and Guo thesis abstracts).
Speed_note: The process plan yields reported deposition and machining times (WAAM 3.7 h deposition plus 0.5 h milling vs CNC 1.3 h), a production-time-only partial model with no lead time (Busachi et al. 2017 review, Sect. 5).

name: Wilson et al. DED turbine-blade remanufacturing (repair vs. replace) assessment
developer: J. M. Wilson, C. Piya, Y. C. Shin, F. Zhao, K. Ramani (Purdue University)
description: Reverse-engineers the missing blade volume from a scanned mesh with a prominent-cross-section algorithm, deposits the repair by laser direct deposition, and validates geometry and tensile strength. A cradle-to-gate comparison of energy and CO2 finds repair favourable when less than ~18% of blade volume is missing.
NRE_note: Geometry reconstruction (PCS points, CATIA spline and sweep, Boolean repair volume) is a step the method performs, but digitising and CAD reconstruction are explicitly excluded from the energy and CO2 analysis and do not enter the repair-or-replace decision (Wilson et al. 2014, secs. 3.1, 4.5).
Production_note: Full paper read: the comparison is energy and CO2 only, and the only dollar figure is a cited DoD estimate of repairable components, not a cost model (Wilson et al. 2014, secs. 1, 4.5).
QA_Qual_note: ASTM E8 tensile tests on two specimens are reported as a finding that the repair matches original strength, but qualification is explicitly excluded from the analysis and does not enter the repair-or-replace decision (Wilson et al. 2014, secs. 3.3, 4.4, 4.5).
QA_Insp_note: A CATIA distance analysis of the repaired blade against the nominal model (max deviation 0.145 mm) is reported as a case result, not a check the method requires or uses in the repair-or-replace decision (Wilson et al. 2014, sec. 4.1).
Storage_note: Full paper read: spares and stock are not analysed; the Corpus Christi Army Depot figure is motivation about repairable components only (Wilson et al. 2014, sec. 1).
Shared_Capital_note: Full paper read: equipment (LENS 750, chiller, lathe) is described only for process and energy, with no machine capital cost or allocation (Wilson et al. 2014, secs. 3.2, 4.5).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read: throughput, capacity and sites are not discussed; capacity appears only as the machine work envelope (Wilson et al. 2014).
Speed_note: Deposition build times (14 and 18 min) are reported and machine hours enter the energy inventory, a print-time-only time model, but repair lead time or turnaround is not analysed (Wilson et al. 2014, sec. 4.2, Table 3).

name: Wilson-Schmitz hybrid AFSD + scanning + CNC activity-based cost model
developer: N. Wilson, R. Patterson, E. Charles, M. Landis, J. Kincaid, R. Garcia, G. Corson, T. Schmitz (University of Tennessee, Knoxville; Oak Ridge National Laboratory MDF; Northwestern University)
description: Activity-based cost models for each step of a hybrid sequence (AFSD deposition, structured-light scanning, milling, turning), with direct costs and indirect costs (space, depreciation, maintenance). The hybrid route cost ~$1,008 vs. ~$834 for machining only, and labour was 65% of the hybrid cost.
NRE_note: Per-step setup labour is costed (18 min AFSD, 60 min scanning, 30 min milling), but part-program generation is explicitly neglected and no redesign or other one-time engineering is costed (NSF PAR full text, Sec. 2.1 and Table 1).
Production_note: Per-part cost is built up step by step from direct (material, labour, energy, tooling) and indirect (space, depreciation, maintenance) costs, about $1,008 for the hybrid route vs $834 for machining only (NSF PAR full text, Secs. 2-3).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper was read and neither the cost model nor the case study contains any qualification or certification term (NSF PAR full text).
QA_Insp_note: Structured-light scanning is a costed per-part metrology step (about $175), but it locates the preform for machining; acceptance inspection of the finished part is only mentioned as possible and is not costed (NSF PAR full text, Secs. 1 and 3.1.2).
Storage_note: The full paper was read; the only storage term is floor space for stored raw material inside the space cost, and parts inventory or holding cost is absent (NSF PAR full text, Eq. 13).
Shared_Capital_note: Straight-line depreciation (equipment cost, 10-year life, salvage) and maintenance are charged by process time, with no utilisation, annual-hours or volume input (NSF PAR full text, Sec. 2.1, Table 1).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper costs one part's process chain on dedicated machines, with no capacity, queue or pooling term (NSF PAR full text).
Speed_note: Per-step process times are reported (469 min AFSD print, scanning and machining times) and drive cost, a partial time model, while lead time is explicitly not examined (NSF PAR full text, Table 1 and Sec. 4).

name: NIST SP 1176 / Thomas & Gilbert AM cost review and taxonomy
developer: D. S. Thomas, S. W. Gilbert (National Institute of Standards and Technology)
decision_levels: Process/machine choice; Adopt or make-vs-buy; Capacity placement/sharing
description: Literature review that sorts AM costs into well-structured costs (material, machine, build-envelope utilisation, build time, energy, labour) and ill-structured costs (build failure, setup, inventory, transport, supply-chain vulnerability). It gives conceptual supply-chain cost equations but no new calibrated model.
