QA_Insp_note: Testing and inspection results are stored with build data, including NDT, visual inspection, accuracy, CT and ultrasonic records in the Sandia schema, data recorded rather than used to decide, and public sources cannot confirm any decision use (CIMdata 2015; Sandia slides).
Storage_note: A materials and process data management system for powders, builds, machine parameters, parts and tests, so spare-part inventory is outside its documented scope (TenLinks 2017; CIMdata 2015).
Shared_Capital_note: Senvol machine data in Granta MI let users identify and compare AM machines by process, manufacturer, part size and cost, so machine capital cost is a selection criterion, but there is no amortisation, utilisation or sharing calculation (3DPI May 2016).
Shared_Capacity_note: As a materials data management and selection system its documented scope does not include production capacity shared across sites or users (CIMdata 2015; 3DPI 2016).
Speed_note: As a data management system it does not estimate part lead time or availability; the only time claim is reduced time-to-market for AM development (CIMdata 2015; TenLinks 2017).

name: Altair Inspire Print3D
developer: Altair Engineering (solidThinking unit at launch); altair.com product pages now redirect to siemens.com (ownership change not separately verified here)
description: SLM design and process-simulation tool. It generates and edits supports with the part, picks orientations that minimize supports, runs a thermo-mechanical solver (build, cooling, cutting, springback), flags deformation, overheating and delamination, and exports a print-ready file. No cost-estimation function was found in fetched sources.
NRE_note: The SLM workflow performs build-preparation and parameter work (orientation, supports, a calibration coupon per material, distortion-compensated STL export), but this is an activity the tool performs and its effort is not costed or used in any decision (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM tool list).
Production_note: Altair claims the tool reduces development and manufacturing costs, but the SLM help describes no cost estimate and the Printer tool takes no cost or hourly rate, so cost enters no decision (3D Printing Industry launch article; Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM tool list and Printer topic).
QA_Qual_note: The SLM help covers thermo-mechanical simulation and calibration of that simulation only and does not address material, process or part qualification (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM tool list).
QA_Insp_note: The SLM help covers no inspection or testing of printed parts; Slice validates geometry before printing and the coupon only tunes the simulation (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM tool list).
Storage_note: Inspire Print3D is a design and print-simulation tool for single SLM builds, so inventory is outside its documented scope (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM tool list).
Shared_Capital_note: The Printer tool sets bed size, laser and recoating parameters only, with no machine cost, rate or utilisation, and no cost function exists in the module (Inspire 2022.2 help, Printer topic).
Shared_Capacity_note: As a single-build design and simulation tool it does not address machine capacity or sharing across sites or users (Inspire 2022.2 help, SLM tool list).
Speed_note: Orientation optimisation evaluates print time (a Time heatmap, with recoating time as a printer input) to minimise it, a print-time-only model; lead time or availability is not computed (Inspire 2022.2 help, Orientation and Printer topics).

name: Cadence Simufact Additive (print cost estimation; formerly Hexagon)
year: Cost estimation added in Simufact Additive 2020 (announced Nov 2019); bundled in HxGN AM Suite Feb 2024
developer: Simufact Engineering, part of MSC Software; Cadence since it acquired Hexagon's design and engineering business (closed February 2026); previously Hexagon Manufacturing Intelligence
description: Metal AM process simulation. It predicts and compensates distortion, residual stress and temperature. Its PBF Process and Defect Analysis module anticipates warping, porosity and incomplete fusion. It also estimates print-job costs for single components or assemblies, extending to downstream cutting, machining, drilling and grinding, to pick the best build variant.
NRE_note: Distortion compensation and the PBF Process and Defect Analysis module are offered to 'significantly reduce trial-and-error' in getting builds right, a claimed benefit; whether the cost estimate or build-variant choice uses one-time build-preparation effort cannot be confirmed from public sources (Hexagon Nexus page).
Production_note: The software estimates print-job cost for single components or assemblies, including subsequent cutting, machining, drilling and grinding, to choose the best build variant, but the cost inputs (machine rate, material, labour) are not publicly documented, so a full per-part build-up cannot be confirmed (Hexagon 2019 release; Industrial Production 2020).
QA_Qual_note: The Nexus page and 2019/2020 releases describe defect prediction (porosity, incomplete fusion) but never mention qualification or certification, and no product documentation was publicly reachable (Hexagon Nexus page; Hexagon 2019 release).
QA_Insp_note: The Nexus page and releases do not mention inspection, and whether the cost estimate's downstream processes can include inspection is not public (Hexagon Nexus page; Industrial Production 2020).
Storage_note: Simufact Additive is process-simulation software with build-job costing, so spare-part inventory is outside its documented scope (Hexagon Nexus page).
Shared_Capital_note: The releases say print-job costs are estimated and compared across build variants for components or assemblies, but whether a machine rate, utilisation or parts-per-plate allocation is used is not public (Hexagon 2019 release; MSC 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: As build-process simulation software its documented scope does not include capacity shared across sites or users (Hexagon Nexus page).
Speed_note: The Nexus page speaks only generally of 'saving time', and the releases do not say whether build time or lead time is output (Hexagon Nexus page; Hexagon 2019 release).

name: Fieldmade Digital Inventory software with NOMAD deployable micro-factories
year: 2016-present; Equinor digital-inventory project 2019-2020; Nomad LW UK distribution Jan 2023; 1000 Kelvin AMAIZE bundle Jan 2024
developer: Fieldmade AS (Norway; founded 2016 as a spin-off of the Norwegian Defence Research Establishment, FFI)
description: Deployable container micro-factories (NOMAD 01/02/03; Nomad LW) paired with Digital Inventory software. The software gives access to aggregated print-ready files with metadata so parts can be printed at the point of need. Fieldmade also offers 3D scanning/reverse engineering and lists 'qualification assessment and control' as an expertise. The 1000 Kelvin AMAIZE AI print-recipe software is bundled with NOMAD.
NRE_note: Fieldmade offers design and digitisation of the part portfolio as a service and NOMAD03 integrates design, scanning and reverse engineering, but whether NRE enters any platform decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (company site; 3DPrint.com 2025).
Production_note: The digital-inventory platform collects quotes, lead times and offers from different vendors but does not itself compute a cost, and whether price enters any platform decision cannot be confirmed (Fieldnode site).
QA_Qual_note: OEMs can pre-select quality standards that produced parts should meet, but the site does not say these gate manufacturers or parts, so use in a decision cannot be confirmed (Fieldnode site).
QA_Insp_note: NOMAD integrates the Plastometrex PLX-Benchtop non-destructive indentation test to give on-site stress-strain data, an inspection capability offered, and whether results gate parts or enter any decision cannot be confirmed from press (3DPrint.com 2025).
Storage_note: The digital inventory is said to reduce inventory build-up and Equinor expects savings 'through reducing inventory', claims not computed by the tool, and whether stock enters any decision cannot be confirmed (Fieldnode site; Techstars 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: No source read (company site, Fieldnode site, Equinor and Techstars articles, 3DPrint.com 2025) says whether machine investment or utilisation is modelled.
Shared_Capacity_note: Deployable NOMAD units add forward capacity and the digital inventory connects IP holders and manufacturers through manufacturing networks, but how orders are routed is not described, so use in a decision cannot be confirmed (company site; Fieldnode site; Equinor article).
Speed_note: Vendor lead times are collected with quotes and press claims parts printed, tested and installed 'in just hours', but the platform is not shown to use lead time to decide, which cannot be confirmed from public sources (Fieldnode site; 3DPrint.com 2025; Equinor article).

name: SPEE3D TwinSPEE3D (cold spray toolpath and printability software)
year: Toolpath algorithm upgrade 2020; TwinSPEE3D listed on DirectIndustry (undated); XSPEE3D fall 2022; Expeditionary Manufacturing Unit May 2024
developer: SPEE3D (Australia)
description: Proprietary software for SPEE3D cold spray printers. It automatically generates print or coating toolpaths, identifies unfeasible part features and suggests design modifications, and simulates the full print before production. No part-screening service, parts catalogue, or cost/lead-time estimator was found for SPEE3D.
NRE_note: TwinSPEE3D automates toolpath generation, flags unfeasible features with suggested design changes and simulates the print, features that cut build preparation, but whether NRE enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (DirectIndustry TwinSPEE3D listing; IMCRC 2020).
Production_note: The vendor listing offers only the slogan 'Save significantly on cost and time' and describes no cost, material-usage or print-time output, so whether per-part production cost is addressed cannot be established (DirectIndustry TwinSPEE3D listing; IMCRC 2020).
QA_Qual_note: The vendor listing and IMCRC article do not mention qualification, and no SPEE3D software documentation or catalogue could be opened (DirectIndustry listing; IMCRC 2020).
QA_Insp_note: The listing describes a print-preview simulation to catch issues before production, not inspection or testing of printed parts, and no documentation could be read (DirectIndustry listing).
Storage_note: TwinSPEE3D is toolpath and print-simulation software, so spare-part inventory is plainly outside its documented scope (DirectIndustry listing).
Shared_Capital_note: Neither the listing nor the IMCRC article says whether machine cost or utilisation is considered, and no documentation could be read (DirectIndustry listing; IMCRC 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: As toolpath and simulation software for an individual SPEE3D printer, its documented scope excludes capacity shared across sites or users (DirectIndustry listing).
Speed_note: IMCRC's 'saves our users valuable time' refers to automated toolpath construction (engineering prep), and the listing's 'cost and time' slogan names no part lead time, print time or availability, so speed of part supply cannot be established (IMCRC 2020; DirectIndustry listing).

name: Markforged Digital Forge (Eiger / Eiger Fleet with Digital Part Inventory; Digital Source)
year: Eiger Fleet Sep 2021; Digital Source Sep 2023; 'Digital Part Inventory' listed on Eiger page 2026
developer: Markforged (Waltham, MA); acquired by Nano Dimension (closed 25 Apr 2025)
description: Cloud print-prep and fleet platform. Eiger Fleet gives centralized control of distributed printers, users and a digital parts inventory (RBAC, SSO, API) and tracks KPIs for time and cost savings. Digital Source lets OEMs upload designs with locked process settings and encrypted build instructions, licensed to customers or approved print-service providers for on-demand 'manufacturer-certified' parts.
NRE_note: Eiger automates print prep with one click and under Digital Source the OEM locks the process settings, features that remove user setup, but whether NRE enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).
Production_note: Eiger computes a per-part cost when a part is sliced, but it is material cost only (labour and energy are a planned enhancement), and the ROI dashboard sets the alternative cost at a flat 10x the Markforged cost (Markforged ROI tools blog).
QA_Qual_note: Digital Source lets OEMs lock printing process settings so licensed customers or approved print-service providers print 'manufacturer-certified parts', but whether qualification enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Digital Source release 2023).
QA_Insp_note: The Eiger page lists automated part scanning with measurement and reporting as a quality-control feature, but whether inspection results enter any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Eiger page).
Storage_note: Eiger has a Digital Part Inventory and Digital Source claims 'reduced inventory costs', but whether stock enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Eiger page; Digital Source release 2023).
Shared_Capital_note: The ROI dashboard tracks savings across an organisation's connected printers and a Utilization Dashboard reports printer use, but this is recorded data and printer capital never enters the material-only cost, so sharing of capital in a decision cannot be confirmed (Markforged ROI tools blog).
Shared_Capacity_note: The Utilization Dashboard reports print jobs, print time and printer utilisation across the cloud-connected fleet, and Digital Source licenses printing at approved service providers, but utilisation has no effect on lead time or service (Markforged ROI tools blog; Digital Source release 2023).
Speed_note: Eiger's Utilization Dashboard reports print time, a partial time model, while lead-time and downtime benefits are only claimed (Digital Source testimonials) and the ROI tools compute cost savings only (Markforged ROI tools blog; Digital Source release 2023).

name: AMPOWER Additive Manufacturing Cost Calculator
developer: AMPOWER (AM consultancy, ampower.eu)
description: Total-cost-of-ownership calculator. Inputs are part material, dimensions, volume, complexity, quantity and build utilization; outputs are cost per part broken down by process-chain step. Covers technician labor (machine prep, unpacking, support removal, optional data prep), heat treatment and consumables, all overridable. Also gives lead time per part, cost vs 1-10,000 parts/yr, service-bureau market price ranges, and side-by-side comparison of technologies.
NRE_note: Optional digital data-preparation time and cost and a machine-setup step are costed in the process chain, but no reverse engineering, redesign or parameter development cost is included (AMPOWER product and shop pages).
Production_note: Cost per part is computed from volume, bounding box, complexity and quantity and broken down along the process chain (material, data preparation, setup, printing, unpacking, sintering, heat treatment), including technician labour, machine investment and consumables (AMPOWER product and shop pages).
QA_Qual_note: The listed process-chain steps include no qualification, but the Excel tool is 'fully customizable with own parameters and processes' and its documentation is not public (AMPOWER shop and tools pages).
QA_Insp_note: The listed process-chain steps include no inspection step, but the calculator is 'fully customizable with own parameters and processes', so whether inspection can be costed is not established (AMPOWER shop and tools pages).
Storage_note: The calculator's documented scope is per-part cost, lead time, throughput, market price and technology comparison, which excludes inventory holding (AMPOWER product page).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment is a main cost driver and cost per part depends on build-volume utilisation and annual quantity (1-10,000 per year), a utilisation and volume assumption (AMPOWER product page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Annual throughput is output for production planning, so machine capacity is modelled, but there is no pooling across sites or users and no capacity effect on lead time (AMPOWER product page).
Speed_note: The calculator reports the time to produce a single part broken down along the process chain from data preparation to heat treatment (called 'lead time' on the product page and 'production time' on the shop page), but no queueing, delivery, availability or downtime value is computed (AMPOWER product and shop pages).

name: Ulu-Huang-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) concurrent structure + process-parameter optimization for minimum-cost metal AM
developer: E. Ulu, R. Huang, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University, Mechanical Engineering)
description: Couples a process-based cost model (material with 1% scrap, machine investment and maintenance amortised over 7 yr at 7,000 h/yr, energy, labour, 3.5% reject factor) with SIMP topology optimisation. Beam power is chosen per element, so structure and process parameters are optimised together for minimum cost under compliance constraints. Concurrent optimisation cuts cost by up to ~15% and build time by ~21% vs. structure-only optimisation.
NRE_note: A constant setup time is part of the costed build time (machine plus labour rate), but design effort, build preparation and parameter development are not costed because costs unaffected by design or process variables are ignored (author PDF).
Production_note: Per-part cost combines material-based costs (with 1% scrap) and time-based costs from build time driven by scan passes, beam power and velocity, with machine, energy and labour rates; post-processing is excluded (author PDF).
QA_Qual_note: Full paper read; qualification is not addressed, appearing only in a reference title (author PDF).
QA_Insp_note: A single 3.5% reject rate covers parts rejected in quality control and destructive testing, with no separate inspection or test line items (author PDF, Table 2).
Storage_note: Full paper read; inventory is not addressed (author PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: The machine rate amortises a $1.1M investment plus maintenance over a 7-year life and an assumed 7,000 operating h/yr, rerun at 2,000 h/yr, so a utilisation assumption sets the capital charge, though packing, batch size and volume are not modelled (author PDF).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read; capacity, queues or multiple sites are not addressed (author PDF).
Speed_note: Build time (setup, melting, powder delivery, cooling) is computed and reported, e.g. 21% faster builds with concurrent optimisation, but it is print time only and not linked to lead time or availability (author PDF).

name: Nie-Jung-Kara-Whitefoot (CMU) part-consolidation optimization for minimum production cost/time with metal AM
developer: Z. Nie, S. Jung, L. B. Kara, K. S. Whitefoot (Carnegie Mellon University)
description: Generates consolidation candidates from an interface connectivity matrix and removes structurally redundant ones with a 'closed-loop filter'. It then optimises build orientation for minimum support, places parts with a 2-D bottom-left layout, and estimates cost or time; a genetic algorithm searches large assemblies. Consolidating 17 components into 4 parts minimises cost (~20% lower unit cost); merging into 2 parts minimises time (~25%). Full consolidation is rarely optimal because support material and removal costs rise.
NRE_note: Batch setup (1.5 h per PBF batch at the machine-plus-labour rate, times the layout-driven number of batches) is costed, but redesign of consolidated parts is explicitly excluded and no one-time engineering cost appears (CMU PDF).
Production_note: Unit cost is built up from build, setup, part and support material, energy, scrap and machine costs plus support removal and assembly of unconsolidated interfaces (CMU PDF).
QA_Qual_note: Full paper read; qualification and certification are absent from the cost terms and the analysis (CMU PDF).
QA_Insp_note: Full paper read; there is no inspection or testing cost, and 'scrap' is powder lost during recovery, not quality rejects (CMU PDF).
Storage_note: The paper states its cost estimates do not include inventory, and fewer part numbers are not linked to stock (CMU PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: The machine rate amortises investment ($1.1M for PBF EBM) over a 7-year life at 7,000 operating h/yr plus maintenance, and parts are 2-D packed into multi-part batches, so capital is spread by a utilisation and multi-part-build assumption (CMU PDF).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read; it optimises production of one assembly and has no shared capacity, queueing or multi-site element (CMU PDF).
Speed_note: Unit production time (build, setup, support removal and assembly) is computed and can be the objective, but lead time, delivery and the value of availability are not addressed (CMU PDF).

name: Piili et al. (LUT/Aalto) laser PBF stainless-steel cost estimation by build scenario
developer: H. Piili, A. Happonen, T. Väistö, V. Venkataramanan, J. Partanen, A. Salminen (affiliations not shown on the accessed record; record held by Aalto University)
description: Estimates part cost from build time, machine, material and energy across build scenarios with optimised machine utilisation. Machine investment dominates while energy and material are minor, so time per part is the main lever. A secondary review reports that building as many parts as possible per build cut cost 81-92% vs. building singly.
NRE_note: Only the abstract and a review summary could be read, and neither says whether design or build-preparation effort is costed; the full paper was not reachable (Aaltodoc abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).
Production_note: Part cost is estimated for each build scenario from calculated build times and machine, material and energy costs (Aaltodoc abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Neither the abstract nor the review summary mentions qualification, and the full paper was not reachable (Aaltodoc abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).
QA_Insp_note: Neither the abstract nor the review summary mentions inspection or post-processing, and the full paper was not reachable (Aaltodoc abstract; Khanna et al. 2024).
Storage_note: The documented scope is per-part manufacturing cost of build scenarios on one machine, which plainly excludes inventory (Aaltodoc abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment, the dominant cost, is spread under optimised machine utilisation and multi-part builds, with full builds cutting cost 81-92% versus single parts (Aaltodoc abstract; Khanna et al. 2024 review).
Shared_Capacity_note: The documented scope is build scenarios on a single research machine, which plainly excludes capacity pooled across sites or users (Aaltodoc abstract).
Speed_note: Build time is calculated per scenario and manufacturing time per part is named the key cost lever, a build-time-only model with no lead time or availability value (Aaltodoc abstract).

name: Barclift et al. (Penn State) CAD-integrated cost estimation and build-orientation optimization for metal PBF
developer: M. Barclift, A. Armstrong, T. W. Simpson, S. B. Joshi (Pennsylvania State University)
description: Pulls part volume and surfaces through the SolidWorks API and generates internal and external supports as solid bodies, then varies build orientation. This lets designers estimate build time and feedstock (including depreciation of reused powder) while designing. An imprecise support angle underestimates support volume by 34% and build time by 20%. Poor orientation and packing can push powder-depreciation cost to nearly twice the material cost.
NRE_note: The 2017 abstract automates support generation and orientation but does not say whether preparation or redesign labour is costed; the 2016 base model costs per-part geometry preparation and excludes redesign, but the paywalled 2017 full text could not confirm what it keeps (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016, Eq. 12, Sec. 5.4).
Production_note: Estimates metal AM build cost from CAD geometry queried through the SolidWorks API (build time, feedstock including generated supports, reused-powder depreciation), extending the 2016 per-part total-cost model (sciencegate abstract; MDPI 2024 review; SFF 2016, Eq. 12).
QA_Qual_note: The documented scope is a design-stage estimate of build time and feedstock cost inside CAD, which plainly excludes qualification, and the 2016 base model leaves powder acceptance to supplier-purchaser agreement (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016, Sec. 3.1).
QA_Insp_note: The documented scope is build time and feedstock, and the 2016 base model it extends names CT only as an unmodelled possible step (sciencegate abstract; SFF 2016, Sec. 5.4).
Storage_note: A design-stage build-cost estimator inside CAD; inventory is plainly outside its documented scope (sciencegate abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The 2016 base model splits a flat $60/h machine rate over the parts in a build, but machine capital is not amortised with a utilisation assumption, and the 2017 abstract's packing result concerns powder depreciation, not machine capital (SFF 2016, Table 1, Eq. 3; sciencegate abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: A single-build, design-stage cost estimate; capacity shared across sites or users is plainly outside its documented scope (sciencegate abstract).
Speed_note: Computes and reports build time from CAD (an imprecise support angle under-predicts it by 20%), a print-time-only time model; lead time and availability are not computed (sciencegate abstract).

name: Budinoff & Shafae geometry-to-cost process-based model for metal L-PBF design alternatives
developer: H. D. Budinoff, M. Shafae (affiliation not shown on accessed page)
description: Process-based cost model of the L-PBF build and post-processing, applied to design alternatives. Costs differ by up to 14% between alternatives, with part mass and build time the strongest predictors. Higher complexity was linked to lower cost but not strongly to reject rates. Scrap and reject rates vary with geometry in conflicting directions.
NRE_note: Only the abstract is readable (Springer paywall; the Arizona accepted manuscript exposes no file link), and it does not say whether design or build-preparation cost is modelled (Springer abstract).
Production_note: A process-based cost model of the L-PBF build and post-processing gives per-design costs that differ by up to 14% between alternatives (Springer abstract).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract does not mention qualification and the full text could not be opened, so whether it is costed cannot be established (Springer abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The cost model carries geometry-dependent scrap and reject rates, i.e. inspection outcomes folded into a reject-rate factor, but no separate inspection or testing cost is shown (Springer abstract).
Storage_note: The documented scope is build and post-processing cost of functionally equivalent design alternatives, which plainly excludes inventory (Springer abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The abstract does not show how machine cost is amortised or whether parts share a build, and the full text could not be opened (Springer abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The abstract says nothing about parts per build, build-volume utilisation or machine capacity, and the full text could not be opened, so whether capacity is modelled cannot be established (Springer abstract).
Speed_note: Build time is estimated per design and reported as one of the two most influential cost groupers (found non-linear in complexity), a print-time-only partial model with no lead time (Springer abstract; Brennan & Hanft, SFF 2024).

name: Sartini et al. (UNIVPM) analytic cost model for bound metal deposition
developer: M. Sartini, I. Bianchi, A. Vita, M. Germani, M. Mandolini (Università Politecnica delle Marche)
description: Analytic per-part cost over pre-processing, printing, debinding and sintering. Each phase sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables, driven by part and support geometry, material, batch quantity and accuracy. Sintering machine and energy dominate the validation case (EUR 565 estimated vs. EUR 576 actual).
NRE_note: Pre-processing labour for set-up and nesting (orientation, supports, slicing, file loading) is costed, with nesting counted only for the first job, but CAD design and parameter development are not (Cambridge PDF).
Production_note: Per-part cost sums material, machine, labour, energy and consumables over pre-processing, printing, debinding and sintering from part and support geometry, accuracy and batch size, validated at EUR 564.60 versus 576.14 actual (Cambridge PDF).
QA_Qual_note: Full paper read; qualification is not modelled, and 'quality' is only a high/low accuracy input that sets layer thickness and nozzle diameter (Cambridge PDF).
QA_Insp_note: Full paper read; no inspection or testing cost term appears in any of the four phases (Cambridge PDF).
Storage_note: Full paper read; inventory is not addressed (Cambridge PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine hourly rates include depreciation, overhead and maintenance at a 57% load factor (4,993 h/yr), and set-up, debind and sinter costs are divided over parts in a batch, with mixed jobs allocated by volume (Cambridge PDF).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read; the model prices one batch on one printer, debinder and furnace, with no shared or pooled capacity or queueing (Cambridge PDF).
Speed_note: Build time is computed from extruder path length and speed (10.42 h versus 11 h actual) and debind and sinter times are fixed inputs, but these only drive cost and no lead time is aggregated or valued (Cambridge PDF).

name: DeBoer-Diba-Hosseini AM cost calculator (FFF and metal bound powder extrusion)
developer: B. DeBoer, F. Diba, A. Hosseini (Ontario Tech University; Fleming College CAMIIT)
description: Cost calculator covering machine (equipment cost over a payback period and operating hours, power, changeover and setup labour), material (adjusted for shrinkage), post-processing (wash, sinter, argon, debind fluid, loading labour), overhead and profit. In the H-yoke case about 85% of part cost was Metal X capital, so BPE was judged uneconomic unless weight is critical.
NRE_note: Per-print setup and material-changeover time are costed at the labour rate (Eq. 12), but design, CAD, file preparation and other one-time engineering are not included (UPEI PDF).
Production_note: Per-part cost is built from machine time, electricity, shrinkage-adjusted material, wash and sinter post-processing and labour, plus overhead and markup (UPEI PDF, Eqs. 3-16).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper has no qualification, certification or first-article term; the only quality mention is the 96% dense final part (UPEI PDF).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper has no inspection, testing or reject term in Eqs. 1-16 (UPEI PDF).
Storage_note: Inventory or storage of parts is not addressed in the full paper (UPEI PDF).
Shared_Capital_note: The hourly machine rate divides purchase cost by a payback period in months x 21.5 days x a user-set operating hours per day, an explicit utilisation input (UPEI PDF, Eq. 11).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper costs single parts on one machine with no multi-machine, queue or pooled-capacity element (UPEI PDF).
Speed_note: BPE print time is computed from slicer time scaled by speed, layer and nozzle ratios (Eq. 14) but only as an input to machine cost; the paper gives no print-time value for the H-yoke, the interface is said to display the manufacturing cost, and no lead time is computed (UPEI PDF, Eqs. 12-16, Fig. 5, Conclusion).

name: Reiher et al. (Paderborn DMRC) holistic approach: part selection through test and verification
developer: T. Reiher, C. Lindemann, U. Jahnke, G. Deppe, R. Koch (Paderborn University, DMRC)
description: Chains the TOM selection matrix (rough cost quote, knock-out criteria, scored sub-criteria) with topology-optimisation redesign, a manufacturing strategy (orientation, supports, thermal stress) and part marking. It adds a three-tier test scheme: part-independent material/process tests, witness specimens in every build, and part-specific NDT (CT, dimensional, surface) plus load tests. The bracket was 60% lighter with buy-to-fly reduced from ~50 to 1.5. AM was cheaper at the forecast volume, although post-processing and quality costs 'had a major impact'.
NRE_note: A redesign workflow (system-context review, FE topology optimisation, voxel smoothing, NURBS re-intersection) follows part selection, but redesign effort or CAD availability is not a TOM criterion or an input to any later decision (Springer full text, Sec. 2-3).
Production_note: TOM computes a rough cost quote from quantities, current cost, dimensions, mass and material under depreciation-time and demand assumptions, and a costing tool compares production, self- and lifecycle costs, but the build-up and figures are not published (Springer full text, Sec. 2, 8).
QA_Qual_note: Prescribes part-independent material and process tests (tensile, SCC, crack growth, fatigue, powder composition and dryness) for new materials or changed parameters and part-specific tests at qualification loads, with no counts by class and no costs (Springer full text, Sec. 5.1, 5.3).
QA_Insp_note: Requires witness specimens in every build (at least tensile and density) and part-specific CT, dimensional and surface checks; quality costs are said to have a major impact but are not itemised (Springer full text, Sec. 5.2-5.3, 8).
Storage_note: Lower inventory, WIP and capital lock-up from storing only raw material are discussed in the supply-chain section, but stock and demand are not TOM criteria and no inventory figure is computed (Springer full text, Sec. 9).
Shared_Capital_note: TOM's rough quote is calculated with depreciation-time and demand assumptions, and high machine prices are said to favour centralised production at near-full workload, but how machine capital is spread is not documented (Springer full text, Sec. 2, 9).
Shared_Capacity_note: Centralised vs distributed production is discussed in the supply-chain section, but it is not a TOM criterion and the approach makes no siting or routing decision (Springer full text, Sec. 9).
Speed_note: On-demand JIT production is claimed to shorten lead and delivery time for the bracket, but lead time is not a TOM criterion and no lead-time value is computed (Springer full text, Sec. 9-10).

name: Siller et al. (TU Berlin) potential-assessment and adaptation method for AM of conventionally made components
developer: N. Siller, S. Werner, V. Molina, D. Göhlich (Technische Universität Berlin, Institute of Machine Design and Systems Technology)
description: A pass/fail prefilter (fits build space, material available, AM-sensitive features acceptable, no legal restriction, conventional production not much cheaper) is followed by 0-4 scored assessments. These cover in-process and post-process restrictions and 'opportunistic' economic, eco-social and functional drivers, weighted by utility analysis. An automatic 'AM adaptation potential' flags parts that minor redesign could make suitable. Below 40% overall means low suitability; above 65% means generally suitable. In the case, 5 of 11 parts failed the prefilter.
NRE_note: An automatic 'AM adaptation potential' score (high at 6 or above) flags parts that marginal non-functional redesign could make suitable, but redesign effort is not costed (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Sect. 3.2.3, 3.3).
Production_note: Cost enters only as a prefilter check that current production is not significantly more cost-efficient and as a 0-4 'Reduces costs' driver (12% weight in the turbine case); no cost is calculated (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Sect. 3.2.1, Table 7, Fig. 8).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper was read; no qualification, certification or testing criterion exists in the prefilter or assessments (the legal prefilter concerns patents), and load-capacity simulation and tests follow outside the method (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Sect. 3.1.1, Table 4).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper was read; support removal, powder removal and post-processing effort are scored, but inspection or quality assurance is not a criterion (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Table 6).
Storage_note: Table 7 scores 'Enables on-demand-manufacturing/build-to-order' and 'Secures/improves supply-chain activities' (21% weight each in the turbine case) as 0-4 drivers, motivated by end-of-service spare supply, but inventory is not named or costed (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Table 7, Fig. 8, Sect. 1).
Shared_Capital_note: The full paper was read; machine capital is not a criterion, with machine performance only adjusting geometric thresholds and build-space fit as a prefilter (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Sect. 3.2.2, Table 4).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper was read; machine capacity, utilisation or pooling is not scored, and 'company capacities' refers only to scheduling backlogged engineering work (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Tables 4-7).
Speed_note: Table 7 includes 'Reduces lead time' as a 0-4 driver (weight 0 in the turbine case for lack of production-time data) and prefilter P9 asks whether the part can be produced or purchased especially fast, but lead time is never quantified (TU Berlin open-access PDF, Table 7, Table 13).

name: Bracken et al. (Penn State) Geometry for Additive Part Selection (GAPS) worksheet
developer: J. Bracken, T. Pomorski, C. Armstrong, R. Prabhu, T. W. Simpson, K. Jablokow, W. Cleary, N. A. Meisel (Pennsylvania State University)
description: Paper worksheet that rates nine literature-backed geometric features known to affect metal PBF printability and totals them into a geometric-suitability score. Example components were rated and compared with expert assessments, and preliminary user feedback is reported.
NRE_note: The worksheet scores nine geometric features so designers can see what hurts printability and modify it, a redesign activity recommended; redesign effort is not a scored factor, and whether the worksheet uses it to decide cannot be confirmed from the abstract (nTop blog; Penn State abstract).
Production_note: The documented scope is nine geometric features scored 1, 3 or 5 and totalled into a suitability score, which excludes per-part cost; failed-print waste is cited only as motivation (nTop blog; Penn State abstract; Cayley et al. 2024).
QA_Qual_note: The documented scope is geometric printability scoring compared with expert raters, which plainly excludes material, process or part qualification (Penn State abstract; nTop blog).
QA_Insp_note: The documented output is a geometric printability score of a design, which excludes per-part inspection scope or cost (Penn State abstract; nTop blog).
Storage_note: The documented scope is geometric suitability of a design for metal PBF, which plainly excludes inventory (Penn State abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The worksheet scores geometric features only, with no machine or cost input, so machine capital is plainly outside its scope (Penn State abstract; nTop blog).
Shared_Capacity_note: The worksheet scores geometric features only, so print capacity is plainly outside its scope (Penn State abstract).
Speed_note: The output is a totalled suitability score, and neither the abstract, the nTop blog nor Cayley et al. mentions a build-time or lead-time estimate (Penn State abstract; nTop blog; Cayley et al. 2024).

name: Lawand et al. (McGill/Chalmers/GKN) dynamic lifecycle-cost model for DED remanufacturing (repair/extend vs. replace)
developer: L. Lawand, M. Panarotto, P. Andersson, O. Isaksson, M. Kokkolaras (McGill University; Chalmers University of Technology; GKN Aerospace Engine Systems)
description: Present-value lifecycle cost over a 700-month service period, with nine categories: material, manufacturing (variable plus fixed tooling), transport (replacement only), fuel, replacement labour, failure-probability-based repair, inventory, salvage, and recertification (supplemental type certificate fee). Nested optimisation (MADS) picks the stiffener design and deposition time. Deposition timing dominates LCC, and the optimal design lifespan is 312-432 months.
NRE_note: None of the nine LCC categories costs design, engineering or deposition-parameter development; the only fixed manufacturing term is machine tooling (Chalmers full text, Eqs. 2-11, Table 1).
Production_note: Material (Inconel 718 price times weight including the deposited stiffener), manufacturing (USD 3.33 per cycle plus fixed tooling), replacement labour and failure-based repair are computed per design over the service period (Chalmers full text, Eqs. 2-8, Table 1).
QA_Qual_note: Recertification is costed only as a single fixed supplemental-type-certificate fee (USD 9,977), with no qualification testing or analysis effort modelled (Chalmers full text, Eq. 11, Table 1).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection, NDT and testing of the deposit are not cost terms anywhere in the model (Chalmers full text, Eqs. 2-11).
Storage_note: Inventory cost C7 is a costed LCC element but is held constant over the service period with no deposition term, so AM's effect on stock is not modelled (Chalmers full text, Eq. 9).
Shared_Capital_note: No DED machine purchase, depreciation, investment or utilisation term exists; the only fixed term is 'machine tooling costs' (USD 20,000) and machine maintenance is only named as one component of the lumped per-cycle manufacturing cost (Chalmers full text, Eq. 3, Table 1).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity, sites or pooled resources are not modelled; the deposition is simply done on site (Chalmers full text).
Speed_note: Downtime, aircraft-on-ground time, lead time and deposition time are not modelled; transport is costed only for replacement (Chalmers full text, Eq. 4).

name: Xu & Feng AM-based remanufacturing cost model (remanufacture vs. new manufacture)
developer: Y. Xu, W. Feng (Cranfield University, School of Applied Sciences)
description: Framework and cost-breakdown structure for an AM-based remanufacturing process, validated by expert judgement, with a case comparing remanufacturing cost against new manufacture.
NRE_note: Pre-production cost (reverse engineering plus data processing, from labour rate and working time) is an explicit term of the total-cost equation, and pre-production activities make up about 44% of the slat-track case total (Springer full text, Secs. 3.2 and 4.2).
Production_note: Per-component cost sums setup, wire material, shielding gas, grinding wheel, depreciation, labour, power and overhead, with times from deposit mass and rates, and new manufacture is costed in SEER-MFG for comparison (Springer full text, Secs. 3.4 and 4.3).
QA_Qual_note: The full paper was read and has no qualification or certification step or cost; 'validation' means expert review of the cost model, not of the part (Springer full text, Sec. 3.6).
QA_Insp_note: The full paper was read; only machine checks (gas/wire, grinding wheel) appear in setup, and part inspection or testing is absent from the cost breakdown and equations (Springer full text).
Storage_note: Only costs on the remanufacturing premises are counted, and inventory and reverse logistics are explicitly left to system-level work (Springer full text, Sec. 5).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation is a time-based term in the depositing and grinding costs, with idle rates inflating machine time, but there is no utilisation, volume or shared-use input (Springer full text, Secs. 3.2-3.4).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full paper costs one remanufacturing job on the premises, with no capacity, queue or pooling (Springer full text, Sec. 5).
Speed_note: Deposition and grinding times appear only inside the cost equations (mass over rate, adjusted for idle rate) and no time value is reported in the case, while lead time is not mentioned anywhere in the full paper (Springer full text, Eqs. 2-3, Sec. 4.2).

name: Baffa (Univ. Florence) WAAM repair-vs-replace sustainability and remanufacturing-viability model
developer: F. Baffa (Università degli Studi di Firenze, doctoral thesis)
description: Develops WAAM repair toolpath strategies, compares the sustainability of repair vs. replacement, and builds a mathematical model of remanufacturing viability (cost and energy) in closed-loop supply chains. It identifies feasible configurations and the parameters that most affect cost and energy.
NRE_note: The thesis is embargoed to 31 Dec 2026 and neither its abstract nor the companion JCP 2024 abstract says whether developing the repair toolpaths, which the thesis does, is costed (FLORE thesis and JCP records).
Production_note: Both abstracts describe a mathematical model that computes the economic and energy viability of remanufacturing versus new parts for steel, aluminium and titanium across three supply chains, with remanufacturing volume and share of material preserved as key inputs, but no cost elements or per-part build-up are public and the JCP abstract does not name WAAM (FLORE thesis and JCP 2024 records).
QA_Qual_note: Only abstracts are public (thesis embargoed, JCP paper closed access) and neither says whether requalification of repaired parts is costed; the thesis aims to meet mechanical requirements but does not describe qualification (FLORE records).
QA_Insp_note: Only abstracts are public and none mentions inspection of the repaired insert (FLORE thesis and JCP records).
Storage_note: The JCP 2024 abstract compares a no-remanufacturing chain with direct and distribution-centre remanufacturing chains, so stock could plausibly enter, but no abstract mentions inventory (FLORE records).
Shared_Capital_note: Remanufacturing volume is the most influential variable, but no abstract says whether WAAM or machining equipment cost is included or how it is allocated (JCP 2024 abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The three scenarios differ in how customer and manufacturer interact, directly or via a distribution centre, and the abstracts say nothing on repair capacity or its sharing (FLORE records).
Speed_note: Only abstracts are public and none says whether repair versus replacement lead time or downtime is valued (FLORE thesis and JCP records).

name: IMPACT 2.0 Techno-Economic Analysis Tool for Selection of Metal Part Manufacturing Processes (Topic 3)
developer: University of Arizona Investment Casting Institute (lead), with PADT and 3Degrees. Funded by the OSD ManTech IMPACT 2.0 call, administered by America Makes and NCDMM.
description: A second OSD ManTech-funded TEA tool, parallel to NIAR's, for choosing a metal part manufacturing process. The NCDMM winners page gives only the topic title and team. It is listed so the survey records that the tool exists, not for what it can do.
NRE_note: The award announcements give only the title, team and a one-line purpose, and the RFP with topic requirements could not be reached, so whether engineering effort is considered cannot be established (NCDMM winners page; 3DPrint.com 2025).
Production_note: The award announcement says the planned tool will help manufacturers choose the most cost-effective metal part manufacturing process, but no inputs, method or output are public, so whether it computes or uses production cost cannot be confirmed (3DPrint.com 2025).
QA_Qual_note: Only the title, team and one-line purpose are public; the call's aim of data-based qualifications applies to the call overall, not to this tool (NCDMM winners page; 3DPrint.com 2025).
QA_Insp_note: No public source describes the tool beyond its title, team and one-line purpose, and the RFP could not be reached (NCDMM winners page; 3DPrint.com 2025).
Storage_note: No public source describes the tool beyond its title, team and one-line purpose, and the RFP could not be reached (NCDMM winners page; 3DPrint.com 2025).
Shared_Capital_note: No public source describes the tool beyond its title, team and one-line purpose, and the RFP could not be reached (NCDMM winners page; 3DPrint.com 2025).
Shared_Capacity_note: No public source describes the tool beyond its title, team and one-line purpose, and the RFP could not be reached (NCDMM winners page; 3DPrint.com 2025).
Speed_note: The call as a whole aims to show lead-time improvements for casting and forging, but no source says whether this tool estimates lead time (NCDMM call page; 3DPrint.com 2025).

name: RAND 3D printing supply-chain impact matrix and fab-lab concept (PE-229)
developer: RAND Corporation (Simon Véronneau, Geoffrey Torrington, Jakub P. Hlavka)
description: A two-by-two matrix in which the impact of 3D printing grows with site isolation and with ad hoc (unpredictable) demand. The paper proposes a four-machine fab-lab and a process flow: incoming inspection, CT, 3D rendering, AM or CNC, post-production, outgoing inspection, tracking and serialization, then return to service. It calls for a total supply-chain cost comparison but gives no cost model and does not rank parts.
NRE_note: The fab-lab flow includes CT-based reverse engineering to 'generate a 3D printable design', and the authors 'estimate that it would take about one hour to characterize a part for which a 3D diagram is not available', a fixed engineering-time assumption with no cost model or redesign costing (RAND PE-229, pp. 11-12).
Production_note: A total supply-chain cost comparison and a 'comprehensive cost-effectiveness evaluation' are called for in words only, and cost does not enter the impact matrix (RAND PE-229, pp. 12, 17).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification appears only as a recommendation to rationalise 'the certification and testing approach for components manufactured by AM technology' and enters neither the matrix nor the fab-lab flow as a criterion (RAND PE-229, p. 18).
QA_Insp_note: Incoming and outgoing inspection and CT scanning are steps in the proposed fab-lab process flow, a concept description that does not change the impact matrix and sets no inspection requirement or scope (RAND PE-229, pp. 11-12, Figure 8).
Storage_note: No inventory or holding-cost analysis, but the impact matrix screens by demand variability ('ad hoc nature (or variability) of the demand') and obsolescence, a screening use of demand criteria (RAND PE-229, pp. 10, 17).
Shared_Capital_note: Read in full: the fab-lab is not costed and sharing its equipment is not discussed; 'pay-per-use' appears only as background on civilian fab-labs and the only equipment price is sub-$500 personal printers (RAND PE-229, p. 10).
Shared_Capacity_note: Fab-lab local production is compared with centralised production in discussion and fab-lab sizing is said to need a throughput estimate, but capacity enters neither the matrix nor any decision (RAND PE-229, pp. 10, 12).
Speed_note: Times such as a noncritical part 'in as little as 45 minutes' or spares within an 8-hour shift are the authors' illustrative estimates, and the matrix's isolation axis is defined as connectivity to the supply chain with no time measure, so lead time is not an input to the matrix or any decision step (RAND PE-229, pp. 10, 12, 17).

name: RAND Europe AM and obsolescence management in defence (PE-171), with Cranfield obsolescence-resolution cost metrics
developer: RAND Europe (eds. Jon Freeman, Giacomo Persi Paoli). Contributors from armasuisse S+T, US Army ARDEC (G. Di Benedetto) and Cranfield University (J. Erkoyuncu, R. Roy, S. Williams, P. Colegrove, F. Martina, A. Busachi). Funded by armasuisse S+T.
description: A collection of expert perspectives, not a model. The nearest decision elements are a 'window of opportunity' test for obsolescence, a list of resolution options (same component, form-fit-function replacement, emulation, redesign), and Cranfield cost metrics (Table 2) for choosing 'the most cost effective solution'. The cost metrics are not AM-specific.
NRE_note: Cranfield Table 2 gives explicit non-recurring obsolescence-resolution costs by integration level (emulation GBP 52,100 to 2.69m; minor redesign GBP 50,100 to 549,000), but these are generic look-up figures, while AM-specific NRE such as the RESTORE 'SCAN to CAD to FAB' workflow is described without cost (RAND PE-171, pp. 9, 14-15).
Production_note: AM production cost is discussed in words only (costs are 'largely predictable' and whether small batches can be made 'at a constant cost' is posed as a question), and no unit cost enters the resolution choice (RAND PE-171, pp. 6, 15).
QA_Qual_note: Requalification of air/safety-critical components is a cost parameter folded into the Table 2 lump non-recurring costs per resolution approach, and qualifying AM equipment, processes and materials is named the best strategy, but there is no AM-specific qualification costing (RAND PE-171, pp. 12, 14-15).
QA_Insp_note: Full text read: per-part inspection is not discussed; the only testing is ARDEC tensile testing of DMLS 4340 specimens for process comparison (RAND PE-171, p. 11).
Storage_note: Proposes keeping designs, specifications and materials 'in digital format' for on-demand remanufacture, and Table 2 lists 'existing stock' only as a GBP 300 resolution option, so inventory reduction from AM does not enter any decision step (RAND PE-171, pp. 9, 15).
Shared_Capital_note: Full text read: AM machine investment or its sharing is not discussed; investment appears only as R&D funding (RAND PE-171, p. 10).
Shared_Capacity_note: A national 'strategic reserve of additive manufacturing capabilities' and 'Mobile AM facilities' for sustainment contracts are raised as ideas, with no rule for assigning work to them (RAND PE-171, pp. 6, 16).
Speed_note: The paper uses a window-of-opportunity test, comparing the time to replace or redesign a component with the window available, to decide whether obsolescence management is needed, and quotes FRCE repairs made with AM 'over a few days' against 'three or more weeks', but time is not computed or valued (RAND PE-171, pp. 11, 13).

name: Braunberger AFIT MODA and metal L-PBF cost model for AM vs DLA procurement (C-130 parts)
developer: 1st Lt Trever J. Braunberger, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (committee: Maj John Situ, Maj Ryan Kemnitz, Alfred E. Thal Jr.)
description: A nine-criterion multi-objective decision analysis. Weights: quality 21.0%, lead time 20.1%, readiness 18.3%, price 14.6%, airworthiness 7.3%, expected life 6.3%, strength 6.2%, weight 4.8%, quantity 1.5%. Score bands: 86–100% is an 'extremely good candidate'; below 60%, use traditional methods. It is paired with an Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model and a guide to AM lab set-up costs ($1.94M for one metal lab). Single-part AM builds averaged $3,174.96 against $2,486.83 DLA prices, 27.6% more. Table 4.3 shows two of six parts cheaper with AM, while the text says three. AM lead times were 9–16 days against 71 to 120+ days.
NRE_note: Pre-processing cost CPRE = (ET x EC) + (TS x CO) puts numbers on per-build engineering and setup (about $69-150 per part, Table 4.3), but one-time reverse engineering and redesign (up to $1M) are SME quotes outside the model (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 3, Table 4.3, ch. 4).
Production_note: Per-part AM cost is built from material, pre-processing, processing (build time x depreciation, energy, maintenance) and post-processing for six parts and batch builds (DTIC full thesis, Eqs. 1-5, Tables 4.3-4.4).
QA_Qual_note: Airworthiness is a weighted MODA criterion (7.3%) and the parts were chosen as non-flight-safety-critical, but approval effort or cost is not quantified (DTIC full thesis, Table 3.1, ch. 2-5).
QA_Insp_note: Eq. 5 includes a test-cost term CTEST and a tensile test is assumed after each build, but CTEST is given no value or formula (only a $1,061 wedge-grip fixture price) and Table 4.3 reports testing, if at all, only inside the post-processing total (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 5, assumptions, Table 4.3).
Storage_note: Inventory storage and transport savings are acknowledged as varying by part and location, but they are not a MODA criterion or a term in the cost equations (DTIC full thesis, pp. 35, 53).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation (8-year amortisation of a $1.105M M290) is charged per build hour against machine hours per year, and multi-part builds are costed explicitly, cutting per-part cost about a third (35% for three bracket mounts per build) (DTIC full thesis, Eq. 4, Tables 4.1, 4.3-4.4).
Shared_Capacity_note: SMEs call for an expanded, integrated network of printing sites for faster turn-around, a recommendation, while the model prices a single machine and does not assign or pool work across sites (DTIC full thesis, Appendix 2, ch. 4).
Speed_note: The cost model computes build time per part and the MODA scores lead time and readiness on user-set bands (e.g. 1-15 days = 10), but the AM delivery days in Fig. 4.2 (9-16 days) were gathered from Haystack Gold and SMEs, not computed, and Table 4.7 is a generic all-10 example (DTIC full thesis, Table 4.3, Fig. 4.2, Tables 4.7-4.8).

name: Crean AFIT metal AM per-part cost model and AM capability fielding costs
developer: Capt Ryan C. Crean, USAF, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Alan W. Johnson)
description: An Atzeni & Salmi-based cost model (material, pre-processing, processing, post-processing) with a layer-based build-time formula. It matched UDRI builds within 0–5.3%. Single builds averaged $3,144.74 per part and maximum batches $2,615.95. Before NRE, only 1 of 7 parts was cheaper with AM in single builds, and 3 with batching. Fielding one metal capability costs about $1.52–1.66M per alloy family.
NRE_note: Build setup is costed (2 h at $45/h, $90 per build) and an engineering-time term sits in Eq. 3, but one-time NRE is excluded from per-part cost and only cited outside the model (AFLCMC ~$1,000,000; Tinker ~40 h) (full thesis, Eq. 3, pp. 57, 60).
Production_note: Per-part cost is built from material (with waste factor), pre-processing, build time x depreciation per machine hour, energy, maintenance, labour ($45/h), heat treatment ($100) and machining, with build time from a layer-based formula validated within 0-5.3% (full thesis, Eqs. 1-5, Table 2).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is discussed as a barrier and technical risk is placed outside scope, and the selected parts are noted as not flight-safety critical, but criticality or qualification is not a screening step of the cost model (full thesis, Ch. I-III, pp. 30, 62).
QA_Insp_note: A per-build test cost is a line item in post-processing: one ASTM E8 tensile coupon per build at $300 ($200 machining, $100 test); volumetric inspection is excluded (full thesis, Eq. 5 and assumptions).
Storage_note: Inventory holding and transport savings are discussed but deliberately left out of the model as hard to calculate (full thesis, ch. III).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine depreciation (EOS M290, ~$1.1M) is charged per machine hour against machine hours per year and spread over multi-part builds (up to 16 parts), cutting average cost from $3,144.74 single-build to $2,615.95 max-batch; sharing across sites is not modelled (full thesis, Eq. 4, Tables 5-8).
Shared_Capacity_note: An enterprise-wide network with metal machines placed at the correct bases is a recommendation in the conclusions, not part of the cost model (full thesis, pp. 60, 62).
Speed_note: Build and post-processing hours are computed (average 88.76 h single-part, 188.22 h max-part builds) and current PLT+ALT is reported, but AM lead time is not totalled or valued and NMC-S cost is left to future work (full thesis, Tables 4-8).

name: AMPAT (Additive Manufacturing Process and Analysis Tool), NPS Navy Expeditionary AM capstone
developer: Leslie J. Amodeo, Brian B. Dick, Charles P. Flynn, Rebecca A. Nagurney and Meagan B. Parker (NPS Systems Engineering capstone). Sponsor: Navy Expeditionary Combat Command (NECC).
description: The user filters a database of AM systems on attributes such as build size, material, process, footprint, print speed, cooling, print quality, post-processing, failure rate, operational availability and environment, then assigns weights. The tool outputs a normalized weighted ranking and plots, for example overall score against initial cost. It covers equipment only, not part selection.
NRE_note: The tool has no NRE attribute; the report only notes that the X-FAB carries a 3D scanner to model existing parts and recommends adding a parts library as future work (DTIC AD1150790).
Production_note: Material cost per pound, consumable cost per 100 hours and component cost are machine attributes normalised to the best value and weighted into a ranking score, but no per-part cost is built up or reported, and per-part price comparison appears only as future AMCAT integration (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2, Equation 4, Future Work).
QA_Qual_note: The tool has no qualification attribute; the report cites the DON goal to rapidly qualify AM components and recommends a unified DoD equipment certification program as future work (DTIC AD1150790).
QA_Insp_note: Print quality (layer thickness) is a machine capability attribute and the report says sailor-printed parts need a validation process, but inspection does not enter the ranking (DTIC AD1150790).
Storage_note: The report argues on-demand AM means fewer spares carried in the field, but the tool's spares attributes cover only the AM system's own spares, so part inventory does not enter the ranking (DTIC AD1150790).
Shared_Capital_note: Each AM system's procurement (component) cost, with maintenance and consumable costs, is entered and plotted against its overall score (e.g. a 3:1 cost benefit), but machine cost is not spread over parts, volume or users (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2, Fig. 38).
Shared_Capacity_note: The tool is meant to inform dispersion and prepositioning of AM capability across the fleet, but the team could not build a dispersion plan and the tool does not assign or route work across printers (DTIC AD1150790).
Speed_note: Print speed, logistics delay time, maintenance downtime and operational availability are machine attributes used to filter and weight the ranking, and the report claims on-demand AM cuts lead time, but no part lead time is entered and no print, build or lead time is computed or reported (DTIC AD1150790, Table 2, Table 4, limitations).

name: Sasson & Johnson 3D printing supercenters concept
developer: Amir Sasson, John Chandler Johnson (BI Norwegian Business School)
description: An invited conceptual paper. Firms use direct digital manufacturing (DDM) to separate out low-volume, disruptive parts even at a higher unit cost, then grow into regional multi-product 'supercenters'. These move spares inventory from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM facilities. There is no quantitative model; the authors call for cost comparisons and simulation studies.
NRE_note: Digital design (creation, modification, copying or scanning) is named as a phase of 3D printing and firms are urged to publish printable component files, but design effort enters no decision in the conceptual paper (BI open author version, '3D printing', 'Discussion').
Production_note: Higher DDM unit cost is argued to be acceptable for low-volume, disruptive parts 'regardless of relative cost', with an anecdote and a hypothetical ($1 vs $1000), so unit cost is not used to decide and cost comparisons are left to future research (BI open author version, 'From Long Tail to DDM Supercenters').
QA_Qual_note: A lack of safety and quality standards is cited as a constraint on adoption and published print files are said to ensure component quality, as discussion with no qualification step in any decision (BI open author version, '3D printing', 'Discussion').
QA_Insp_note: The full paper was read and does not discuss inspection or testing of printed parts; the out-of-spec RiverCo trial is attributed only to insufficient engineering evaluation criteria (BI open author version).
Storage_note: Spares inventory is argued to shift from finished goods at company plants to raw material at shared DDM supercenters, with lower lot sizes and safety stocks, as a concept that quantifies nothing and decides nothing (BI open author version, 'Supply Chains and DDM Supercenters', 'Discussion').
Shared_Capital_note: Supercenters are argued to raise utilisation of printing capacity by serving other firms' demand and to gain economies of scope, as a concept with no numbers or decision rule (BI open author version, 'Background', 'Supply Chains and DDM Supercenters').
Shared_Capacity_note: The authors envisage orders redirected to center B when center A is full, as long as extra distribution cost is below customer queuing cost, by analogy with a search engine redirecting customers from fully booked hotels, but this is a conceptual mechanism, not a rule a tool applies (BI open author version, 'Background').
Speed_note: The authors predict that manufacturers 'will allocate expedite orders for low and sporadic demand parts to 3D printing' and claim local printing cuts lead times, with no criteria or quantification (BI open author version, 'Introduction', 'From Long Tail to DDM Supercenters').

name: Strong et al. hybrid-AM hub facility-location model (uncapacitated and p-median, 2018)
developer: Danielle Strong, Michael Kay, Brett Conner, Thomas Wakefield, Guha Manogharan (Penn State)
description: An uncapacitated facility-location model places hubs by geography, demand and hybrid-AM processing cost. Hubs land at demand centroids, and location depends only on AM utilization rate. A constrained p-median model grows from 22 to 44 hubs as demand rises. Outputs are candidate US counties, fixed, operating and transport costs, and hub utilization. Transport cost was not a significant factor.
NRE_note: Only the abstract and a trade summary could be read, and neither mentions design or engineering effort; the full paper was not reachable (Penn State Pure abstract; 3DPrint.com).
Production_note: Hybrid-AM processing and operational cost enter the hub-location model at hub level, with no per-part build-up from geometry, material and machine (Penn State Pure abstract).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract mentions meeting GD&T, surface-finish and mechanical-property requirements but not qualification, and the full paper was not reachable (Penn State Pure abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract names post-processing steps (machining, grinding, heat treatment, HIP) but not inspection, and the full paper was not reachable (Penn State Pure abstract).
Storage_note: Neither the abstract nor the trade summary mentions inventory, and the model formulation was not reachable (Penn State Pure abstract; 3DPrint.com).
Shared_Capital_note: Because shops find metal AM equipment too costly to own, the model pools capacity into hubs and trades fixed hub cost against hub count (22 rising to 44 with demand), with location driven by the AM utilisation rate (Penn State Pure abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Hub capacity utilisation is an output of the constrained model and adding capacity to existing hubs is recommended, but no effect on lead time or service is reported (Penn State Pure abstract; 3DPrint.com).
Speed_note: The abstract and trade summary report transport cost but no lead or delivery time, and the full paper was not reachable (Penn State Pure abstract; 3DPrint.com).

name: ISO/ASTM TS 52930:2021 Qualification principles: installation, operation and performance (IQ/OQ/PQ) of PBF-LB equipment
developer: ISO/TC 261 and ASTM F42 (joint), adopted by CEN as CEN ISO/ASTM/TS 52930
description: Recommended practices for IQ, OQ and PQ of PBF-LB/M machines and connected equipment. Feedstock qualification and post-processing beyond powder removal are excluded. The public scope gives no test list, sample sizes or tiering by part criticality.
NRE_note: The scope excludes only process mapping, risk assessment and validation planning and keeps process issues where they support machine qualification, while OQ is defined as establishing process control limits and the OQ clause body (6.3) was not visible, so whether parameter development falls inside the standard is not established (ISO scope; iTeh SIST sample cl. 1, 3.2).
Production_note: The documented scope is recommended practice for machine qualification, per-part cost is plainly outside it and the TOC has no cost clause (ISO scope; ANSI TOC preview).
QA_Qual_note: The standard prescribes IQ (FAT/SAT, environment, utilities, procedures, software control, calibration), OQ and PQ for PBF-LB/M machines plus revalidation and a normative SPC annex, with tests repeated as needed, but no test counts or part-class tiering are visible (iTeh SIST sample cl. 6.1-6.2; ANSI TOC).
QA_Insp_note: Clause 5 requires the machine user to identify, monitor and document critical process variables under SPC (Annex A) and names in-process and end-product testing as quality determinants, but no per-part inspection scope by part class or cost is visible (iTeh SIST sample cl. 5).
Storage_note: Inventory is plainly outside the documented scope, which is IQ/OQ/PQ of the equipment that directly influences material consolidation (ISO scope; ANSI TOC).
Shared_Capital_note: Only the scope, TOC and clauses 5-6.2 were seen; qualification is machine-centric for serial production but clause 6.1 also calls for validation when a new product is introduced, and the revalidation clause body is not visible, so whether qualification is reused across parts or users is not established (iTeh SIST sample; ANSI TOC).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity pooled across sites or users is plainly outside the documented scope of single-machine qualification (ISO scope).
Speed_note: Lead time and availability are plainly outside the documented scope, and the scope and TOC have no scheduling or availability element (ISO scope; ANSI TOC).

name: EASA CM-S-008 Additive Manufacturing, Issue 04 (3 Sept 2025)
developer: European Union Aviation Safety Agency (EASA); revision discussed at FAA-EASA AM Workshop WG1
earlier_versions: CM-S-008 Issue 01 (4 Apr 2017): first issue. | CM-S-008 Issue 02 (3 Nov 2020): added supporting text for the basic CS materials requirements, guidance on AM in non-critical parts, and emphasis on knowledge transfer and training; issued for public consultation (3-24 Nov 2020). | CM-S-008 Issue 03 (30 Apr 2021): incorporated the comments from the Issue 02 consultation.
description: Adopts the ASTM F3572-22 Class A-D scheme. Section 3 policy covers only new parts or repair-by-replacement of no/low criticality (Class C and D); higher classes are said to be hard to certify near-term. All AM parts need early authority engagement, a threat and design safety assessment, M&P specifications and process control documents, KPPs, statistically covered design values (A/B/C/D/S-basis per MMPDS/CMH-17), and machine OQ plus process PQ over multiple builds. Class C/D may use S-basis data, a minimal representative coupon set and simplified means of compliance; Class D may qualify for minor change approval. POA must treat a new AM process as a significant change.
NRE_note: Calls for identification of key variables and key process parameters and for process control documents supported by M&P specifications, a parameter-development activity required for certification, with no effort or cost (CM-S-008, secs. 3.1.1-3.1.2).
Production_note: Full CM read; per-part production cost is not addressed, the only cost reference being a passing 'commercially driven material and process selection decision' (CM-S-008, sec. 3.1.2).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is tiered by class (Class C/D may use S-basis data, a minimal representative coupon set and reduced MoC; OQ and PQ need statistical relevance over multiple builds), but no build or coupon counts are set and Class A/B are left to the future (CM-S-008, secs. 1.1, 1.3.2, 3.1.2).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection appears only in definitions and design considerations (defects judged against acceptance criteria, flaws by NDT detectability, 'access for inspection', defects 'challenging to detect by inspection'), and the CM prescribes no NDI, first-article, witness-coupon or acceptance activity beyond a general POA conformity duty (CM-S-008, secs. 1.3.2, 3.1.2, 3.5, App. 2).
Storage_note: Full CM read; spares, stock and inventory are not mentioned, the scope covering only new parts and repair by replacement (CM-S-008, sec. 1.1).
Shared_Capital_note: Reuse of prior qualification is a rule of the procedure, without numbers: applications within previous regulatory agreement avoid case-by-case agreement, and simplified MoC may rest on equivalence to an established, accepted database, though part families and machine equivalency are not covered (CM-S-008, secs. 1.3.2, 3.1.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full CM read; production capacity, multiple machines and sites are not mentioned, only the organisation's AM scope and capability (CM-S-008, secs. 3.1.2, 3.5).
Speed_note: Full CM read; lead time and availability are not mentioned (CM-S-008).

name: FAA Advisory Circular AC 33.15-3 Powder Bed Fusion AM Process for Aircraft Engine Parts (with FAA 2020 AM Report to Congress)
developer: Federal Aviation Administration (Aircraft Certification Service)
description: Design values should be statistically based (MMPDS-level rigor) from a frozen process and stable feedstock. Specimens should span builds, build locations, orientations, thicknesses and powder lots, with debits for features and thermal exposure. Key process variables are frozen within validated windows; changes need requalification; each machine is validated separately. Powder reuse limits are required, ISO/IEC 17025 labs are expected, and periodic destructive sampling is based on SPC. No sample sizes are given. There are no criticality tiers beyond noting that life-limited parts need more (33.14/33.70). The 2020 report says acceptable risk is set by part criticality but defines no formal tiers.
NRE_note: Requires one-time engineering to identify key process variables, complete parametric studies (process validation) and freeze the process before qualification, with no effort or cost stated (AC 33.15-3 secs. 5.2, 8.1, 8.1.3).
Production_note: The AC does not address production cost; the bundled 2020 Report to Congress states in words that AM parts save cost, as background with no cost model or inputs, and no step of the AC uses cost (FAA 2020 report sec. 4.2; AC 33.15-3).
QA_Qual_note: Prescribes qualification test sets (MMPDS-rigour design values from specimens spanning builds, locations, orientations and powder lots; feature and thermal debits; per-machine validation; requalification on key-variable change) but gives no specimen counts and no part classes beyond noting life-limited parts need more (AC 33.15-3 secs. 5.2, 6.1.1, 6.4, 11.5).
QA_Insp_note: NDI (including CT) is one option alongside process monitoring, proof testing and periodic destructive sampling whose frequency is set from demonstrated SPC, with no quantities or class-specific scope (AC 33.15-3 secs. 10.3, 10.6, 10.9, 11.4.2).
Storage_note: Full AC and report read: inventory is absent and outside the AC's materials-compliance scope, and the 2020 report mentions spare parts only as AM applications that maintenance organisations raise case by case, with no stock-reduction claim (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report sec. 4.2.2).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine investment is outside the AC's scope, and each machine needs its own process validation even with identical parameters, so qualification is explicitly not spread across machines (AC 33.15-3 secs. 11.5-11.6).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full AC and report read: production capacity, utilisation and pooling are not addressed and lie outside the AC's scope (AC 33.15-3; FAA 2020 report).
Speed_note: The AC does not address lead time; the bundled 2020 report claims schedule savings and faster builds as background, and no step of the AC uses lead time (FAA 2020 report secs. 4.2, 5; AC 33.15-3).

name: MMPDS Volume II guidelines for AM allowables (2026 handbook edition)
year: 2021-2026 (AM data guidelines presented 2021-2023; Volume II first released 1 July 2024; 2026 edition 1 July 2026; no AM allowables published yet)
developer: Battelle (MMPDS Secretariat) with the MMPDS General Coordinating Committee (FAA, DoD, industry)
earlier_versions: Draft AM allowables guidelines presented by Battelle (Hall, 2021 and 2023): C-, D- and S-basis data minima on which the survey ratings rest. | MMPDS-2024 Volume II (released 1 July 2024): first edition; data-generation and analysis framework only, no material allowables yet (Battelle press release, Aug 2024). | MMPDS 2025 Volume II: annual edition listed on SAE Mobilus; changes not checked.
description: Volume II adds C-basis (lower of spec minimum or T99), D-basis (T90) and S-basis allowables for AM metals, each requiring 'further showing'. Mandatory S-basis minimums: 30 samples per strength property from 3 heats, 3 manufacturing lots, 3 machines and 3 build cycles (fewer for modulus and density). Recommended D-basis: 100 samples, 10 heats, 10 lots, 5 machines, 10 builds. C-basis: 100 samples, 10 heats, 20 lots, 5 machines, 20 builds. If no parametric fit is possible, 299 samples are needed. C-basis needs 20 builds or lots, against 10 lots for conventional A-basis. Lot-release values are being derived for several AMS AM specs.
NRE_note: Documented scope plainly excludes it: Volume II 'publishes the framework for generating and analyzing the data' for material allowables, so part design files, reverse engineering and per-part parameter development are outside it (SAE Mobilus Volume II page; Hall 2021/2023).
Production_note: Documented scope (material allowables data framework) plainly excludes per-part production cost, and neither slide deck mentions cost (SAE Mobilus page; Hall 2021/2023).
QA_Qual_note: Sets costable data minima per allowable basis (S-basis 30 samples, 3 heats, 3 lots, 3 machines, 3 build cycles; D-basis 100/10/10/5/10; C-basis 100/10/20/5/20; 299 samples without a parametric fit), but basis is not tied to part class: S-basis for low-criticality parts was only under FAA-EASA discussion (Hall, AMSC 2021, Items 19-20; Hall, NRC 2023).
QA_Insp_note: Handbook sec. 9.2.2, which applies to AM materials in Volume II, requires a specification whose quality controls 'shall include' lot-release acceptance criteria for composition and mechanical properties, with Battelle deriving the lot-release values, but per-part inspection or NDI is not addressed (Hall, NRC 2023).
Storage_note: Inventory is plainly outside the documented scope of a material-allowables data framework (SAE Mobilus page; Hall 2021/2023).
Shared_Capital_note: Allowables pooled across machines, heats and builds are published for all users and AMS 7032 sends machine-qualification data to Battelle, but this describes shared data rather than a rule that uses capital sharing to decide, and the slides cannot confirm more (Hall, NRC 2023; Hall, AMSC 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity is plainly outside the documented scope of a material-allowables handbook (SAE Mobilus page; Hall 2021/2023).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is outside the documented scope; the only time figure is that 'Two to five new alloys are added each year' to MMPDS (Hall, NRC 2023).

name: JMADD: Joint Metal Additive Database Definition (America Makes project 5511.001), public B/A-basis allowables framework for L-PBF Ti-6Al-4V
developer: Wichita State University NIAR (presenter; fabrication and testing) with Battelle, Auburn University, Beehive Industries, EOS, Boeing and Penn State CIMP-3D; America Makes project funded by OSD ManTech (AFRL agreement FA8650-20-2-5700)
description: Budget: $4.24M ($1.8M government + $2.44M cost share) over Oct 2020 to Oct 2024. Inputs: three fabricators, three powder suppliers, 19 feedstock lots in Qual 1 and 10+ heats.
