About 1,733 specimens were defined for Qual 1, covering tension, shear, compression, bearing and fracture toughness, with a CT subset of 216. Qual 2 uses 60 builds. The overall program was described as about 3,600 specimens. Planned follow-ons are machine equivalency (GE M2 vs EOS M290, 18-24 months) and fatigue curves (360 specimens, 8 builds, 24 months).
NRE_note: JMADD drafts an NCAMP L-PBF process specification (NAPS 065) and machine-specific process control documents that users can adopt instead of developing their own parameters, a deliverable whose saving is claimed, and whether NRE enters any decision cannot be confirmed from the briefings (NIAR JMADD 2024 presentation; FAA REDAC 2022).
Production_note: JMADD is an allowables database and specification effort, a documented scope that plainly excludes per-part production cost (FAA REDAC 2022; NIAR JMADD 2024 presentation).
QA_Qual_note: It prescribes a costable material-qualification test matrix (e.g. tension, compression and shear 100 x 3 = 300 each across 5 machines and 10 heats, bearing 600, fracture toughness 90; about 1,733 Qual-1 specimens) at a programme cost of $4.24M, but for material and process only, with no part-class qualification counts or cost model (NIAR JMADD 2024 presentation; NIAR AFRL-2024-1140 briefing).
QA_Insp_note: The programme specifies a lot-release tensile test from each build, which is lot-level acceptance; CT of about 216 specimens is nondestructive inspection of the allowables test specimens, not per-part production inspection (NIAR AFRL-2024-1140 briefing; NIAR JMADD 2024 presentation).
Storage_note: JMADD is a material allowables and specification effort, so parts inventory is outside its documented scope (FAA REDAC 2022; NIAR presentations).
Shared_Capital_note: Allowables and specifications are to be published through NCAMP and America Makes so qualification data are reused across users and machines, a claimed benefit not quantified, and whether reuse enters any decision cannot be confirmed from the briefings (NIAR JMADD 2024 presentation; FAA REDAC 2022).
Shared_Capacity_note: JMADD's documented scope is material data and specifications, which plainly excludes print capacity (FAA REDAC 2022; NIAR presentations).
Speed_note: JMADD's documented scope is material data and specifications, which plainly excludes part lead time or availability (FAA REDAC 2022; NIAR presentations).

name: MASAAG Paper 124 Issue 2 (2022): qualification and certification of AM parts for military aviation
developer: Military Aircraft Structures Airworthiness Advisory Group (MASAAG), UK Ministry of Defence
earlier_versions: MASAAG Paper 124 Issue 1 (17 Oct 2018): first issue covering structures, propulsion and metals; Issue 2 added Systems and Polymers chapters, a graphical abstract and updated recommendations.
description: Grade A structural parts and Critical engine parts get the full recommendations: the MCRI (Military Certification Review Item) process, a PCD supplied with airworthiness documentation, B-basis allowables per failure mode with minimum coupon and batch counts, and a test pyramid up to component tests. Grade B is at the designer's discretion. Non-critical parts need a consequence-based subset agreed with the TAA. Statistical guidance: about 100 measurements for direct A/B values, 30 as an interim B-value. NDI detectable crack size is linked to inspection intervals for inspection-based fatigue substantiation.
NRE_note: One-time engineering deliverables are required without cost or hours: a PCD for critical AM parts, calibration builds when the alloy changes, pre-qualification builds on machines outside the qualification, and retention of the qualified CAD/STL file (MASAAG 124, REC6.1, REC6.5, REC6.8, REC6.9).
Production_note: Standard text read (chapters 1-6 and the start of 7): no per-part production cost; the only cost-related words are that real spin tests are 'expensive' and powder reuse economics (MASAAG 124, 4.6.1, 6.4).
QA_Qual_note: Grade A structure gets costable counts (B-basis allowables per failure mode, Table 3-3 fallback of at least 15 coupons with 5 per source and 3 batches, 100 or interim 30 measurements, MCRI, PCD, test pyramid), while Grade B is at the designer's discretion and non-critical parts get a TAA-agreed subset, so counts exist for the top class only (MASAAG 124, 3.1.6, 3.6.1, REC3.1, REC4.14).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection scope is set for the top class only: each Grade A part (and Class 1/Group 1 engine and Grade A systems part) gets NDI of 100 percent of its surface plus structurally significant internal areas, while Grade B gets no inspection recommendation and non-critical parts a TAA-agreed subset; per-build witness specimens are recommended for all powder-bed builds, but their content is illustrative ('could include but are not limited to') and not tied to class (MASAAG 124, REC3.7, REC3.9, REC6.43, Sec. 6.6.1).
Storage_note: Parts inventory and spares are not addressed; storage appears only as evidence that feedstock properties have not deteriorated (MASAAG 124, REC6.2; chapters 1-6 read).
Shared_Capital_note: Qualifying a process for a range of parts within a part family is described only as a future possibility, and REC6.8 allows other machines after pre-qualification builds, a qualification requirement rather than any spreading of machine cost across parts or users (MASAAG 124, 3.8.1, 4.7.2.2, REC6.8).
Shared_Capacity_note: Capacity across sites or users is not addressed; moving production to other machines is treated only as a pre-qualification requirement (MASAAG 124, REC6.8; chapters 1-6 read).
Speed_note: Lead time, availability and obsolescence are not addressed; inspection 'intervals' concern in-service fatigue inspection, not part supply (MASAAG 124, 4.5.1; chapters 1-6 read).

name: Lloyd's Register LR-GN-046 guidance notes for AM metallic parts (June 2024)
developer: Lloyd's Register (with TWI for the 2016/2017 editions)
earlier_versions: LR/TWI Guidance Notes for Additive Manufacturing (March 2017 edition, read in full; an earlier 2016 edition is reported but not confirmed): joint LR-TWI goal-based guidance for LMD, L-PBF and WAAM parts; LR-GN-046 (2024) refocused it on marine and offshore use.
description: The 2017 edition is goal-based with no fixed part categories. Testing depends on design code, criticality and a functional study. Five certifiable stages (design, materials, manufacturing, post-processing, inspection/testing) can be certified separately by different organisations. Minimum per part: 100% visual and 100% dimensional examination. NDE methods are set by quality level, complexity and criticality. For PBF, good practice is a density block, retained-powder capsule and one tensile set per build. Build parameters are machine-specific. The 2024 edition adds facility approval but its categories were not seen.
NRE_note: Requires a manufacturing plan for each AM part design and further testing when certified parts move to a different machine, and lists reverse engineering as a criterion for deciding whether AM suits a part, none costed; the 2024 text sits behind Regs4ships sign-up and was not read (LR/TWI 2017 secs. 3, 7.1.1, 10).
Production_note: Material cost, production size and shipping time and cost are criteria to be considered in deciding whether AM is the most suitable process for a part, with no cost calculation (LR/TWI 2017 sec. 3).
QA_Qual_note: Defines five separately certifiable stages and machine-specific parameter qualification, with mechanical testing specific to part geometry and application and agreed case by case, but no class-specific counts (LR/TWI 2017 secs. 4, 5, 9.3; LR guidance notes page).
QA_Insp_note: Sets costable minimums for every part and build (100% visual and 100% dimensional examination, a powder capsule preserved for each PBF build, density block and tensile set as good practice) but leaves NDE extent to quality level, complexity and criticality (LR/TWI 2017 secs. 7.2.2, 9.1).
Storage_note: The full 2017 text does not mention inventory or spares, and the 2024 edition's stated scope (manufacturer requirements; testing, qualification and certification) excludes it (LR/TWI 2017; LR guidance notes page).
Shared_Capital_note: Says certification of individual stages 'can reduce the effort' for later part designs and contracts and that pre-certified organisations can cut certification cost, stated benefits rather than a rule that carries certification across parts (LR/TWI 2017 sec. 4).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacity and pooling are absent from the full 2017 text and outside the documented certification scope of the 2024 edition (LR/TWI 2017; LR guidance notes page).
Speed_note: Lead time and shipping time are criteria to be considered in deciding whether AM suits a part, and pre-certified organisations are said to shorten certification lead times, without figures (LR/TWI 2017 secs. 3, 4).

name: ABS Requirements for Additive Manufacturing
year: 2018 (Guidance Notes, Sept 2018); 2021 (Guide, April 2021); Requirements edition date Unknown (a linked PDF file name suggests July 2022)
developer: American Bureau of Shipping (ABS)
earlier_versions: ABS Guidance Notes on Additive Manufacturing (Sept 2018): four-stage maturity approval (feasibility, verification, pre-production validation, production); specimen counts agreed case by case; read in full. | ABS Guide for Additive Manufacturing (April 2021): first ABS Guide, covering facility and part approval for PBF and DED; later reissued as the Requirements, which also cover material extrusion (2025 trade coverage); not read.
description: The 2018 Guidance Notes define four maturity stages: feasibility, verification of a cradle-to-grave file, pre-production validation builds witnessed at hold points, and production with monitoring. Qualification depth scales with the part's ABS Tier of Approval; specimen counts are agreed case by case. A critical process-parameter change triggers requalification. A 2023 ABS briefing describes AM Test Levels 1-3 set by risk (likelihood x consequence, consequence mapped to ISO 5817 classes). It lists standard approval tests and rapid-qualification options: in-situ monitoring replacing NDT, reduced scope using existing data, and part- or feature-family qualification. It states only that approval cost is high.
NRE_note: ABS reviews the cradle-to-grave file at each stage and requires converted or transferred build files to be checked for units and origin before builds, prescribed preparation steps that are not costed (ABS Guidance Notes 2018, Secs. 2/2, 5/1, 6/3; current Requirements portal not read).
Production_note: The full 2018 guidance sets facility and part approval steps with no per-part cost content, and ABS describes the current Requirements as 'a structured approval and certification process', a scope that plainly excludes production costing; the page's 'cost-effectively' line describes AM in general, not the Requirements (ABS Guidance Notes 2018 full text; ABS AM page).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is staged with ABS review and its depth 'should correlate with the applicable Tiers of Approval', and 2023 Test Levels are set by risk, but 'the amount and type of testing varies on a case-by-case basis' with no class-specific specimen counts or test sets (ABS Guidance Notes 2018, Secs. 2/1.4, 4/6; Qiao ABS slides 2023).
QA_Insp_note: Production NDE and its probability of detection must be described, a test artifact in each build is recommended and in-situ monitoring may replace NDT, but inspection frequency is agreed case by case by volume and criticality with no class-specific scope (ABS Guidance Notes 2018, Secs. 2/1.4, 4/3.1, 6; Qiao slides 2023, slide 21).
Storage_note: Spare-part inventory is absent from the full 2018 guidance (storage appears only for feedstock), the 2023 slides mention spare and obsolete parts only as cases where standard qualification fits poorly, and approval requirements plainly exclude inventory (ABS Guidance Notes 2018; Qiao slides 2023).
Shared_Capital_note: ABS lists qualification 'by Part Family or by Design Feature Family' within AM Levels 3-1 and reduced test scope using recognised data as rapid-qualification routes, only qualification by material group being labelled 'potential', though qualified processes 'may be specific to the serial number of a particular AM machine'; no numbers (Qiao ABS slides 2023, slide 21; ABS Guidance Notes 2018, Sec. 6/4).
Shared_Capacity_note: The guidance says one AM service provider 'can act as the equivalent of multiple qualified factories' serving many clients 'under one roof', a foreword remark that does not enter its procedure (ABS Guidance Notes 2018, Foreword).
Speed_note: The guidance says AM's value is producing 'a low number of complex parts faster than traditional manufacturing methods', a claim with no lead time used in its procedure (ABS Guidance Notes 2018, Sec. 1/2).

name: Indian Register of Shipping Classification Notes: Additively Manufactured Metallic Parts for Marine and Offshore Applications
developer: Indian Register of Shipping (IRClass)
description: Parts are 'class items' (must meet IRS Rules; IRS approves feedstock and manufacturer) or 'certified items' (meet industry/OEM standards; manufacturer qualifies feedstock and design). Criticality is set separately: critical = primary/secondary essential services, non-critical = habitability. Qualification specimen counts are tabulated per category. PBF: tensile 5 (class) vs 3 (certified critical), impact 3 sets vs 1, hardness 6 vs 3, microstructure 4 vs 2, density 3 vs 3. DED tensile: 6 vs 3. Coupons and components get visual and surface NDT; components also get embedded-flaw NDT. Production sampling frequency is set in an agreed inspection and test plan.
NRE_note: Requires one-time engineering steps (CAD or drawing review and approval for class items, a design-analysis report for topology-optimised parts, and AMPS qualification over a parameter range) without costable effort (IRClass CN secs. 1.6.2, 3.2.3, 5.1.2).
Production_note: Full notes read: production cost is not mentioned and is outside a class-approval document's scope (IRClass CN, July 2025).
QA_Qual_note: Tables 19-21 prescribe qualification specimen counts per test for each in-scope category (certified critical vs class items) and process, e.g. PBF tensile 3 vs 5, hardness 3 vs 6, microstructure 2 vs 4, while non-critical parts are left to manufacturer's certification by the notes' scope (IRClass CN July 2025, secs. 1.1.1, 1.5.1, Tables 19-21).
QA_Insp_note: Sets costable per-part minimums (100% visual examination and NDT of every delivered part, component surface and embedded-flaw checks) but leaves NDT extent and production test frequency to an agreed NDT plan and ITP rather than setting scope by part class (IRClass CN secs. 7.3.8.1-7.3.8.2, Tables 19-20).
Storage_note: Full notes read: spare-parts inventory is not addressed, and storage appears only as feedstock shelf life and handling (IRClass CN, July 2025, Table 7).
Shared_Capital_note: Qualification is reused across parts and machines without numbers: certified critical items may be approved as a part family with a risk analysis, and a new serial number of the same machine model is not a change of machine (IRClass CN sec. 6.4.3; Annex 2 Table 37 note 1).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full notes read: capacity pooling is not addressed, and the manufacturer only declares estimated annual production, frequency and maximum part sizes for approval (IRClass CN, Annex 2).
Speed_note: Full notes read: lead time or availability is not mentioned (IRClass CN, July 2025).

name: AIA Recommended Guidance for Certification of AM Components, Rev. A (Oct 2025)
developer: Aerospace Industries Association (AIA) Additive Manufacturing Working Group, with FAA participation
earlier_versions: AIA Recommended Guidance for Certification of AM Components, initial report (2020): first AIA AM Working Group guidance; Rev. A (2025) restructured it, added guidance for higher-criticality parts (damage-tolerance, crack-growth and fracture-toughness data, expanded NDI, witness coupons) and aligned with ASTM F3572-22.
description: Criticality is set by FMECA rather than ASTM F3572 classes, and requirements scale with consequence of failure. Higher criticality brings fatigue and damage-tolerance allowables, tighter KPV control, more frequent machine maintenance and stricter requalification. Inspection development needs limits of detection and POD. Performance qualification ends in first-article inspection, and witness coupons are built into production for high-criticality parts. Every machine serial number is qualified independently, though PCDs can be reused. Equivalency is shown statistically. Requalification triggers include software, firmware, component or relocation changes. A section on part-family allowables exists but was not read.
NRE_note: Prescribes process development (DOE over 8-10 parameters, a parameter set per material and machine make/model, fixed PCDs, qualification of each build definition) without effort or cost (AIA 2025, secs. 6.3, 6.4, 7.2).
Production_note: Cost appears only in words (maximising parts per platform generally lowers cost per part; point-design allowables are called uneconomic for many parts) and enters no requirement or decision step (AIA 2025, secs. 6.9.3, 8.2.1).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification rigour scales with FMECA criticality (KPV control, allowables, part-family scrutiny, PQ per machine serial number), but no build, lot or specimen counts are set for any criticality level (AIA 2025, secs. 5.1, 7.3, 8).
QA_Insp_note: First article inspection is in general a 100% dimensional verification, critical parts retain 100% sampling of select PCS and non-critical lot acceptance names a minimum test set (composition, tensile, hardness), but NDI method and acceptance criteria are left to part criticality with no class mapping (AIA 2025, secs. 13, 14.1, 14.2).
Storage_note: Full guidance read in two passes; inventory and spares stocking are not addressed, the only related text being a possible part replacement strategy for in-service anomalies (AIA 2025, sec. 14.5).
Shared_Capital_note: Qualification reuse is set by rules without numbers: PCDs from the first machine can be reused on others and test data pooled across a part family once similarity is shown, though every machine needs full PQ (AIA 2025, secs. 7.3.2, 8.2.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: The guidance sets a qualification route for when more than one machine, at one or more part producers, is needed to meet a part's demand, but it does not assign or route work across machines or sites (AIA 2025, sec. 7.3.2).
Speed_note: Full guidance read; part lead time, availability and schedule are not addressed, time appearing only as build-time minimisation in parameter optimisation and 'flow time reduction' as a general AM adoption driver (AIA 2025, sec. 6.4).

name: Peron/Cantini qualification-cost model for AM vs conventional spare parts (Cantini et al. 2025)
developer: Peron (NTNU), Cantini (Politecnico di Milano / Univ. Firenze), Coruzzolo and Lolli (Univ. Modena e Reggio Emilia), De Carlo (Univ. Firenze)
earlier_versions: Peron, Cantini & Coruzzolo 2023, IFAC-PapersOnLine 56(2):6537-6542 (doi:10.1016/j.ifacol.2023.10.303, open access): base model pricing DNV-ST-B203 class-dependent qualification and production tests; AM break-even falls from 42 parts to 8 (C2) and 6 (C3).
description: Adds three qualification cost blocks to a production-cost comparison. Build process qualification is one-time for all classes (12 tensile, 3 impact, plus hardness, microstructure, porosity, chemistry and visual). Part qualification is one-time and C3 only, covering the full test set including surface and volumetric NDT and dimensional checks. Production testing is per build job: full set for C3, reduced for C2, negligible for C1. A CM batch shares one production test, while each AM build job needs its own. Test prices run from $10 (visual) to $150 (hardness or volumetric NDT), plus $20 per part for transport. Reported break-even quantity below which AM wins: 42 parts without qualification, 42 for C1, 8 for C2, 6 for C3. Sharing a build job among 4 parts raises the C3 break-even to 9. The 2025 extension embeds qualification costs in a spare-parts inventory cost model with holding and backorder costs (abstract only).
NRE_note: The 2023 full paper costs no design-file or parameter preparation and names design routines and their costs as future work, and the 2025 abstract adds only qualification costs (IFAC 2023 full text, Conclusions; PPC 2025 abstract on Polimi record).
Production_note: Explicit per-part unit costs by technology are model inputs (AM $560.55/part; CM $22.68/part plus a $22,366 fixed cost spread over quantity), taken from Atzeni and Salmi rather than computed from geometry (IFAC 2023 full text, case study).
QA_Qual_note: One-time build-process qualification (12 tensile, 3 impact, hardness, microstructure, porosity, chemistry; all classes) and part qualification (highest class only) are priced per test by DNV-ST-B203 criticality class (IFAC 2023 full text, Eqs. 2-3, Tables 2 and 4).
QA_Insp_note: Production testing is priced per build job by class (full set C3, reduced set C2, visual only C1) with per-job transport cost, cutting the AM break-even from 42 parts to 8 (C2) and 6 (C3) (IFAC 2023 full text, Eqs. 4-6, Table 4).
Storage_note: The 2023 paper has no inventory terms, and the 2025 paper is framed around spare-parts inventories with prior models covering holding and backorder costs, but its full text is not on the Polimi, UNIMORE or UNIFI records and the DOI is blocked, so a holding-cost term is not established (PPC 2025 Polimi record).
Shared_Capital_note: One-time qualification cost is spread over part quantity through the break-even, and production tests are shared across parts in a build job (four parts per job raises the C3 break-even from 6 to 9), but AM machine capital itself is not modelled (IFAC 2023 full text).
Shared_Capacity_note: The 2023 full paper does not address machine capacity, sites or utilisation, and the 2025 abstract mentions none (IFAC 2023 full text; PPC 2025 abstract).
Speed_note: The 2023 paper cites AM's shorter lead time only as motivation, and the 2025 extension, whose abstract names backorder costs in prior models, could not be read, so backorder or lead-time computation is not established (IFAC 2023 full text; PPC 2025 Polimi record).

name: Verna et al. quality-inspection cost model for low-volume and AM production (2022)
developer: Politecnico di Torino (Verna, Genta, Galetto, Franceschini)
earlier_versions: Verna et al. 2020, Planning offline inspection strategies in low-volume manufacturing processes (Quality Engineering, doi:10.1080/08982112.2020.1739309): earlier inspection-planning model trading inspection cost against alpha/beta errors; the 2022 model adds per-part production cost and a return on inspection investment.
description: A probabilistic model per output characteristic covering defect probability p, false-alarm α, missed-defect β, inspection cost, necessary and unnecessary repair cost, and external failure cost. It yields D_tot (expected undetected defects) and C_tot (quality cost) to compare inspection strategies (2020). The 2022 paper adds quality costs to a per-part production cost model, with a return-on-inspection metric (ROII). In the L-PBF case, production cost was 18.56 €/part and quality-related costs were 14.40-31.69 €/part across three alternatives. In 2020, the most effective strategy cost about 4x the cheapest (€168.81 vs €42.36) with fewer undetected defects. CT was mentioned but not modeled.
NRE_note: Per-job AM system setup (2.5 h) and software job preparation (1.5 h) are costed at 2.97 EUR/part, but no one-time design or parameter development cost is included (2022 manuscript).
Production_note: The model computes per-part material and manufacturing cost from powder, machine and operator rates and pre-, in- and post-process times, giving 18.56 EUR/part in the L-PBF case (2022 manuscript).
QA_Qual_note: Full manuscript read; qualification and certification do not appear, and only inspector skill affecting error rates is discussed (2022 manuscript).
QA_Insp_note: Per-part inspection cost (operator plus equipment rate x inspection time, e.g. 3.38-12.50 EUR/part by characteristic) is traded against Type I and II errors, repair costs and external failure costs across three inspection strategies (2022 manuscript).
Storage_note: Full manuscript read; inventory is not addressed (2022 manuscript).
Shared_Capital_note: The EOS M290 is charged at about 38 EUR/h from a 700 kEUR price depreciated over five years at 50% utilisation, and job costs are divided over 60 parts per job (2022 manuscript).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full manuscript read; capacity, pooling and throughput are not addressed beyond the utilisation input to the machine rate (2022 manuscript).
Speed_note: Full manuscript read; build time (18 h/job) and handling times are fixed inputs multiplied by cost rates, no time quantity is computed or reported as an output, and lead time, delivery, throughput or availability do not appear (2022 manuscript).

name: CT vs electromechanical-impedance per-specimen verification cost estimate for metal AM (Strutner et al.)
year: Unknown (SAMPE conference paper; neither the NSF PAR record nor the PDF gives a date; latest reference is 2018)
developer: Virginia Tech (Strutner, Tenney, Tarazaga, Williams) with Northrop Grumman (Kwas); NSF award 1635356
description: Builds a simple per-specimen CT cost estimate. In-house 220 kV CT: $600k capital over 5 years x 2,000 h, i.e. $60/h, scaled to $240/h at a 25% duty cycle. A 2-hour scan therefore costs $480 machine time, plus about $1,000 analysis labour (about 8 h), for about $1,480 per specimen. A service bureau costs about $2,300 ($450/h + $1,000 labour + $400 shipping). Larger parts may cost 5-10x more to analyse. The EMI alternative is estimated at about $324 per specimen (about 90 min).
NRE_note: The full paper's cost items are powder, machine time, de-caking labour, CT and EMI only, with no design, parameter-development or other one-time engineering cost (NSF PAR full text, Sect. 3.4).
Production_note: Each EBM specimen's cost is built from powder (about USD 160), depreciated machine time for a quarter of a 10 h build (about USD 188) and de-caking labour (about USD 600), giving at least USD 947 each (NSF PAR full text, Sect. 3.4.1).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification or certification is not discussed in the full paper; EMI is presented only as post-production screening (NSF PAR full text).
QA_Insp_note: Per-specimen inspection cost is built up explicitly for in-house CT (USD 1,480), a CT service bureau (USD 2,300) and EMI now (USD 324) and with a clamp-on fixture (USD 103) (NSF PAR full text, Table 3).
Storage_note: Inventory, stock or spares are not discussed anywhere in the full paper (NSF PAR full text).
Shared_Capital_note: Equipment capital is amortised with explicit utilisation: the USD 600k CT over 5 x 2,000 h at a 25% duty cycle (USD 240/h) and the USD 1.5M Arcam over 5 x 4,000 h with a quarter-build share per specimen (NSF PAR full text, Sect. 3.4, Table 3).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity contention is not modelled; the only capacity remarks are that in-house CT scans one specimen per day and that an external CT service can be used (NSF PAR full text, Sect. 3.4.2).
Speed_note: The 10 h print, 12 h de-caking, 2 h CT scan, about 8 h analysis and about 90 min EMI are observed or assumed durations multiplied by hourly rates to give cost; no build or production time is computed as an output and no lead time, turnaround or total time per specimen is reported (NSF PAR full text, Sect. 3.2-3.4, Table 3).

name: Multivariate equivalency testing framework for AM requalification (Lynch et al., UTEP) with R package MultivariateEquivalency
developer: University of Texas at El Paso W.M. Keck Center and collaborators (Lynch, Villalobos, Valadez Mesta, Gomez Guillen, Mireles, Wicker)
description: Feature-wise equivalence tests on percentile bins of the reference process, with family-wise error control across measured attributes. Simulations map trade-offs among power, detectable effect size, feature count and fabrication/measurement cost. Validation used 40 observations per process and three geometric features. The authors position it as a requalification screen, not a replacement for formal qualification.
NRE_note: The full text was read; the framework screens equivalence after a machine, parameter, facility or measurement change for candidates already supported by prior engineering evidence and does not cost design or parameter development (JMMP full text, Sec. 1).
Production_note: The full text was read; per-part production cost is not modelled, and an illustrative artifact cost ($4,165) enters only as Omega in the requalification cost function (JMMP full text, Sec. 3.5, 6).
QA_Qual_note: The framework models requalification test cost as C = n* x Omega x (1 + p x delta), combining artifact fabrication and per-feature measurement, and picks the minimum-cost sample size and feature count, comparing it against a $424,500-$1,269,255 conventional tensile procedure (JMMP full text, Sec. 3.5 Eq. 9-14, Sec. 3.6, 6).
QA_Insp_note: The full text was read; measurement cost applies only to requalification artifacts, and per-part production inspection is not addressed (JMMP full text, Sec. 3.5, conclusion).
Storage_note: The full text was read and inventory is not addressed (JMMP full text).
Shared_Capital_note: The framework is meant to show that a candidate machine, scanner, facility or workflow stays equivalent to a qualified reference, so a qualified baseline can be extended to added machines, but that reuse is not tied to machine capital or utilisation (JMMP full text, abstract, Sec. 1).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full text was read; capacity pooling is not addressed, with build-plate occupancy and machine time mentioned only as batch constraints on test artifacts (JMMP full text, Sec. 3.5).
Speed_note: The full text was read; sequential stopping cuts requalification sample sizes and test-campaign duration, but part lead time or availability is not addressed (JMMP full text, Sec. 2.1, 5.1, conclusion).

name: NAVAIR Additive Manufacturing Capability initiative: licensed Material Process Combination (MPC) qualification data packages (Colibrium Additive contract) and FRCE depot certification
year: 2026 (FRCE first certified metal AM parts reported April 2026; Colibrium MPC award reported May 2026)
developer: Naval Air Systems Command (NAVAIR AM Team) with Colibrium Additive (GE Aerospace); Fleet Readiness Center East (FRCE) depot
description: NAVAIR licenses six alloy Material Process Combinations. Each includes characterization data and curves, optimized parameters, consolidated material and process specifications, and design allowables for the tested properties, plus thin-wall fatigue characterization and workforce training. FRCE, working with the NAVAIR AM Team and Fleet Support Teams, qualified, produced and certified its first metal AM parts in under six months, which it called the fastest such effort in NAVAIR. The parts were an AH-1Z pylon fitting, a V-22 landing-gear door stop fitting and a C-130 blanking plate, in aluminum, described as non-flight-critical. No contract value, cost or tiered criteria are public.
NRE_note: The licensed packages supply optimized process parameters and manufacturing process instructions, removing part of parameter development, but this is something the initiative buys rather than an item it uses to decide, as far as press sources show (GE Aerospace release Apr 2026).
Production_note: The GE release, TCT, AM Media and the Navy story give only the $31M contract value and say nothing about per-part production cost, which could plausibly sit in an unpublished NAVAIR business case (all four sources).
QA_Qual_note: The initiative buys alloy qualification packages (material and process specifications, property data, design allowables, thin-wall fatigue data) to 'enable expedited testing, qualification and certification', and FRCE parts were qualified and certified before fleet delivery, but no qualification cost is isolated because the $31M also buys four printers and training (GE release; TCT; Navy.mil).
QA_Insp_note: The sources say only that parts meet 'the same safety and quality requirements as traditionally manufactured parts' and that training covers quality teams; per-part inspection is not described (Navy.mil; GE release).
Storage_note: The Navy story says in-house, on-demand production addresses parts 'difficult to obtain through the traditional supply chains' but makes no stock or inventory claim (Navy.mil).
Shared_Capital_note: Each licensed MPC is an alloy-level package bought 'to support the additive manufacture of NAVAIR components' generally, so reuse of qualification across parts is implied, but no rule or decision using it is public (GE Aerospace release; AM Media).
Shared_Capacity_note: The Navy story names FRCE, Lakehurst, NAVAIR HQ and Fleet Support Teams as collaborators, but no source says where the four printers go or whether sites share capacity (Navy.mil; TCT).
Speed_note: The release says the packages will 'shorten lead times for critical components' and the Navy says in-house production reduces maintenance lead times, claims that public sources do not show entering any decision (GE release; Navy.mil).

name: ROK procedure for applying 3D-printed repair parts in operational units (DMSMS / FMECA / localisation screening with DT&E-OT&E qualification)
developer: S. Yoo (ROK Ministry of National Defense), J. Hur (ROK Naval Academy), H. Lee (ROK Navy Force Support System Project Group)
description: Qualitative screening built on existing parts-localisation procedures. Candidates come from three pools: DMSMS-tracked obsolete parts, FMECA risk level 2-3 parts with poor MTBF/MKBF/MRBF, and foreign-sourced parts with high import-substitution value. Each passes DT&E, an installation test, OT&E and a military-suitability determination before being catalogued in a parts database. The programme (since 2017) was extended by a 2025 industry-defence ministry agreement.
NRE_note: Digital drawings, scanners and reverse engineering appear only as background and software functions, and approved parts' drawings are stored after the suitability decision, so NRE is not a screening criterion or decision factor (Yoo et al. 2019, Sec. 2.1, Table 3, Sec. 4.2 step 6).
Production_note: Ease of manufacture and cost screen the localisation pool and an economic feasibility review is required, with the F-15K cover plate cited at 90% lower cost, but no cost is computed (Yoo et al. 2019, Secs. 2.2, 4.2).
QA_Qual_note: The procedure prescribes a feasibility review, DT&E, an installation test, OT&E if needed and a military-suitability decision before cataloguing, but gives no class-specific test counts or costs (Yoo et al. 2019, Sec. 4.2.1).
QA_Insp_note: The procedure requires development testing against quality-evaluation criteria, but the KCL inspection items (tensile and impact strength, hole and angle precision) appear only as background and no per-part inspection is required (Yoo et al. 2019, Sec. 3.2, Table 3, Sec. 4.2.1).
Storage_note: One of the three candidate pools is parts discontinued or expected to be discontinued under the DMSMS management plan, so obsolescence is a screening criterion, but no stock or holding cost is modelled (Yoo et al. 2019, Sec. 4.2).
Shared_Capital_note: Full paper read: it calls for expanding military printing facilities and a Defense Center for development and test management, but never addresses spreading machine investment across units or parts (Yoo et al. 2019, Sec. 4.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read: no printer counts, capacity or pooling of printing across units or services is described, and the Defense Center manages development and testing, not production (Yoo et al. 2019).
Speed_note: Lead time appears only as motivation and in an F-15K case that cut procurement by more than 30 days, while the candidate pools screen on obsolescence, FMECA risk and reliability rather than lead time or availability (Yoo et al. 2019, Secs. 2.2, 4.1-4.2).

name: Satair/Airbus AM spare-part pre-assessment and RapidSpares recertification route
year: 2015-2020 (AM team since c. 2015; first certified metal flying spare 2020)
developer: Satair (Airbus aftermarket subsidiary) AM team with Airbus RapidSpares design offices; production at Airbus Filton Reference Manufacturing shop
description: When a part becomes non-procurable or an AOG order arrives, Satair's AM team runs a short pre-assessment and hands candidates to Airbus RapidSpares design offices for redesign and recertification. In the A320ceo wingtip fence case, AM beat both re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining. Satair reports more than 300 AM-certified part numbers.
NRE_note: Non-recurring cost decided the route: AM was chosen over re-tooling the casting and redesigning for machining, whose cost and lead time were 'not competitive', with AM NRC reported 45% lower in the wingtip-fence case, but no method is published (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
Production_note: Printing the four-part shipset in one 26-hour build is said to cut cost per piece, a claimed benefit, and whether per-part cost enters the route's decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
QA_Qual_note: Candidates pass to RapidSpares design offices for redesign and recertification, and the part was recertified within five weeks under a new certification process and ships with EASA Form 1 from a process-qualified shop, with no qualification effort or cost modelled (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
QA_Insp_note: The press accounts say post-processing steps make the part airworthy but say nothing about inspection or testing, and no fuller description of the route is public (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020; TCT 2020).
Storage_note: The route is triggered when a part is no longer procurable (here after repeated supplier mould losses), so obsolescence acts as a screening trigger, but stock levels or holding cost are not discussed (Satair press release 2020; TCT 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: Four parts are printed together to cut cost per piece and build time per part, a claimed benefit of the build, and whether machine cost or utilisation enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (the 'more than 300 part numbers' figure is Satair's overall AM count) (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: The press names the Filton shop and notes four more customers requested the same part, which is demand rather than capacity allocation, and no source says how print capacity is shared (Metal AM 2020; TCT 2020).
Speed_note: The route is AOG-triggered and machining redesign was rejected partly because its lead time was not competitive, with shorter lead time and lower AOG risk claimed without figures (Satair press release 2020; Metal AM 2020; TCT 2020).

name: ST Engineering AM parts screening, business case and certification workflow (with EOS Additive Minds)
developer: ST Engineering Aerospace (Advanced Manufacturing Design Centre, Singapore), with an EOS Additive Minds capability transfer
description: A late-2018 capability-transfer programme gave ST Engineering a process for parts screening and selection, DfAM, business case analysis and critical-to-quality requirements. ST then built its own workflow covering DfAM, powder management, printing, inspection and post-processing. Parts are printed on demand from certified files under EASA/FAA/CAAS approvals, and more than 120 part numbers are in a production digital catalogue.
NRE_note: Design for AM and assembly consolidation are steps the workflow performs, but redesign effort is not shown as an input to part selection or the business case, whose contents are not published (EOS/AM Chronicle case study).
Production_note: Business case analysis is a named step of the screening and selection method and the brochure quotes '>20% weight and cost savings' on one IN625 part, but the analysis's cost inputs are not published (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC brochure 2025).
QA_Qual_note: Parts are printed from certified files after an aviation qualification campaign (B-basis design values, full proof-load tests) and EASA STC, DOA and POA approvals obtained before installation, a certification step the workflow requires, with qualification effort not modelled or set by part class (EOS/AM Chronicle case study).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is listed as one stage of the printing workflow from powder management to post-processing, but its methods, scope and whether results gate part release are not described (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC page).
Storage_note: A virtual inventory is being built and on-demand printing is said to reduce non-moving inventory, claimed benefits; the screening criteria are not published, so whether stock or obsolescence is used to select parts cannot be confirmed (EOS/AM Chronicle case study).
Shared_Capital_note: The business-case step is named but its contents, including any machine investment or utilisation input, are not public, and only a vendor case study, brochures and a web page describe the method (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC brochure 2025).
Shared_Capacity_note: Certified print files let parts be produced close to aircraft sites and the brochure lists 5 qualified machines, but no routing of work across printers or sites is described, so its use in decisions cannot be confirmed (EOS/AM Chronicle case study; AMDC brochure 2025).
Speed_note: Shorter lead time from on-demand printing is claimed and case results are quoted (duct lead time down 90%, a part installed within 7 days of enquiry), but the screening criteria are not published, so whether lead time enters part selection cannot be confirmed (AMDC brochure 2025; EOS/AM Chronicle case study).

name: Leonardo Aircraft Division AM spare-part candidate criteria (safety, feasibility, lead time >180 days, unscheduled removal rate band)
developer: Leonardo S.p.A. Aircraft Division Customer Support (Caselle, Turin) with Politecnico di Torino (A. Pochettino MSc thesis; builds at IAM@PoliTo)
description: Four screening criteria: non-safety-critical (binary); feasibility (geometry, material, volume, cost); procurement lead time over 180 days; and unscheduled removal rate of 0.050-0.500 per 1,000 flight hours. They yielded three use cases: a C-27J main landing gear bracket, an M-346 clevis and an M-345 connector. Leonardo reports more than 100 metal AM parts qualified and flying. This is separate from the earlier pass's Viano business-model entry for the same division.
NRE_note: The feasibility criterion screens on 'design and geometry' for printability, and the bracket was remodelled in SolidWorks from the drawing, but redesign effort or CAD availability is not used to accept or reject candidates (Pochettino thesis, Table 1.1 and Sec. 2.1).
Production_note: The feasibility criterion uses cost only as a filter (AM must be more cost-effective than conventional manufacturing at small to medium volumes); the later AMOtool figures (Table 2.1: EUR 105, 96, 69, not stated as per part or per job) come from a post-selection run whose calculation is not shown, so the criteria build up no per-part cost (Pochettino thesis, Table 1.1, Sec. 2.2.2).
QA_Qual_note: Safety criticality is a binary gate (candidates 'must be non-safety critical'), and the work leans on Leonardo's existing qualification route (over 100 metal parts qualified) without costing qualification; the AlSi10Mg result is judged against Leonardo's internal specification (Pochettino thesis, Sec. 1.1, 1.3, Ch. 5).
QA_Insp_note: Leonardo's procedure builds every order in two copies and the second, sacrificial 'first article' is submitted for dimensional, chemical-physical and mechanical testing, a fixed one-extra-copy-per-order acceptance sample, but the test set is not fixed and nothing is costed (Pochettino thesis, Sec. 2.1, p. 40).
Storage_note: The unscheduled removal rate band (0.050-0.500 per 1,000 FH) screens parts by demand, and on-demand production is presented as 'the digitization of the warehouse', but stock is never quantified (Pochettino thesis, Ch. 1, Table 1.1).
Shared_Capital_note: Read in full: the criteria and the thesis contain no machine investment, hourly rate, depreciation or utilisation; the only build sharing is the thesis author's AMOtool run 'occupying the building platform at best' (16, 14, 68 parts per job) with its calculation hidden, a post-selection case step (Pochettino thesis, Table 1.1, Sec. 2.2.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Read in full: neither the four criteria nor the rest of the thesis treats print capacity, sites or pooling; 'Delocalized production of spare parts, possibly close to the end-user' is one item in a background list of AM benefits, the BEAMIT deal is a single-supplier contract, and parts were built on one EOS M270 (Pochettino thesis, pp. 3-4, 46).
Speed_note: Procurement lead time over 180 days is a screening threshold, with AOG as motivation; the only times reported are case build durations (18 h AlSi10Mg, 15 h Ti6Al4V), not computed by the criteria (Pochettino thesis, Table 1.1, Sec. 2.2.1).

name: EDF case-by-case AM of obsolete nuclear auxiliary-circuit parts and EDF Hydro WAAM programme
developer: EDF (R&D, nuclear fleet and EDF Hydro) with partners incl. CIH, Institut de Soudure and INOVSYS
description: EDF selects obsolete parts case by case and limits nuclear use to auxiliary circuits, not the primary circuit. Worn parts are 3D-scanned and rebuilt, either printed directly (a valve plug by SLM) or cast from a printed mould. The process is chosen by part size and use (SLM, cold spray or WAAM). EDF says it has not yet entered an industrial phase.
NRE_note: Worn obsolete parts are 3D-scanned and rebuilt by AM, an activity EDF performs, with no sign that engineering effort enters its case-by-case part choice (EDF R&D pages).
Production_note: Lower manufacturing and sourcing cost and cost gains from cold spray are claimed in words; whether cost enters EDF's case-by-case selection cannot be confirmed (EDF R&D pages).
QA_Qual_note: EDF works only on parts in auxiliary circuits, not the primary circuit or nuclear zones, and requires AM parts to have mechanical properties at least as good as conventional ones, a safety-class screening gate; qualification is also named as a main obstacle and RCC-M does not yet cover AM (EDF R&D pages).
QA_Insp_note: EDF calls NDT 'essential' but is still adapting NDT methods to AM and names inspectability as a main unknown, an R&D challenge rather than a described inspection step parts must pass (EDF R&D page 'les bénéfices pour la production').
Storage_note: EDF selects parts that have become obsolete, case by case, an obsolescence screening criterion, while its principle of storing only metal powder or wire plus 3D designs in a digital catalogue is not quantified (EDF R&D pages).
Shared_Capital_note: EDF reports major investments, including two cold-spray laboratories, but no source says whether machine cost or its spread across parts or fleets enters part decisions (EDF R&D pages).
Shared_Capacity_note: EDF Hydro works with CIH and Institut de Soudure and EDF cites subcontractors and several fleets, but production capacity or its pooling is not discussed (EDF R&D pages).
Speed_note: EDF claims AM can cut manufacturing lead time by a factor of 3 or 4 and names shorter spare-part lead times as its main goal, but whether lead time enters part selection cannot be confirmed (EDF R&D pages).

name: Siemens Energy (Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery) Finspang AM burner repair and spares programme
developer: Siemens Industrial Turbomachinery AB, Finspang (now Siemens Energy); Materials Solutions, Worcester (acquired 2016)
description: Problem-driven adoption: eroded burner tips are repaired by machining off the worn section and reprinting it, instead of buying new burners. A digital thread (NX, Teamcenter, MOM tracking powder reuse) supports the work. No formal part screening or business-case method is published.
NRE_note: The burner head was redesigned from many machined and welded pieces into one unit (22% lighter, goal 50%), a case activity, and no published method uses engineering effort in a decision (Metal AM article; Siemens blog).
Production_note: Repair is presented as a 'lower-cost alternative' to new burners, but no cost figures or repair-or-replace rule are published, so whether cost enters a decision cannot be confirmed (Siemens 2019 blog; Metal AM article).
QA_Qual_note: Siemens aimed to 'repair and re-certify burners', with lasting the required duty cycles called the true test, but no certification step or gate for repaired burners is described (Siemens 2019 blog; Metal AM article).
QA_Insp_note: An AM monitor rates layer images 0-1 in near real time and burners were checked after 20,000 operating hours, but neither is shown gating parts or entering a decision (DN Siemens feature; Metal AM article).
Storage_note: Spares printed on demand when turbines signal a need is a future vision, not used in any decision (Metal AM article).
Shared_Capital_note: Press reports a large investment and eight new machines in 2016 but nothing on how machine investment or sharing enters part decisions, and only press describes the programme (Metal AM article).
Shared_Capacity_note: The Siemens AM Network linking part designers with AM service providers is named as a concept, with nothing showing the programme routing work across it (Metal AM article).
Speed_note: A 70% cut in repair turnover time and lead times 'reduced by up to 90 percent' are reported outcomes, and no published method uses lead time in a decision (Siemens 2019 blog; DN Siemens feature).

name: GE annual part audit and per-part ROI screen for casting-to-AM conversion (LM9000 bleed air adapter caps)
developer: GE Aviation (now GE Aerospace) with GE Additive; parts for Baker Hughes LM9000 turbines
description: In GE's 2020 annual part audit, the team reviewed hundreds of purchased castings, found 180 suitable for AM, and calculated ROI for each. It chose four CoCr bleed air adapter caps as the most profitable and checked them against quotes from four outside vendors. Reported results: ~35% lower manufacturing cost and 10 months from identification to prototypes.
NRE_note: Available engineering resources were a prioritisation criterion when narrowing candidates, but engineering effort is not entered as a cost term (The Fabricator 2021).
Production_note: Per-part ROI was calculated with the teams' own production and financial models, whose inputs are not documented, and checked against four vendors' casting quotes (about 35% lower) as a case result (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
QA_Qual_note: Candidates were gated on using well-characterised materials already run on the M2 machines, but no qualification effort or cost is described (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
QA_Insp_note: Both trade-press accounts describe the screen (size, features, post-processing, machining, brazing) without mentioning inspection or testing, and no GE description of the method is public (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
Storage_note: 3DPI says the project de-risked the caps' supply chain for future spare sourcing, an outcome rather than an inventory criterion, and neither article mentions stock or inventory (3DPI 2021; The Fabricator 2021).
Shared_Capital_note: The team re-laid the M2 build plate to fit four parts instead of three, a case result, but whether machine cost or utilisation enters the ROI screen cannot be confirmed from public sources (The Fabricator 2021).
Shared_Capacity_note: The Fabricator notes only that pandemic downtime unexpectedly left machine and post-processing time free at GE's Auburn facility, and neither article shows that capacity, pooling or lead-time effects enter the audit or ROI screen, with no GE description public (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).
Speed_note: Time to market is quoted from the case (10 months from identification to final prototypes vs 12-18 months for castings), but whether the screen uses lead time in its ROI or ranking cannot be confirmed from public sources (The Fabricator 2021; 3DPI 2021).

name: Sandvik-Boliden on-demand printed drill-rig spare parts trial
developer: Sandvik Mining and Rock Solutions with Boliden
description: Proof-of-concept trial installing redesigned metal-printed parts on Boliden drill rigs to test local on-demand supply. The parts are bushes, brackets and drill parts replaced every 3,000-4,000 h. Costs, IP, warranty and liability are listed as open questions.
NRE_note: The trial prints 'a set of specially redesigned components', a case activity whose effort the trial does not use in any stated decision (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
Production_note: Sandvik lists 'What will the costs be?' as an open business-model question the trial is meant to answer, with no figures or method (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
QA_Qual_note: Part performance is to be evaluated in service on Boliden drill rigs as a proof of concept, with warranties and liabilities unresolved and no qualification procedure or gate described (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022; IOM3 2022).
QA_Insp_note: The release and trade reports describe only in-service performance monitoring and do not mention inspection or testing of the printed parts (Sandvik release; IOM3; Metal AM).
Storage_note: Sandvik says it cannot tie up capital to stock all these parts and Boliden cites reduced storage needs, claims that the trial does not use in any stated decision (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
Shared_Capital_note: The accounts leave open who does the printing but do not mention machine investment or how it would be spread, and no fuller trial description is public (Sandvik release; Metal AM).
Shared_Capacity_note: Parts are printed at one Sandvik-managed facility in Italy and who prints in future (OEM, miner or third party) is an open question, so no routing of work across printers or sites is described (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).
Speed_note: Faster supply and 'shorter delivery times' are claimed benefits of local printing, not used in any stated decision (Sandvik news release, Mar 2022).

name: Additive Manufacturing Initial General Assessment (AMIGA)
developer: XSB, Inc. for the Defense Logistics Agency
description: A tool that helps DLA procurement and engineering staff make a quick first call on whether a legacy part 'can be made using Additive Manufacturing, and should it be', using DLA internal and commercial data. It was announced as an extension of XSB's DLA contract. XSB co-authored the 2016 LMI prescreening study, so AMIGA is probably a follow-on (inference).
NRE_note: The XSB release says stakeholders currently evaluate logistics and technical data by hand and AMIGA automates the screen, but it does not say whether technical-data availability, reverse engineering or redesign effort is assessed (XSB press release 2020).
Production_note: Cost from various sources is one of the screening factors, but no cost method or AM cost estimate is documented (XSB press release 2020).
QA_Qual_note: The tool checks where a part will be used to flag critical safety issues affecting AM suitability, a criticality screen with no qualification effort estimated (XSB press release 2020).
QA_Insp_note: The press release does not mention inspection or testing, and the tool's full criteria are not public (XSB press release 2020).
Storage_note: Stocking issues are a screening factor, with no inventory or holding-cost calculation (XSB press release 2020).
Shared_Capital_note: The release says AM machine physical and logistical properties are assessed but does not mention equipment or capital cost, and the internals are not public (XSB press release 2020).
Shared_Capacity_note: The release covers part and machine properties but does not say whether production capacity or sites are considered (XSB press release 2020).
Speed_note: A part's production lead time is a screening factor, but lead time is not computed or valued (XSB press release 2020).

name: Additive Manufacturing Cost and Time (AMCAT) decision tool
year: 2016–2022 (tasked Oct 2016; described as in use in Sept 2022)
developer: Navy Price Fighters (NPF), NAVSUP Weapon Systems Support
description: A web-based cost and time model that compares AM side by side with the existing supply chain, standardizes AM data collection and metric reporting, and produces a business case and ROI. It is calibrated with data from DoD AM production sites. NAVSEA cites the 'Price Fighter AM cost/part tool' as the input to its 'buy or print' Mission Impact Analysis.
NRE_note: Non-recurring engineering, in labour hours and equipment purchases, is an explicit cost category the tool collects from real DoD AM production-site data (navy.mil 2022).
Production_note: The tool outputs a projected AM cost per part ('AM cost/part tool') intended to capture all AM costs, with some inputs named (NRE labour hours, equipment, shipping, contracting, transportation), but material, machine-time and post-processing build-up is not published (navy.mil 2022; NAVSEA NRC briefing slide 6).
QA_Qual_note: Only the Navy article and the NAVSEA briefing describe the tool, and neither says whether qualification or certification costs are included (navy.mil 2022; NAVSEA NRC briefing).
QA_Insp_note: The article names NRE, shipping, contracting and transportation costs but not inspection or testing, and the tool's internals are not public (navy.mil 2022).
Storage_note: The tool compares AM with established supply systems, but neither source says whether inventory holding or storage cost is part of that comparison (navy.mil 2022; NAVSEA NRC briefing).
Shared_Capital_note: Equipment purchases are entered as a cost within NRE from real site data, but whether machine cost is amortised across parts, volume or users is not documented (navy.mil 2022).
Shared_Capacity_note: The tool is built around engineering processes at DoD AM production sites, but the public description does not say whether capacity across those sites is modelled (navy.mil 2022).
Speed_note: The tool is said to 'calculate both AM cost and time' and compare AM with traditional supply chain solutions, but neither the article nor the NAVSEA slides say the computed time is lead time, availability or readiness rather than AM production time, and no lead-time figures or method are given (navy.mil 2022; NAVSEA NRC briefing 2020).

name: Army AI for AM Part Selection (Army SBIR topic A224-001)
developer: Solicited by US Army SBIR program (Solicitation 22.4); no awardee found
description: A requested AI system that analyzes Army technical data to judge whether a component is an AM candidate. Goals include cutting engineering analysis time by up to 80% and expanding the candidate pool. Phase I criteria 'may include Material, Tolerance, Size, System, Supplier, and Item owner'.
NRE_note: The solicitation asks AI to automate engineers' analysis of technical data, cutting analysis time by up to 80%, but does not say whether per-part design or reverse-engineering effort would be estimated, and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
Production_note: The topic automates a 'Can Print / Should Print' analysis but defines no cost criterion among its listed criteria (material, tolerance, size, system, supplier, item owner), and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and certification are not mentioned in the listed criteria or description, though they could enter later phases, and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection and testing are not mentioned, and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
Storage_note: The topic mentions logistics but not inventory, stock or demand, and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
Shared_Capital_note: Equipment or capital cost is not mentioned, and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacity and sites are not mentioned, and no delivered tool is public (Govly listing).
Speed_note: The aim to 'enhance logistics and readiness through increased use of additive manufacturing' is motivation and the 80% figure is engineering analysis time; whether the requested system would use part lead time in its decisions cannot be confirmed from the solicitation, whose example criteria do not include it (Govly listing; Army SBIR topic).

name: Army EXORD 050-18 AM decision tree (risk-based approach for commanders)
year: 2017 (issued December 2017 per DoD IG DODIG-2020-003; described publicly in 2019)
developer: Headquarters, Department of the Army
description: An execution order that covers printer types, price thresholds, uses, limits and approvals for unit-bought printers. It includes a decision tree to help commanders decide when and how to use AM, within policy, training and certification limits. AM parts may be used as temporary replacements until the conventional part arrives.
NRE_note: The EXORD text is not public, and neither the army.mil description nor the DoD IG audit says whether it addresses design, scanning-to-CAD or other engineering effort (army.mil; DODIG-2020-003 p. 8).
Production_note: The descriptions mention printer price thresholds for purchases, not part production cost, and the EXORD itself is not public (army.mil; DODIG-2020-003).
QA_Qual_note: A risk-based gate: commanders use 'a risk-based approach to determine which part to produce using AM', within 'policy, training, and certification limits as defined in the EXORD', with no class-specific requirements described (DODIG-2020-003 p. 8; army.mil).
QA_Insp_note: Army policy under EXORD 050-18 requires that AM parts 'must still meet the performance requirements of its intended use and are analyzed after being used', a required evaluation without method, cost or class-specific scope (DODIG-2020-003 p. 8, fn. 8).
Storage_note: Neither description mentions inventory or stock, and the EXORD text is not public (army.mil; DODIG-2020-003 p. 8).
Shared_Capital_note: The EXORD sets printer types, price thresholds and approvals for unit purchases, but whether printer cost is shared or amortised across parts or units is not described (army.mil).
Shared_Capacity_note: The army.mil article describes multi-echelon AM placement under the Army AM Campaign Plan in separate paragraphs and does not tie it to the EXORD, whose text is not public (army.mil).
Speed_note: Under the policy an AM part serves 'as a temporary replacement until the traditionally manufactured part arrives', a use limit and availability benefit; neither source shows the decision tree using lead time or part availability as a criterion (DODIG-2020-003 p. 8; army.mil).

name: Multi-staged business case analysis for AM part selection (Army Advanced Manufacturing Directive 2019-29 context)
developer: US Army DEVCOM Armaments Center, Quality Engineering and System Assurance Directorate, Advanced Manufacturing Cell (F. Gagliardi, M. Sloane)
description: A proposed staged business case analysis: a strategic/performance review first, then technical analysis of the AM process and end item compared with traditional sources, an activity-based cost assessment (direct and indirect costs, with AM-specific distinctions), and scheduling and supply chain effects.
NRE_note: The strategic stage asks as a guiding question whether the design has been optimised for AM's geometric freedom, but redesign effort is not an input to any stage of the analysis (National Defense viewpoint).
Production_note: A cost evaluation against traditional sources, split into direct and indirect costs, is one of the analysis stages, with no published model or inputs (National Defense viewpoint).
QA_Qual_note: The full viewpoint does not mention qualification, certification or testing; its technical stage covers the AM process and end item only (National Defense viewpoint).
QA_Insp_note: The full viewpoint does not mention inspection (National Defense viewpoint).
Storage_note: Whether parts serve manufacturing lines that have become obsolete is a strategic-driver consideration in the first stage, which decides whether AM is strategically useful before the comparison stages, with no inventory calculation (National Defense viewpoint).
Shared_Capital_note: The full viewpoint mentions AM machines only in a warning against bolting them onto existing processes and does not address their cost or sharing (National Defense viewpoint).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full viewpoint does not address capacity shared across sites or users (National Defense viewpoint).
Speed_note: The scheduling stage requires estimates that 'must account for supply chain variations' from AM's effect on sourcing, manufacturing, shipping, receiving and distribution, described without any calculation (National Defense viewpoint).

name: USAF Candidate AM Part Selection Process (crawl-walk-run)
developer: US Air Force (as reported in the FY2017 DoD AM Report to Congress)
description: A standardized, risk-graded down-select of candidate parts that weighs technical complexity, part size, material, application, economics, lead time and risk. The DoD IG (2019) found the Air Force tracked AM parts in Access and Excel, with engineers and subject-matter experts approving parts.
NRE_note: The Report to Congress lists selection criteria without reverse-engineering or technical-data effort, and the internal process is not public (FY2017 Report to Congress, Section 3.3.5).
Production_note: Economic considerations are a selection criterion within a value-chain approach weighing economic and readiness criteria, with no cost method described (FY2017 Report to Congress, Section 3.3.5).
QA_Qual_note: Risk and component application are screening criteria in a crawl-walk-run down-select that starts with low-risk items, and engineers and SMEs approve parts, with no qualification cost or test sets (FY2017 Report to Congress 3.3.5; DoD IG DODIG-2020-003).
QA_Insp_note: Neither the Report to Congress selection paragraph nor the DoD IG audit describes inspection or testing in the selection process, and the internal process is not public (FY2017 Report to Congress 3.3.5; DoD IG).
Storage_note: The selection criteria include no inventory or stock term and the internal process is not public (FY2017 Report to Congress 3.3.5; DoD IG).
Shared_Capital_note: The selection paragraph does not mention equipment cost, which appears only in separate Innovation Center purchasing policy, and the internal process is not public (FY2017 Report to Congress 3.3.1, 3.3.5).
Shared_Capacity_note: The selection paragraph does not mention capacity or sites, with Innovation Centers at the Air Logistics Complexes described separately, and the internal process is not public (FY2017 Report to Congress 3.3.1, 3.3.5).
Speed_note: Lead time is a named selection criterion and readiness criteria enter the value-chain approach, without quantification (FY2017 Report to Congress, Section 3.3.5).

name: DoD Additive Manufacturing Strategy (2021) decision guidance
developer: OUSD(R&E) / Office of the Secretary of Defense
decision_levels: Part selection; Adopt or make-vs-buy; Capacity placement/sharing
description: A strategy that names considerations without giving a tool. It recommends starting with low-risk, non-critical parts such as support equipment and tooling; calls AM 'well suited for low-volume, out-of-production or long lead time parts'; calls for risk-based qualification; and lists 'cost modeling' as a policy still to be defined.
NRE_note: Reverse engineering for legacy systems, DfAM, standard AM technical data and data access in contracting are named as approaches and goals, but the strategy uses NRE in no decision step (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 5, 6, 9).
Production_note: Reduced manufacturing cost is claimed and cost modeling and cost-benefit analysis are listed as work still to be done, so no cost enters any decision (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 5, 8, 15).
QA_Qual_note: The strategy calls for developing a risk-based, tailorable qualification and certification process that considers consequences of failure and recommends starting with non-critical parts, goals rather than prescribed qualification activities or a gate (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 9, 12).
QA_Insp_note: Standardizing AM inspection and metrology practices, NDI validation and in-situ sensing are called for as future work, and the strategy sets no inspection requirement in any decision (DoD AM Strategy 2021, p. 18).
Storage_note: Reduced obsolete-part risk and DMSMS mitigation are claimed and the RAPTOR and JAMMEX digital part repositories are cited, but stock and obsolescence enter no decision step (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 5, 6, 8, 16).
Shared_Capital_note: Sharing data and standards across the Services is said to 'reduce the time required to develop and certify' and MIIs are called national resources, but no capital or qualification sharing enters any decision (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 11, 16).
Shared_Capacity_note: The strategy states that AM production 'can be distributed and scaled across multiple machines and locations' and calls for networked machines, a vision with no assignment of work across sites (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 5, 17).
Speed_note: The statement that AM is 'currently well suited for low-volume, out-of-production or long lead time parts' is an assessment rather than a selection rule, and reduced time-to-use is claimed without entering any decision (DoD AM Strategy 2021, pp. 5, 9, 12).

name: UK Defence Advanced Manufacturing Strategy decision principles
developer: UK Ministry of Defence
description: Strategy that tells MoD to weigh the cost of lost availability against the cost of a part, builds a digital thread from design libraries to production sites, and sets certified production capabilities feeding mobile production 'spokes' near the point of use.
NRE_note: The strategy describes parts designed for AM from the outset or reverse engineered when no longer available and calls for policy favouring AM at the design stage, but sets no decision step that uses design or reverse-engineering effort (GOV.UK strategy, Sections 4 and 7.2).
Production_note: The strategy notes that cost comparisons are still made back to the traditionally made part and proposes considering the cost of loss of availability against the cost of a part, but as an action with no method or criterion, so part cost enters no decision rule (GOV.UK strategy, Section 7.7).
QA_Qual_note: The strategy requires AM items accepted into the defence inventory to pass the same scrutiny as conventional ones and aims for production capabilities qualified against unnamed international standards, but prescribes no qualification activities or gate of its own (GOV.UK strategy, Sections 4, 7.2 and 7.5).
QA_Insp_note: Full strategy read; AM items must pass 'the same levels of scrutiny' as conventional items to enter the inventory, but inspection, non-destructive testing or acceptance testing are not named or costed (GOV.UK strategy, Section 7.2).
Storage_note: The strategy says AM is enabled by a digitised inventory and calls for policy driving a 'strategically selected digital inventory' against a 1.3M-item physical inventory, but gives no selection criteria and stock enters no decision (GOV.UK strategy, Sections 5, 7.6 and 8.2).
Shared_Capital_note: Full strategy read; it notes most unit AM machines lack through-life support and proposes commoditised equipment supply, but does not discuss spreading machine investment across parts or users (GOV.UK strategy, Section 7.5).
Shared_Capacity_note: The strategy describes a hub-and-spoke network of certified industry production capabilities and dispersed qualified suppliers feeding mobile production near the point of use, a concept that assigns no work across sites (GOV.UK strategy, Sections 4 and 5).
Speed_note: The strategy names inventory items with excessive lead times as targets, proposes weighing the cost of loss of availability against part cost and assumes reduced lead times, but gives no method, threshold or figures, so lead time enters no decision rule (GOV.UK strategy, Sections 5, 7.1 and 7.7).

name: RAPiD-e Additive Manufacturing Digital Repository Concept and Framework
developer: NATO Allied Command Transformation (contracted study)
description: Four-month study to define a secure repository for storing, searching and licensing 3D-printable part data among Allies; bidders to stratify equipment by security level and propose proof-of-concept items.
NRE_note: The ACT notice asks for a repository concept for secure storage and sharing of technical data packages and does not say whether design or reverse-engineering effort is covered; the study deliverables are not public (ACT NOI 022062; FBO notice).
Production_note: The UK export notice asks bidders to 'confirm, delimit or reject ACT's presumption of the viability of the business proposition', a business check of the repository concept rather than per-part production costing, and the deliverables are not public (defenceonline/UK export notice; ACT NOI).
QA_Qual_note: Neither notice nor the NSPA follow-on article mentions part qualification or certification, and the study outputs are not public (ACT NOI; FBO; defence-industry.eu).
QA_Insp_note: Neither notice nor the NSPA follow-on article mentions inspection, and the study outputs are not public (ACT NOI; FBO; defence-industry.eu).
Storage_note: The repository is for 'secure storage and sharing of digital technical data packages for NATO and nations' and the UK notice mentions 'the potential for a digital warehouse with the 3D printing of parts on demand', a digital-inventory concept; whether it uses stock in any decision cannot be confirmed from the solicitation (ACT NOI 022062; defenceonline/UK export notice).
Shared_Capital_note: Neither notice nor the follow-on article mentions machine investment or sharing (ACT NOI; FBO; defence-industry.eu).
Shared_Capacity_note: The NSPA follow-on describes a platform where 'nations and industry can collaborate, request and share files' and reports NSPA printing a British Army file on-site at Denmark's request, but no source shows the repository assigning or routing print work (defence-industry.eu 2023; ACT NOI).
Speed_note: The notice frames the repository around 'an in-field production capability for NATO operations' and the follow-on cites printing spare parts 'on-site and on-demand', availability claims; whether lead time enters any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (ACT NOI; defence-industry.eu 2023).

name: Re-design and re-manufacturing methodology for discontinued Bundeswehr spares
developer: Montero, Paetzold, Bleckmann, Holtmannspoetter (affiliations not shown on fetched page); case from the German Federal Armed Forces
description: Methodology for handling data across reverse engineering, redesign and AM production of a discontinued spare, shown on a Bundeswehr case. Decision-level fit is weak; it is a workflow for the NRE step.
NRE_note: The method is itself the reverse-engineering and redesign workflow (laser scanning, point-cloud repair, feature recognition, redesign, verification against the scan, STL hand-over), but it makes no decision in which that effort is an input and gives no hours or cost (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
Production_note: Full paper read; production on the SLM 125 is described but no production cost, machine time or material cost is given or modelled (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
QA_Qual_note: Full paper read; part approval, certification or airworthiness sign-off is not discussed, only that manufacturing verifies the construction is viable (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
QA_Insp_note: Full paper read; the only check compares the redesigned CAD model with the scan point cloud (about 0.1 mm deviation), and the printed part is not inspected or tested (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
Storage_note: The paper motivates on-demand AM because such spares are rarely in the warehouse and notes that repeat orders need only the STL file, but stock does not enter the method (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
Shared_Capital_note: Full paper read; equipment is only listed, and machine investment or its sharing across parts or units is not addressed (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
Shared_Capacity_note: Full paper read; deployed designers send STL files to a manufacturing department, a single hand-off with no pooled capacity or network (DESIGN 2018 full paper).
Speed_note: The method is motivated by deployed equipment idle for lack of a spare and claims AM 'saves a lot of time in the logistics process' overseas, but lead time or downtime does not enter the method (DESIGN 2018 full paper).

name: AM spare part candidate identification for Danish defence logistics (FMI)
year: Unknown (poster undated; the resulting SDU PhD thesis was defended in August 2023)
developer: University of Southern Denmark (J. Foshammer, PhD project) with FMI
description: PhD project to identify spare part candidates with the highest AM potential to build a feasible business case, studying how data literacy shapes the selection method and building knowledge sharing within FMI.
NRE_note: The thesis abstract says identified parts come out 'for redesign or 1:1 substitution' depending on participants' design or supply-chain background, a finding about participants rather than a use of redesign effort to decide, and whether NRE enters selection cannot be confirmed from the abstract (Foshammer PhD thesis abstract, SDU 2023).
Production_note: The poster aims at 'a feasible AM business case' and the thesis abstract at 'solid business cases', but neither abstract shows whether per-part production cost is assessed, and the IJPE full text was bot-blocked on both open repositories (SDU poster; thesis abstract; Foshammer et al. 2022 abstract).
QA_Qual_note: None of the poster, thesis abstract, project page or IJPE abstract mentions qualification or certification, and the full paper with the AHP criteria could not be reached (Foshammer et al. 2022 abstract).
QA_Insp_note: No reachable source mentions inspection or testing, and the full paper with the AHP criteria could not be reached (Foshammer et al. 2022 abstract).
Storage_note: The poster mentions decommissioning 'obsolete equipment and material' and USAF obsolete B-52 spares as context, but no reachable source shows whether inventory effects are assessed by the identification method (SDU poster).
Shared_Capital_note: No reachable source mentions printer investment, amortisation or sharing, and the full paper could not be reached (poster; thesis abstract; project page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Mapping 'printers and capabilities throughout the DMoD' and building an organisation to use them are planned project steps, a network concept, and whether the selection method uses shared capacity cannot be confirmed from public sources (SDU project page).
Speed_note: Improved soldier uptime is an expected benefit and a US Navy case of lead time cut 'from days /weeks to hours' is quoted as background, and whether the method uses lead time to select parts cannot be confirmed from public sources (SDU poster).

name: Maritime defence AM part suitability framework (Austal/Curtin/AMCRC)
developer: Austal (lead), Curtin University, Additive Manufacturing Cooperative Research Centre (AMCRC)
