description: Develops a streamlined acceptance framework for AM products and a joint common framework for Qualified Parts/Manufacturers List specifications across 'JAMA risk categories'.
NRE_note: The NCMS announcements and DLA notice describe acceptance, source approval and QPL/QML work but do not say whether design or engineering preparation effort is treated (NCMS JAMA Phase II and III pages; DLA JAMA IV notice).
Production_note: Partners supply 'supply chain, cost analysis, and engineering technical expertise' and Phase III targets the cost of the acceptance process, but no source says whether per-part production cost is treated (NCMS Phase II; Phase III).
QA_Qual_note: The framework builds QPL/QML specifications 'across the JAMA risk categories', which DLA describes from Category 0 (no risk) to Category 3 (severe risk, e.g. CSI) with vendors needing qualification, so the category sets the qualification path, but no class-specific test counts are public (NCMS Phase II and III; DLA JAMA IV notice).
QA_Insp_note: The Phase II announcement does not mention inspection or testing, the later 'Quality Assurance and Testing' workstream is only a title, and the DLA notice's 'first article inspection (FAI) data may be required' is first-article work from a parts buy, so per-part inspection is not established (NCMS Phase II and III pages; DLA notice SP4701-24-I-MH01).
Storage_note: The documented scope, an AM product-acceptance and source-approval framework feeding QPL/QML specifications, plainly excludes spare-part inventory, and no announcement or the DLA notice mentions stock (NCMS JAMA pages; DLA notice).
Shared_Capital_note: A joint common framework for Qualified Parts and Manufacturers Lists, so one approval serves many procurements, is the project's stated objective; the announcements do not show reuse of approvals applied as a rule, and give no numbers (NCMS Phase II and III).
Shared_Capacity_note: The framework expedites approval of commercial AM vendors and JAMA IV invites many vendors to bid, but no source describes pooling or redirecting capacity (NCMS Phase III; DLA notice).
Speed_note: The initiative aims to 'reduce the overall cost, lead time and failure rates of the product acceptance process', a claimed saving in acceptance time with no figures, and nothing shows part lead time used in a decision (NCMS Phase III).

name: Siemens NX Parts Order Management (AM and CNC job costing/quoting)
year: Current product page (2026). The URL of the 2018 Siemens Additive Manufacturing Network now 302-redirects here; Siemens does not state the relationship.
developer: Siemens Digital Industries Software
description: Order-management software for RFQs, configurable pricing and quoting, and order tracking across internal production and external sourcing. It claims 'flexible cost calculations to accurately price CNC machining and additive manufacturing jobs'. No AM-specific cost function was found in Teamcenter Product Cost Management or NX AM.
NRE_note: The product page says cost elements are customisable across quote templates but does not say whether engineering or setup effort is included, and no product documentation was found (Siemens Parts Order Management page).
Production_note: The page claims cost calculations to price AM and CNC jobs with customised cost elements, but the inputs and method are not documented (Siemens Parts Order Management page).
QA_Qual_note: The product page does not mention qualification or certification, and no documentation was found (Siemens Parts Order Management page).
QA_Insp_note: The product page does not mention inspection; quality control and quality reports appear only on the older Siemens AM Network supplier page, whose relationship to this product Siemens does not state (Siemens POM page; AM Network page).
Storage_note: Parts Order Management handles RFQs, quotes and order tracking for a manufacturer, so spare-part inventory is plainly outside its documented scope (Siemens Parts Order Management page).
Shared_Capital_note: The product page does not say whether machine rates, depreciation or utilisation enter the cost calculations (Siemens Parts Order Management page).
Shared_Capacity_note: The page offers visibility of order progress across internal production and external sourcing and in-shop scheduling, but describes no pooling of print capacity or redirection of work between sites, and the 'printer allocation' feature appears only on the older AM Network page whose link to this product is unstated (Siemens Parts Order Management page; AM Network page).
Speed_note: The page speaks of staying aligned with delivery commitments and on-time production, but does not say whether lead or build times are estimated (Siemens Parts Order Management page).

name: Mitterbaur (TU Wien) data-driven spare-part identification for AM from digitized legacy drawings
developer: M. Mitterbaur (advisor F. Ansari; co-advisor T. Madreiter), TU Wien Institute of Management Sciences
description: Uses deep-learning object detection and text recognition plus image processing to find title blocks and BOM tables in scanned drawings, convert them to a spreadsheet, and extract printability-relevant attributes. Assemblies and standard parts are then filtered out to shortlist AM spare-part candidates. Evaluated on an industrial use case.
NRE_note: The thesis discusses reverse engineering a legacy part (a railway example produced in four weeks) and its tool digitises title-block and BOM tables from legacy drawings, but it creates no design files and uses no design or reverse-engineering effort as a criterion (thesis full text, Sect. 1.1-1.2).
Production_note: AM cost savings are claimed in the benefits section (e.g. a literature case cutting procurement cost from EUR 100 to EUR 1), but the demonstrator applies no cost criterion and financial characteristics are left to future work (thesis full text, Sect. 4.10, 5.1).
QA_Qual_note: The full thesis applies no qualification or criticality criterion; its filters exclude only standard parts and assemblies (thesis full text, Sect. 4.6.3, 4.8, 5.1).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is not addressed; the extracted attributes are weight, materials, standards, tolerances and surface properties (thesis full text, Sect. 4.8).
Storage_note: Reduced inventory from printing spares on demand is claimed as motivation and benefit, but no stock or inventory criterion is applied and supply-chain characteristics are future work (thesis abstract; Sect. 4.10, 5.1).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine capital or its sharing is not addressed in the full thesis; capital appears only as inventory binding capital (thesis full text, Sect. 2.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: The full thesis has no capacity, pooling or network element beyond a passing claim about decentralised production (thesis full text; reposiTUm abstract).
Speed_note: Shorter lead times from on-demand AM are claimed and a literature figure of up to 67% lead-time reduction is quoted, but no time criterion is applied in the filter (thesis full text, Sect. 1.1, 4.10).

name: DoDI 5000.93 Use of Additive Manufacturing in the DoD (Change 1, July 6, 2021)
developer: OUSD(R&E) (approved by Barbara McQuiston); incorporates and cancels DTM-19-006
earlier_versions: DTM-19-006 'Interim Policy and Guidance for the Use of Additive Manufacturing (AM) in Support of Materiel Sustainment' (March 21, 2019): interim directive-type memorandum, incorporated and cancelled by DoDI 5000.93. | DoDI 5000.93 original issuance (June 10, 2021): Change 1 (July 6, 2021) only removed a duplicate responsibility entry in paragraph 2.3.
description: The instruction requires a 'risk-informed approach' but prescribes no decision method, scoring model or cost-benefit tool. Maintenance activities must 'consider and evaluate AM's technical and economic practicality.' Contracts should identify parts that 'are, or could be, produced using AM.' Organizations that share approved AM data across organizations must adopt JAMMEX.
NRE_note: The instruction directs acquiring only the AM data and license rights needed and flagging AM-capable parts in the bill of materials, but it prescribes no decision method and TDP creation or reverse engineering enters no decision (DoDI 5000.93, §§3.1.c, 3.1.d, 3.4).
Production_note: Maintenance activities must 'consider and evaluate' AM's economic practicality, but the instruction gives no method or criterion, so per-part cost is not used in any decision it prescribes (DoDI 5000.93, §3.3.c).
QA_Qual_note: Requires policies to define the level of qualification, certification, risk evaluation and approval authority for using an AM part, with no class-specific activities or costs (DoDI 5000.93, §3.2.a).
QA_Insp_note: AM data must include testing requirements and acceptance or rejection criteria and parts must meet established quality control criteria, with no cost or class-specific inspection scope (DoDI 5000.93, §§3.1.b(2), 3.2.d).
Storage_note: JAMMEX is set up as a repository for approved AM data and AM part data and demand must flow to DLA for cataloguing, records that the instruction does not use to decide stock (DoDI 5000.93, §§2.4.d, 3.3.g(1), (4), (7)).
Shared_Capital_note: Full instruction read: equipment appears only in industrial-base assessment and data-system terms, and sharing machines or spreading capital across users is not addressed (DoDI 5000.93, §§2.3.e, 3.5).
Shared_Capacity_note: The instruction directs organizations to leverage organic AM capabilities, answer AM part-sourcing requests, list proven sources and keep capacity available, a policy description of a sourcing network that assigns no work and sets no capacity rule (DoDI 5000.93, §§2.3.e, 3.3.b, 3.3.g(2), (6)).
Speed_note: Quick manufacture 'consistent with demand urgency' and readiness in contingency or combat environments are stated aims, and no lead time or urgency criterion enters a decision step (DoDI 5000.93, §§2.5.a, 3.3.b).

name: NASA In-Space Manufacturing spares-logistics case (MSFC briefings citing Owens & de Weck 2016 and Cirillo et al. 2011)
developer: NASA Marshall Space Flight Center In-Space Manufacturing (ISM) project (R. G. Clinton Jr.; T. Prater, N. Werkheiser, F. Ledbetter), citing analyses by Owens & de Weck (2016) and Cirillo et al. (2011)
description: NASA's case for ISM rests on spares logistics. About 95% of corrective spares will never be used, and about 3,000 kg/yr of upmass compares with about 18,000 kg of ground spares ready to fly. Cited analyses report spares-mass cuts of 78.3% (ISM plus recycling) and 97.7% (the Owens & de Weck case). For a fluid-flow parts case, about one-third of components were assumed printable in space. No other NASA cost or part-selection tool was found besides NASA-STD-6030, which is scored elsewhere.
NRE_note: The underlying analysis notes only that component redesign for ISM 'may also be explored' and the briefings are silent, so design work does not enter the spares-mass analysis (Owens & de Weck 2016, Sec. V.D).
Production_note: The full underlying analysis has no cost metrics (outputs are logistics mass and crew risk, with feedstock mass rather than part cost) and the briefings give no per-part cost; Cirillo et al. was not opened (Owens & de Weck 2016; Clinton 2017).
QA_Qual_note: Developing an on-orbit, in-process certification process is a roadmap item and spaceflight-environment testing is noted as a need, but qualification does not enter the spares-logistics analysis (Clinton 2017 slide 8; Owens & de Weck 2016).
QA_Insp_note: ISM specimens are inspected by structured-light scanning (+/-12.7 um), CT and ASTM D638 tensile tests and in-process NDE is a stated need, but inspection does not enter the spares-logistics analysis (Prater et al. 2018; Clinton 2017).
Storage_note: The underlying analysis optimises spares holdings to a target probability of sufficiency and computes logistics mass with and without ISM (17,232 kg traditional, 12,323 kg with ISM, 11,254 kg with ISM and recycling), reported in the briefings (Owens & de Weck 2016 Sec. IV.B; Clinton 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: The spares analysis excludes the mass of the ISM system and addresses no printer cost or sharing, and the only related text is a project-overview description of the AMF as 'a commercial, multi-user facility'; Cirillo et al. was not opened (Owens & de Weck 2016 Sec. IV; Prater et al. 2018).
Shared_Capacity_note: The spares analysis does not address printer capacity, print time or queueing (its common pool is feedstock material, not printer capacity), and the briefings only call the AMF a multi-user facility; Cirillo et al. was not opened (Owens & de Weck 2016 Sec. IV.A.1; Prater et al. 2018).
Speed_note: The underlying analysis computes probability of sufficiency (spares available when failures occur) and its crew-risk contribution, showing ISM cuts median P(LoC) contribution from 0.0270 to 0.0167 (33% printable) and 0.0084 (50%) (Owens & de Weck 2016 Sec. II.C, IV, Table 1).

name: Meisel et al. decision support for AM deployment in remote or austere environments (tiered-funnel machine/material selector)
developer: Nicholas A. Meisel, Christopher B. Williams, Kimberly P. Ellis, Don Taylor. Affiliations are not shown in the record opened; C. B. Williams is Virginia Tech per the LMI/DLA entry.
description: An interview-derived framework for deployable AM. User constraints fall into process, machine, part, material, environmental and logistical categories, and these feed a 'tiered funnel' tool that narrows a database of candidate machines and materials. The paper calls itself a 'user-driven tool for selecting a process and material'. Scores are from the abstract only.
NRE_note: Only the abstract is available (Emerald paywall, no open copy), and it does not say whether design or engineering effort is a funnel criterion (British Library record; Emerald abstract).
Production_note: The abstract lists process, machine, part, material, environmental and logistical constraint categories but does not say whether machine, material or part cost is a funnel attribute (British Library record; Emerald abstract).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract does not say whether qualification or part-quality requirements are funnel criteria, and the full text is unavailable (British Library record).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract does not mention inspection and the full text is unavailable (British Library record).
Storage_note: The paper's premise is that deployable AM can shorten the supply chain by making an array of spare parts from a single raw-material source, motivation that the abstract does not show entering the tiered-funnel machine and material selection (British Library record abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The abstract does not mention equipment cost or sharing and the full text is unavailable (British Library record).
Shared_Capacity_note: A logistical constraint category exists, but the abstract does not say whether capacity across sites is considered and the full text is unavailable (British Library record).
Speed_note: The abstract does not say whether build time or time to part is a criterion, and the full text is unavailable (British Library record).

name: Draudt AFIT Advanced Intermediate Manufacturing (AIM) facility supply-chain simulation
developer: Eric S. Draudt, Air Force Institute of Technology (advisor Frank W. Ciarallo)
description: An anyLogistix simulation comparing the current supply chain with single, dual and quadruple AIM facilities and with high, medium and low utilization. A single facility cuts lead time from over 800 days to about 104 days. The thesis recommends starting with one facility to keep investment costs under control.
NRE_note: Only the abstract could be read (the AFIT PDF link returns a client error and no other copy was found); it does not mention engineering, reverse engineering or technical data (AFIT Scholar record).
Production_note: Only the abstract could be read; it mentions investment costs but not production cost per part (AFIT Scholar record).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not mention qualification or certification (AFIT Scholar record).
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not mention inspection or testing (AFIT Scholar record).
Storage_note: Only the abstract could be read; it does not say whether inventory is modelled in the anyLogistix supply-chain simulation (AFIT Scholar record).
Shared_Capital_note: The abstract recommends starting with one AIM facility to keep investment costs under control, an author conclusion; whether the simulation itself uses facility capital cost cannot be confirmed from the abstract (AFIT Scholar record).
Shared_Capacity_note: The simulation varies the number of AIM facilities (one, two or four) and three utilisation-driven demand cases, but the abstract does not show parts contending for shared facility capacity or that capacity, rather than production location, drives the lead-time result, and the full thesis PDF could not be opened (AFIT Scholar etd/7712 abstract).
Speed_note: Lead time is a simulated output, falling from over 800 days to about 104 days with one AIM facility (AFIT Scholar abstract).

name: Holmström et al. rapid-manufacturing capacity-deployment alternatives for spare parts
developer: Jan Holmström, Jouni Partanen, Jukka Tuomi, Manfred Walter
description: A conceptual comparison of centralized rapid-manufacturing (RM) deployment by OEMs with distributed deployment near the point of use by generalist service providers. One variant replaces regional distribution-center inventory with AM capacity. Distributed RM could improve service and cut inventory at the same time, but centralized OEM deployment is judged most feasible. RM spares supply is feasible only in particular situations because few parts can be made. Khajavi et al. (2018) note the authors did not use a case study to show which alternatives are feasible.
NRE_note: Only the abstract and two secondary descriptions could be read (full text paywalled), and none mention design or engineering effort (Emerald abstract; Khajavi et al. 2018; Abidar & Chaabane review).
Production_note: A review classes the paper as qualitative with production cost as its decision variable, but no cost calculation or rule is reported, so whether the comparison applies production cost in a decision cannot be confirmed from the abstract and secondary sources (Abidar & Chaabane review, Table 2, Sec. 8).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract and secondary descriptions do not mention qualification, which could be discussed in the paywalled text (Emerald abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract and secondary descriptions do not mention inspection, and the full text was not available (Emerald abstract).
Storage_note: Replacing regional distribution-centre inventory with AM capacity is one conceptual alternative and 'simultaneously improved service and reduced inventory' is a claimed outcome, so whether the comparison uses stock in a decision cannot be confirmed from the abstract (Emerald abstract; Khajavi et al. 2018).
Shared_Capital_note: The authors conclude that decentralized deployment is feasible when AM machine capacity utilization is high, a finding rather than a rule the comparison applies, and the full text was not read (Khajavi et al. 2018 describing Holmström et al.).
Shared_Capacity_note: The paper conceptually compares centralized OEM capacity with point-of-use capacity run by generalist service providers, without a model or case, so whether capacity deployment drives any decision rule cannot be confirmed from the abstract (Emerald abstract; Khajavi et al. 2018).
Speed_note: Improved service from point-of-use deployment is claimed conceptually, and whether lead time or availability enters any decision cannot be confirmed from the abstract (Emerald abstract).

name: Sirichakwal & Conner AM spare-parts inventory model
developer: I. Sirichakwal, B. Conner (affiliations not verified)
description: According to Knofius et al. (2021), the model assumes AM reduces holding costs and lead times and evaluates the effect on stock-out probability. It finds that 'holding cost reductions typically reduce the stock-out probability'. It does not consider cost, so the monetary effect is unclear.
NRE_note: The paper was not opened and neither Knofius description says whether design or engineering effort is modelled (Knofius et al. 2021; Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2).
Production_note: The paper was not opened; Knofius says the authors 'do not consider cost', yet the model uses holding costs and is said to show positive effects on total inventory costs, so whether AM unit production cost appears is not established (Knofius et al. 2021; Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2).
QA_Qual_note: The paper was not opened and neither Knofius description says whether qualification is addressed (Knofius et al. 2021; Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2).
QA_Insp_note: The paper was not opened and neither Knofius description says whether inspection is addressed (Knofius et al. 2021; Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2).
Storage_note: Per Knofius, the model applies a continuous-review base-stock policy at a single stockpoint in which AM's holding-cost and lead-time reductions change the stock kept (lower holding costs mean more stock; integer stock levels shift), so stock levels are computed, though not monetised (Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2; Knofius et al. 2021).
Shared_Capital_note: The paper was not opened and neither Knofius description says whether equipment investment is addressed (Knofius et al. 2021; Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: The paper was not opened and neither Knofius description says whether AM capacity is modelled (Knofius et al. 2021; Knofius 2018, sec. 1.4.2).
Speed_note: Stock-out probability, an availability measure, is the evaluated output, driven by AM-imposed production lead times and holding-cost changes (Knofius 2018 thesis, sec. 1.4.2; Knofius et al. 2021).

name: Kunovjanek & Reiner AM diffusion and raw-material inventory model
developer: Maximilian Kunovjanek, Gerald Reiner
description: A dynamic evaluation model that uses the Bass diffusion model to estimate how AM adoption changes raw-material inventories. AM can cut raw-material inventory by about 4%, and the speed of diffusion depends on the technology's utility. It is not a spare-parts model. The user may instead mean Kunovjanek et al. (2020), 'Additive manufacturing and supply chains – a systematic review', which Abidar & Chaabane cite.
NRE_note: Only the abstract is public (paywalled paper, no open copy found) and it does not say whether design or engineering effort enters the model (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
Production_note: The abstract says AM uses raw material only where needed but does not describe whether per-part production cost is computed (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract is public and it does not mention qualification (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract is public and it does not mention inspection (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
Storage_note: The dynamic model quantifies AM's effect on inventory (raw-material stock about 4% lower as AM diffuses), but the stock is feedstock reduced through lower material use, not spare parts printed on demand (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract is public and it does not say whether equipment investment or its sharing is modelled (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Only the abstract is public and it does not mention capacity or pooling (IDEAS/RePEc abstract).
Speed_note: Only the abstract is public; a dynamic supply-chain model could include lead times, but neither the abstract nor the university summaries say so (IDEAS/RePEc abstract; AAU news item).

name: Chekurov et al. perceived value of AM digital spare parts (focus groups and a conceptual distribution network)
developer: Sergei Chekurov, Sini Metsä-Kortelainen, Mika Salmi, Irene Roda, Ari Jussila. Related to the VTT/Aalto DIVA project scored elsewhere; individual affiliations not verified.
description: Checks the literature's claimed benefits of digital spare parts against industry experience. It surfaces post-processing needs, supplier quality parity, and ICT and file-format gaps, and builds a conceptual distribution network for digital spare parts. OEMs estimated that 2–75% of their spare-parts libraries could be printed, with most estimates at 5–10%. The paper concludes that long-tail parts are deployable now.
NRE_note: 3D model unavailability, file version management and imprecise scanning are raised by participants as obstacles implying more modelling work, but the study uses NRE in no decision step (Chekurov et al. 2018, sec. 4.3 Table 6).
Production_note: High AM machine-hour and material cost is an obstacle that participants judged offset for long-tail parts by lower warehousing and transport costs, a focus-group view that enters no decision step (Chekurov et al. 2018, Table 6, sec. 7).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification and certification for spare-part production, material approval per application and supplier quality parity are raised as barriers, with no qualification step in any decision (Chekurov et al. 2018, sec. 1.1, Table 1).
QA_Insp_note: States, citing literature, that for the strictest applications each material batch needs quality verification, and participants raised variable quality between machines as an obstacle, but inspection enters no decision step (Chekurov et al. 2018, sec. 1.1, Table 6).
Storage_note: Lower inventory and holding cost is confirmed by participants as a perceived benefit, which the study does not use in any decision (Chekurov et al. 2018, Table 7, sec. 6).
Shared_Capital_note: Participants proposed a service centre jointly owned by OEMs that centralises machinery and sells machine time to smaller companies, an idea with no numbers or decision rule (Chekurov et al. 2018, sec. 4.5).
Shared_Capacity_note: A conceptual distribution network (administrator, AM service providers, maintenance site) with a preferred international service-bureau network is built from participant input, a diagram that does not assign work (Chekurov et al. 2018, sec. 4.5, Fig. 1).
Speed_note: Shorter delivery and repair times from distributed manufacturing are confirmed by participants as perceived benefits, which the study does not use in any decision (Chekurov et al. 2018, Table 7, sec. 6).

name: Durão et al. distributed AM spare-parts production use cases (Germany–Brazil network)
developer: Luiz Fernando C. S. Durão, Alexander Christ, Eduardo Zancul, Reiner Anderl, Klaus Schützer
description: A use-case study of how centralization and independence change between a central factory and a distributed AM site. Connected technologies created a flexible, focused factory near the client, with specialization kept at the central factory. Work organization, network performance and IP protection are also evaluated.
NRE_note: Design and engineering in Germany supply the product model to the Brazilian AM site and information exchange is named as the main challenge, a description of the network; whether engineering effort enters any decision cannot be confirmed from the abstracts (2017 abstract; 2016 companion abstract).
Production_note: Only abstracts were readable (the 2017 full text is paywalled); they cite falling AM machine and material costs and lower logistics costs but do not say whether part production cost is analysed (2017 abstract; 2016 companion abstract).
QA_Qual_note: Only abstracts were readable, and neither mentions qualification of parts, materials or processes beyond a vague reference to standards challenges (2017 abstract; 2016 companion abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The companion paper names quality control across distributed sites as a main challenge, a barrier; whether inspection enters the use-case evaluation cannot be confirmed from the abstract (2016 companion abstract, Procedia CIRP 57).
Storage_note: The companion paper claims distributed AM may reduce inventory where inventory and logistics costs are high, with no quantification; whether stock enters the evaluation cannot be confirmed from the abstract (2016 companion abstract, Procedia CIRP 57).
Shared_Capital_note: Only abstracts were readable; they say the Brazilian site provides the machines and that machine costs are falling, but not whether machine investment or its sharing is analysed (2016 companion abstract; 2017 abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: The study characterises centralisation and independence between a central factory and a distributed AM site across four use cases, a description of network configurations; whether work is allocated across sites in any decision cannot be confirmed from the abstract (2017 abstract).
Speed_note: Shorter delivery lead time from producing near the client is the stated motivation; whether lead time is used in the evaluation cannot be confirmed from the abstract (2017 abstract).

name: Muir & Haddud AM impact on spare-parts inventory performance (mechanical engineering and medical industries)
developer: M. Muir, A. Haddud (affiliations not verified)
description: Investigates 'the possible impact of AM adoption on inventory performance and customer satisfaction in a spare parts supply chain' and concludes that 'AM has the potential to improve a firm's inventory performance' (Abidar & Chaabane). It is cited for lead-time and inventory-cost reduction as AM objectives (Durham review). The research method was not verified.
NRE_note: The paper could not be opened and the two reviews that describe it do not say whether design or engineering effort is addressed (Durham review; Abidar & Chaabane review).
Production_note: The reviews attribute only inventory and customer-satisfaction findings, so whether production cost is addressed cannot be established without the paper (Abidar & Chaabane review).
QA_Qual_note: The two reviews do not say whether qualification is addressed, and the paper could not be opened (Durham review).
QA_Insp_note: The two reviews do not say whether inspection is addressed, and the paper could not be opened (Durham review).
Storage_note: The reported finding that AM can improve a firm's inventory performance is the authors' conclusion as cited in reviews, and whether the study's method uses stock or inventory data cannot be confirmed from secondary sources (Abidar & Chaabane review; Durham review).
Shared_Capital_note: The reviews do not say whether equipment investment or sharing is addressed, and the paper could not be opened (Durham review).
Shared_Capacity_note: The reviews do not say whether shared capacity is addressed, and the paper could not be opened (Durham review).
Speed_note: One review attributes inventory performance and customer satisfaction to the study and the other cites it in a group placed after 'inventory cost reduction', so neither shows that lead time or availability is addressed, and the paper could not be opened (Abidar & Chaabane review Sec. 2.2; Durham review Sec. 5).

name: Zanoni et al. supply chain implications of AM: case-study synthesis
developer: Simone Zanoni, Milad Ashourpour, Andrea Bacchetti, Massimo Zanardini, Marco Perona (University of Brescia)
description: Synthesizes qualitative and quantitative cases to argue that AM must be assessed across every supply chain stage and lifecycle phase (design, preparation, production, use). It finds that AM vs conventional comparisons are 'exhaustive only when all features of productions and logistics networks are evaluated simultaneously'.
NRE_note: The synthesis discusses AM's consequences for the design and preparation phases across its cases, but the abstract shows no rule using one-time engineering effort, so its role cannot be confirmed (Springer abstract; IRIS UNIBS abstract).
Production_note: The collection includes quantitative cases benchmarking AM against conventional technologies, case results the synthesis reports; whether it applies any production-cost rule cannot be confirmed from the abstract (Springer abstract, keywords).
QA_Qual_note: Only the abstract was readable (IRIS full text restricted), and it does not say whether qualification is assessed (Springer abstract; IRIS UNIBS record).
QA_Insp_note: Only the abstract was readable, and it does not say whether inspection is assessed (Springer abstract).
Storage_note: Only the abstract was readable; it covers every supply chain stage and cites spare-parts inventory studies, but does not say whether inventory effects are assessed (Springer abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: Only the abstract was readable, and it does not say whether equipment investment or sharing is assessed (Springer abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Only the abstract was readable; it calls for joint evaluation of production and logistics networks but does not say whether capacity sharing across sites is assessed (Springer abstract).
Speed_note: Only the abstract was readable, and it does not say whether lead time is assessed (Springer abstract).

name: Ashour Pour et al. (2019) JELS model of AM in a two-level supply chain
developer: Milad Ashour Pour, Simone Zanoni, Andrea Bacchetti, Massimo Zanardini, Marco Perona (University of Brescia)
earlier_versions: 'Additive Manufacturing Supply Chain: Modeling and Performance Evaluation' (2016), Nineteenth International Working Seminar on Production Economics, vol. 3, pp. 25-36: conference version of the same JELS model, adding discussion of centralized vs decentralized manufacturing; the journal article was first published online in 2017.
description: A JELS analytic model that compares traditional and AM supply chains using the same parameters, from inventory and logistics standpoints. The 2016 proceedings version also gives insights on centralized vs decentralized manufacturing. A review table classifies 'Ashour Pour et al. (2017)' as an analytical total-cost model: homogeneous demand; holding, stock-carrying, ordering and transport costs; traditional vs centralized AM. It reports that 'AM adoption adds flexibility'. A related paper, Ashour Pour & Zanoni (2017, Procedia Manufacturing 11:610–618), covers merging components with AM in spare-parts management; it is not scored because only its keywords were seen.
NRE_note: Only the abstracts and a review table were readable (full texts restricted), and they do not say whether design or engineering costs are in the model (IRIS UniBS records; Abidar and Chaabane preprint).
Production_note: The review table lists only holding, stock-carrying, ordering and transport costs, and whether production cost terms enter the JELS model cannot be seen without the restricted full text (Abidar and Chaabane preprint; IRIS UniBS records).
QA_Qual_note: The abstracts and review table do not mention qualification and the full text is restricted (IRIS UniBS records; Abidar and Chaabane preprint).
QA_Insp_note: The abstracts and review table do not mention inspection and the full text is restricted (IRIS UniBS records; Abidar and Chaabane preprint).
Storage_note: The JELS model assesses AM adoption from an inventory and logistics standpoint, computing total cost from holding, stock-carrying, ordering and transport costs for traditional versus AM supply chains (IRIS UniBS abstract; Abidar and Chaabane preprint Table 2).
Shared_Capital_note: The abstracts and review table do not show whether machine investment or its allocation is modelled, and the full text is restricted (IRIS UniBS records; Abidar and Chaabane preprint).
Shared_Capacity_note: The 2016 version draws insights on centralised versus decentralised manufacturing and the journal model compares traditional with centralised AM configurations, author findings rather than a capacity rule, and whether pooled capacity enters the model cannot be confirmed from abstracts (IRIS UniBS 2016 abstract; Abidar and Chaabane preprint Table 2).
Speed_note: The abstracts and review table do not say whether lead time or backorders enter the JELS model, and the full text is restricted (IRIS UniBS records; Abidar and Chaabane preprint).

name: GWU spare parts model for AM (hybrid AM/traditional maintenance-spares simulation)
developer: George Washington University doctoral dissertation; author not shown on the record (the PDF file name begins 'Togwe'; a related 2019 Engineering Management Journal paper on an AM aviation spares inventory model is by Thembani Togwe, Timothy J. Eveleigh and Bereket Tanju)
description: A simulation comparing a baseline of traditionally made spares with a hybrid of AM and traditional spares. Replacing 15% of maintenance spares with AM parts cut system replenishment lead time by 14.4%, from 98.4 to 84.2 days. Argues a hybrid strategy is viable because unused spares become obsolete or are damaged, lost or stolen.
NRE_note: Only the dissertation abstract (and the related EMJ 2019 abstract) could be read; neither says whether design or engineering effort is costed, and the record exposes no PDF link (GWU ScholarSpace).
Production_note: The related EMJ abstract says the work defines lifecycle variables that AM introduces but does not name them, so production cost coverage cannot be established (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).
QA_Qual_note: Only abstracts were read; they do not mention qualification or certification (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).
QA_Insp_note: Only abstracts were read; they do not mention inspection or testing (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).
Storage_note: Obsolescence, damage, loss and theft of unused spares are given only as motivation and the abstract reports only replenishment lead time for a 15% AM spares mix; whether inventory levels or holding cost enter the model cannot be confirmed from public sources (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).
Shared_Capital_note: Only abstracts were read; they do not mention machine investment or its allocation (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).
Shared_Capacity_note: Only abstracts were read; they do not say whether AM production capacity or sites are modelled in the replenishment simulation (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).
Speed_note: System replenishment lead time is a simulation output: a 15% AM share cut it 14.4%, from 98.4 to 84.2 days (the 2019 EMJ paper reports up to 33% at 35% AM) (GWU ScholarSpace; BL record).

name: Farghali et al. optimal AM and external-sourcing mix for spare-parts inventory
developer: Tamer Farghali, Regina Padmanabhan, Majed Hadid, Laoucine Kerbache (record in the HBKU repository)
description: A mathematical model that finds the 'optimal mix of AM and external sourcing' to minimize total cost and lead time, subject to cost factors and production capacities.
NRE_note: The abstract mentions only unnamed 'various cost factors', and the full text could not be reached (HBKU abstract).
Production_note: The model chooses between in-house AM production and external ordering to minimise total cost, but its cost factors are not itemised, so production cost inputs are undocumented (HBKU abstract).
QA_Qual_note: The abstract does not mention qualification and the full text could not be read (HBKU abstract).
QA_Insp_note: The abstract does not mention inspection and the full text could not be read (HBKU abstract).
Storage_note: The study is framed as spare-parts inventory management and claims on-demand AM helps keep optimal inventory levels, but the abstract shows no inventory or holding term in the model, so whether it uses stock cannot be confirmed (HBKU abstract).
Shared_Capital_note: The abstract does not say whether AM machine investment is a cost factor and the full text could not be read (HBKU abstract).
Shared_Capacity_note: Production capacities are explicit constraints on the AM/external mix, but the abstract does not show contention for shared printer capacity setting lead time, nor cross-site pooling (HBKU abstract).
Speed_note: The abstract states the mathematical model minimises total costs and lead times when choosing the AM/external mix, so lead time is a computed objective (dollar value not required); how lead time is formed is not shown (HBKU abstract).

name: ISO/ASTM 52920:2023 Qualification principles: requirements for industrial AM processes and production sites
developer: ISO/TC 261 and ASTM F42 (joint), with CEN/TC 438; TÜV SÜD offers third-party site certification against it
description: Site-level qualification standard. Clauses cover: infrastructure (machine installation, feedstock storage, FOD, maintenance/calibration); manufacturability assessment (design and manufacturing review); qualification of additive system operations (process mapping, risk assessment, master validation plan, IQ/OQ/PQ, manufacturing plan specification, traceability); and QA (personnel, non-conformities, production-run approval, part approval; informative annex on post-processing and part approval). The preview shows no tiers by part criticality.
NRE_note: Requires a manufacturability assessment and review, data preparation and a manufacturing plan specification, none costed (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, cl. 6; TOC 7.5, 7.7).
Production_note: A site and process qualification standard whose scope is activities and sequences within an AM production site, which plainly excludes per-part cost; cost appears only in the introduction and a note on downtime opportunity cost (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, scope, Introduction, cl. 5.9 note).
QA_Qual_note: Prescribes a risk-based choice of part-specific or process-generic qualification, process mapping, risk assessment, a master validation plan, IQ/OQ/PQ and requalification after changes, but sets no class-specific test counts (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, cls. 7.2-7.3; TOC 7.4).
QA_Insp_note: Requires risk-assessment output to 'define requirements for inspections according to AM part and AM process categories', plus production-run and part approval, but sets no inspection levels per category itself (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, cl. 7.3.2; TOC 8.5, Annex A).
Storage_note: Storage in the standard means feedstock storage at the site; spare-part inventory is plainly outside the scope of a production-site qualification standard (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, cl. 5.5, scope).
Shared_Capital_note: Clause 7.2 makes a risk-based choice between part-specific and 'process generic' qualification, the latter clearing a process for producing changing parts of the same material, so one qualification is reused across many parts, without numbers (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, cl. 7.2).
Shared_Capacity_note: Clause 5.9 mentions planning machine capacity utilisation and feedstock at a single site under the manufacturing-management requirement, but nothing pools or routes work across shared printers, users or sites, so shared capacity is not used in any decision step (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, cl. 5.9).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is plainly outside the scope of a production-site qualification standard; the only time-related text is a note that resource planning reduces machine downtime (ISO/ASTM 52920 sample, scope, cl. 5.9 note).

name: AMSC Standardization Roadmap for AM v3.0 (2023), with gap progress reports to 2026
developer: America Makes and ANSI Additive Manufacturing Standardization Collaborative (AMSC)
earlier_versions: AMSC Standardization Roadmap v1.0 (2017): first America Makes/ANSI roadmap after the AMSC launched in 2016. | AMSC Standardization Roadmap v2.0 (June 2018): update; replaced by v3.0 in July 2023 (141 gaps, 60 new).
description: 141 gaps (54 high, 64 medium, 23 low priority; 60 new). The Q&C chapter has 26 gaps (13 high), including QC2 (AM part risk classification), QC4 (process approval for DoD-procured parts), QC17 (AM part material development timeline), QC18 (OQ/PQ know-how) and QC20 (certifying-agency KPV checklist). The NDE chapter has 12 gaps, including fracture-critical acceptance criteria, NDT reliability and CT IQIs. The prioritization matrix ranks standards gaps, not parts. No cost figures were found.
NRE_note: Design-documentation effort is discussed as a standards gap (typical data packages are 'not sufficient to procure parts made via these processes'; gap DE17 asks for a standard on complete data packages), but the roadmap ranks standards gaps and uses no NRE in any decision about parts (AMSC Roadmap v3.0, Sec. 2.1.5.1, DE17).
Production_note: Cost appears as claims in words (AM 'offers significant potential cost savings'; designers should weigh 'reliability, cost assessment, logistics, and risk assessment'; design for post-processing 'can reduce overall program costs'), not as an input to any decision the roadmap makes (AMSC Roadmap v3.0, Sec. 1, 2.1.2, 2.1.2.5).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is catalogued as standards gaps calling for future standards (QC2 part risk classification, QC4 process approval for DoD-procured parts, QC17 material development timeline, QC18 OQ/PQ know-how, QC20 KPV checklist), so the roadmap prescribes no qualification activities itself (AMSC Roadmap v3.0 TOC; v3.0 overview).
QA_Insp_note: Inspection is named through NDE standards gaps calling for future standards (NDE9 effect of defects, NDE10 in-service inspection, NDE11 NDT reliability, NDE12 CT image quality indicator), not inspection steps the roadmap requires (AMSC Roadmap v3.0 overview).
Storage_note: The PDF text could be extracted only to about Sec. 2.2.3.4 (500,000-character cap), and the readable chapters (intro, design, precursor materials, process control, part of post-processing) contain no inventory or spares text, but the Maintenance and Repair (2.5) and Data (2.6) chapters could not be read, so absence is not confirmed (AMSC Roadmap v3.0).
Shared_Capital_note: Readable chapters mention only that the NIST AM materials database 'will aid in developing AM process chain'; the Finished Material Properties, Q&C and Data chapters, where shared allowables or pedigreed data would sit, lie beyond the extractable text, so sharing of qualification across users is not established (AMSC Roadmap v3.0, Sec. 2.1.3.3).
Shared_Capacity_note: Readable chapters only mention 'Distributed Manufacturing (DM) and Point-of-Care (POC) manufacturing that FDA has identified' (medical design) and forward-deployed machine environments (PC6), neither a capacity-sharing treatment, and the Maintenance and Repair chapter could not be read (AMSC Roadmap v3.0, Sec. 2.1.4.3, 2.2.2.6).
Speed_note: The roadmap claims AM offers 'shortening of the supply chain by allowing parts to be manufactured on-site rather than at a distant supplier', a benefit stated in words that enters no decision (AMSC Roadmap v3.0, Sec. 1, p. 29).

name: US Army AMCOM Command Policy Memorandum 070-062 on advanced/additively manufactured aviation parts (six-category scheme)
developer: US Army Aviation and Missile Command (AMCOM, Army airworthiness authority); drafted by DEVCOM Aviation and Missile Center (AvMC) engineers
description: Parts fall into six categories, from items that support maintenance operations up to aviation critical safety items. Each category prescribes the allowed materials and the appropriate testing method. Category definitions and requirements are not public. Army officials said it was too early to predict cost and time savings.
NRE_note: The memo is not public, and the articles describe H-60 2D-to-3D model conversion as a separate digital-twin effort without saying whether the memo sets engineering or technical-data requirements (Army Sustainment article; DLA reprint).
Production_note: The memo is not public; the Army article says the guidance aims to balance safety, readiness improvements and escalating costs, but no per-part cost element is described (Army.mil 2020 article).
QA_Qual_note: Parts fall into six categories, from maintenance support articles up to aviation critical safety items, each prescribing allowed materials and testing methodology, but the category requirements are not public so no costable test sets can be shown (Army.mil 2020 article; DLA reprint).
QA_Insp_note: Each category prescribes an 'appropriate testing methodology', so testing is required by category, but its scope, counts and cost are not public (Army.mil 2020 article).
Storage_note: The memo's documented scope is manufacturing, use and airworthiness qualification of AM parts, which excludes inventory, and neither article ties the memo to stock (Army Sustainment article; Army.mil 2020 article).
Shared_Capital_note: The memo is not public, so whether a qualification under a category carries across parts or sites, or whether equipment cost is addressed, cannot be established (Army.mil 2020 article; DLA reprint).
Shared_Capacity_note: The memo's documented scope is airworthiness categories with materials and testing, which excludes pooled print capacity, and neither article describes shared printing (Army Sustainment article; Army.mil 2020 article).
Speed_note: The article claims AM parts will end waits on back-ordered parts, but officials said time savings cannot yet be predicted and nothing shows lead time used in categorising parts (Army.mil 2020 article).

name: ASTM AM CoE Strategic Guide to Certification of Additively Manufactured Parts in Defence Applications (UK MOD Project TAMPA)
developer: ASTM International Additive Manufacturing Center of Excellence, funded by and developed with UK MOD (Project TAMPA)
description: Four-tier part classification (Class A-D) that links expected certification evidence to safety criticality. Evidence areas: feedstock control, machine and process qualification, and product verification/NDE. Two certification courses of action, one based on process qualification and one based on testing, chosen in proportion to criticality. Consolidates existing expectations rather than adding requirements.
NRE_note: Only news coverage was reachable (the guide is not listed on the AM CoE publications page fetched), and it names 'machine and process qualification' as an evidence area without saying whether process or design development effort is treated (TCT; VoxelMatters).
Production_note: The guide's documented scope is certification evidence tied to failure consequence, which plainly excludes per-part production cost; the only cost text in coverage concerns 'full qualification campaigns' (TCT; Interesting Engineering).
QA_Qual_note: A four-tier classification (Class A-D) links expected certification evidence to safety criticality, with two courses of action (process qualification or testing), but per-class test counts are not visible in any reachable source (VoxelMatters; TCT).
QA_Insp_note: 'Product verification and non-destructive evaluation' is one of the evidence areas the guide expects, but per-class inspection scope is not visible in coverage (TCT; VoxelMatters).
Storage_note: Inventory is plainly outside the documented scope of a criticality-based certification signposting guide, and no coverage mentions stock or spares (TCT; VoxelMatters; IMTS).
Shared_Capital_note: The process-qualification course of action might let one qualification cover several parts, and coverage notes duplicated testing when one branch's qualification is not accepted by another, but no source shows the guide itself provides for reuse (Interesting Engineering; VoxelMatters).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity is plainly outside the guide's certification scope; the 'planned network of certified AM production shared with allies' in the press release is attributed to Project TAMPA and UK strategy, not the guide (IMTS; TCT).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is plainly outside the guide's certification scope, and no coverage mentions lead time, readiness or spares for the guide (TCT; VoxelMatters; Interesting Engineering).

name: EDA Additive Manufacturing Feasibility Study & Technology Demonstration (EDA-AM, deployable AM factory)
developer: European Defence Agency (contract EDA-16.ESI.OP.144); performed by Fundacion Prodintec and MBDA France
description: EDA-commissioned study mapping defence AM applications, value chains and limitations, with a State of the Art Report and a Strategic Report. A self-contained AM 'factory' module was deployed in an EDA-sponsored airlift exercise to gather data on AM in operations. No part selection method, business case or cost model is published.
NRE_note: Only a poster, factsheet and news items describe the study and its reports are not public, so whether design or reverse-engineering effort is treated cannot be established (EDA poster; EDA activity page).
Production_note: The poster says only that 'substantial economic benefits are also expected', which does not refer to per-part production cost, and the reports that might cost production are not public (EDA poster; EDA activity page).
QA_Qual_note: Standardisation and certification are named among the 'solid limitations' the study found, a barrier; whether the study uses qualification in any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (EDA poster; EDA activity page).
QA_Insp_note: None of the poster, factsheet or news items says whether inspection is considered, and the reports are not public (EDA poster; factsheet).
Storage_note: 'Digital spare part storage and on-demand production' is listed as an example opportunity for the study to identify; whether the study uses stock in any decision cannot be confirmed from public sources (3D Printing Industry, 11 Apr 2017).
Shared_Capital_note: No public source says whether machine investment or sharing is assessed, and the reports are not public (EDA poster; activity page).
Shared_Capacity_note: One self-contained AM lab was airlifted to test deployability and then based at Zaragoza to make test parts, but no source describes pooling or sharing its capacity across units or sites, and the deployment report is not public (EDA poster; EDA news June 2017).
Speed_note: Expected benefits include 'on-site and on-demand field repair & maintenance' and 'ensuring platform availability', claims whose use in any decision of the study cannot be confirmed from public sources (EDA activity page; EDA factsheet).

name: DGA industrial orientation note on additive manufacturing (defence AM action plan incl. in-service support/MCO)
developer: Direction generale de l'armement (DGA), France; defence AM working group launched early 2023
description: Policy note stating that AM complements rather than replaces conventional manufacturing, and that design offices should use AM where useful but not for every part. Its action plan covers defining MCO use cases and business models, a common agile qualification process, large machines serving the whole defence industry, and sharing demand forecasts with subcontractors. No scoring or cost method is given.
NRE_note: Redesign effort is discussed as a benefit of AM (design offices 'devront exploiter les possibilités offertes', topology optimisation as a performance gain) but the note does not use NRE in any decision step (DGA NOI, working-group findings and 'Enjeux pour les armées').
Production_note: Cost is compared in words only (conventional methods 'resteront dans certains cas les plus adaptés et les plus rentables'), a finding the note does not turn into any cost rule or decision step (DGA NOI, working-group findings).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification appears only as a future action-plan item ('Établir un processus de qualification agile, robuste et généralisable' with a shared normative standard), not as a step or gate the note applies (DGA NOI, action plan).
QA_Insp_note: Full text read: inspection, NDT and control are not mentioned; post-processing appears only as a value-chain item ('intrants, imprimantes 3D, post-traitements, logiciels sécurisés') (DGA NOI).
Storage_note: Stock reduction is claimed (MCO costs could fall 'grâce à l'optimisation des stocks par la suppression des rechanges aisément et économiquement reproductibles') but the note uses no stock criterion in any decision (DGA NOI).
Shared_Capital_note: Shared large French machines 'afin de répondre aux besoins de l'ensemble des industriels de l'armement' and SME consolidation are described as policy, not used in any decision step (DGA NOI, working-group findings).
Shared_Capacity_note: Sharing defence-industry needs with subcontractors and setting up 'un réseau multi-filières' are action-plan measures with no routing or capacity rule in the note (DGA NOI, action plan).
Speed_note: Responsiveness is claimed (AM improves 'la réactivité du MCO pour réparer ou fabriquer des pièces de rechanges qui ne sont pas en stock') but lead time is not used in any decision step (DGA NOI).

name: DGA OptiFab study: AM anti-blast protection and pre-qualified spare parts catalogue for light armoured vehicles
developer: DGA (with the Agence de l'innovation de defense) and ARQUUS; testing at DGA Techniques aeronautiques, Toulouse
decision_levels: Part selection; Process/machine choice; Capacity placement/sharing
description: DGA study that compares several manufacturing methods to pick the best for anti-blast parts. It also tests whether light-vehicle spares could be made additively in maintenance workshops. 'Cloned' AM parts are characterised against the originals, first on the bench and then on vehicles, toward a catalogue of pre-qualified spare parts.
NRE_note: The study 'clones' original light-vehicle parts for additive manufacture, a reverse-engineering activity; whether that effort enters any decision cannot be confirmed from press sources (3Dnatives, Sep 2020).
Production_note: The study compares 'plusieurs techniques de fabrication' to pick the best for anti-blast parts, but the comparison criteria are not given and cost is not mentioned; the AID page could not be read (server error) (3Dnatives).
QA_Qual_note: Cloned AM parts are characterised against the originals and validated on a test bench and then on vehicles to enter 'un catalogue de pièces détachées qualifiées en amont', with no counts or burden given (3Dnatives).
QA_Insp_note: Trade press describes characterisation and bench/vehicle validation (qualification) but not whether per-part inspection of workshop-printed spares is required; the AID page could not be read (3Dnatives).
Storage_note: Stock reduction is claimed ('l'impression 3D réduit les stocks et améliore les chaînes d'approvisionnement'), but whether the study uses stock in any decision cannot be confirmed from press sources (3Dnatives).
Shared_Capital_note: Trade press does not say whether printer investment or sharing is assessed, and the AID page could not be read (3Dnatives).
Shared_Capacity_note: Spares made in military maintenance workshops and printers installed on some bases, including OPEX theatres, are described, but whether the study assigns or routes work across these sites cannot be confirmed from press sources (3Dnatives).
Speed_note: Time benefits are claimed ('réduire les délais de production', parts made 'sans attendre un ravitaillement'), but whether the study uses lead time in any decision cannot be confirmed from press sources (3Dnatives).

name: EPRI Quick Insight Brief: Additive Manufacturing to Support Spare and Replacement Items (3002019767)
developer: Electric Power Research Institute (EPRI)
decision_levels: Part selection; Adopt or make-vs-buy; Capacity placement/sharing
description: Short brief listing considerations for using AM for replacement items. They are process limits, QA scope (reverse-engineering measurements, CAD/CAM, fabrication), material equivalency for safety-related items, software control and counterfeiting. It gives utility examples and plans a member capability inventory, an application library and best-practice guidance.
NRE_note: Reverse engineering by laser and structured-light scanning is described and QA provisions 'need to address' reverse-engineering measurements and CAD/CAM data, listed as challenges; the brief has no decision step using engineering effort (EPRI 3002019767).
Production_note: Cost appears only as quoted case figures (connector about $150 each with no minimum vs an OEM quote of about $120,000 with a 100-piece minimum per type), and the brief applies no cost method or rule (EPRI 3002019767).
QA_Qual_note: Establishing equivalency of AM material to the original for safety-related items is listed under 'Challenges', with equivalency evaluations still to be developed, and the brief sets no qualification procedure or gate (EPRI 3002019767).
QA_Insp_note: QA techniques for verifying that items meet design are named as a challenge, with no inspection methods, scope or requirement set (EPRI 3002019767).
Storage_note: AM is presented as a way to manage obsolescence and avoid minimum order quantities, a claimed benefit the brief does not use in any decision (EPRI 3002019767).
Shared_Capital_note: The brief notes the 'potential to share resources such as additive manufacturing and laser light measurement machines' among members, a discussion point with no decision step or figures (EPRI 3002019767).
Shared_Capacity_note: A member and supplier AM capability inventory that could lead to regional AM centres is a planned next step, not a method that routes work (EPRI 3002019767).
Speed_note: Lead-time savings are quoted from cases (OEM about 46 weeks vs about 3 weeks; a 3-month quote vs under one week for 100 pieces) and are not used in any decision by the brief (EPRI 3002019767).

name: Anglo American spare parts inventory analysis and local on-demand AM pilot (with CSIR and Ivaldi)
developer: Anglo American with South Africa's CSIR and Ivaldi Group
description: Two-step project: analyse Anglo American's spare parts inventory and the impact of a digitally distributed supply chain, then digitise, produce locally and test selected parts at South African operations. No screening criteria or metrics are published.
NRE_note: Digitising the selected parts is the second project step, an activity the pilot performs, and whether its effort enters part selection cannot be confirmed from public sources (Anglo American press release, May 2021).
Production_note: The release names only logistics costs as reduced and quotes Ivaldi's general claim of 'significant savings for businesses', which is not tied to part production cost, so whether production cost is assessed cannot be established and no project outputs are public (Anglo American press release, May 2021; Engineering News).
QA_Qual_note: Locally produced parts are to be tested at South African operations in a planned trial with no published criteria, so whether qualification gates adoption cannot be confirmed from public sources (Anglo American press release, May 2021).
QA_Insp_note: The sources mention testing parts at the operations, read as a field trial, but do not say whether per-part inspection is considered, and no project outputs are public (Anglo American press release; Mining Magazine).
Storage_note: The project begins with an analysis of the spare-parts inventory and a 'files, not physical spare parts' model, but no selection criteria are published, so whether stock data are used to choose parts cannot be confirmed from public sources (Anglo American press release, May 2021).
Shared_Capital_note: None of the accounts says whether machine investment or its sharing is assessed, and no project outputs are public (Anglo American press release; Engineering News; Mining Magazine).
Shared_Capacity_note: Ivaldi sending files to local on-demand manufacturers describes a distributed network, but no rule assigning work across sites is published (Anglo American press release, May 2021).
Speed_note: Press coverage claims shorter delivery lead times; whether the platform uses lead time in its decisions cannot be confirmed from public sources (Anglo American press release, May 2021).

name: AWS D20.1/D20.1M:2019 Specification for Fabrication of Metal Components using Additive Manufacturing (2019)
year: 2019 (1st edition); revision and new wire-process D20.2 targeted for summer 2026
developer: American Welding Society (D20 Committee on Additive Manufacturing; D20A Subcommittee for powder processes)
description: Specification for qualifying, fabricating and inspecting metal AM components made by PBF or DED. The Engineer assigns each component Class A (critical), B (semi-critical) or C (noncritical) by consequence of failure, and the class grades the requirements: machine qualification with a standard qualification build (at least 54 tension specimens for PBF, 9 for DED) is required for Class A and B but not C, every Additive Manufacturing Procedure Specification must be qualified with a preproduction test build, and Class A and B PBF builds carry witness specimens. Clause 8 sets the nondestructive and destructive tests and acceptance criteria for production components.
NRE_note: One-time preparation steps are mandatory but not costed: the Additive Manufacturing Procedure Specification must be qualified through a Procedure Qualification Record before production, and a preproduction test build must use the production build file, post-processing and parameters within qualified limits (Coughlin, NRC workshop slides, Clauses 5.1-5.2.3).
Production_note: A fabrication specification, so per-part production cost is plainly outside its scope, and neither the committee slides nor the 2026 revision article mention cost (Coughlin, NRC workshop slides; Barnhart, AWS Welding Digest, Aug 2026).
QA_Qual_note: Qualification is prescribed by class in countable form: machine qualification is required for Class A and B and not for C, using a standard qualification build of at least 54 tension specimens for PBF (9 for DED) across orientations plus visual, dimensional, radiographic, density and metallographic examination, followed by procedure qualification and a preproduction test build (Wells, NASA slides 11-12, Table 5.1; Coughlin, NRC workshop slides, Clause 5.2).
QA_Insp_note: Witness specimens are required on Class A and B PBF builds, and Clause 8 prescribes visual, dimensional, penetrant, magnetic particle, radiographic and density examination plus tension, metallography and chemical analysis with acceptance criteria, but the slides read give no witness specimen counts or per-class inspection extent (Coughlin, NRC workshop slides, 4.3 and Clause 8; Mohr, SME AM Standards Forum slides 5 and 8).
Storage_note: A fabrication and qualification specification, so spare-part inventory is plainly outside its scope and no source mentions it (Coughlin, NRC workshop slides; Wells, NASA slides).
Shared_Capital_note: One-time machine qualification is reused across procedures without numbers: the Machine Qualification Record is kept separate from the Procedure Qualification Record, and Tables 5.2 (PBF) and 5.3 (DED) set which variable changes require requalifying the machine, the procedure or both (Coughlin, NRC workshop slides, 5.1.1 and Tables 5.2-5.3).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity shared across sites or users is plainly outside the scope; machines enter only as the unit qualified by a Machine Qualification Record (Coughlin, NRC workshop slides; Wells, NASA slides 11-12).
Speed_note: Part lead time or availability is plainly outside the scope; the only schedule content is the revision's summer 2026 release target (Barnhart, AWS Welding Digest, Aug 2026).

name: QuesTek ICMD Fatigue Toolkit (microstructure-sensitive fatigue life prediction; AFRL accelerated AM qualification)
developer: QuesTek Innovations LLC (Whelan, Gong, Olson)
description: Predicts fatigue life from alloy, microstructure and loading by building a statistical 3D digital twin of grains, inclusions and porosity and running crystal plasticity FE, small-crack and long-crack models, from crack incubation to long-crack growth, at coupon or component scale. The models are calibrated to a subset of tensile, LCF and crack-growth tests so that the remaining loading scenarios of a fatigue qualification matrix can be simulated as minimum-life predictions.
NRE_note: The paper cites roughly $1 million of fatigue testing per new alloy or process parameter set as motivation, but the toolkit outputs fatigue life and does not cost or decide on design-file or parameter-development effort (Whelan, Gong and Olson, ICAF 2023).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is outside the documented scope; cost appears only as claimed savings in testing and in over-engineering from large safety factors (ICAF 2023; QuesTek ICMD page).
QA_Qual_note: The framework's qualification procedure calibrates its crystal plasticity and crack-growth models to a subset of tensile, LCF and crack-growth tests and simulates the remaining loading scenarios as minimum fatigue lives, but the 500+ test, $1 million baseline is background and the claimed 70% testing-cost and $2 million AFRL savings are not computed by the tool (ICAF 2023; Metal AM, Mar 2025).
QA_Insp_note: X-ray CT or SEM sections characterise porosity and inclusions as inputs to the microstructure twin, and the model finds AM Ti64 pores under about 10 um do not initiate HCF cracks, but the paper sets no per-part inspection scope or acceptance criterion and inspection does not enter the tool's output (ICAF 2023).
Storage_note: A fatigue-life prediction tool, so spare-part inventory is plainly outside its documented scope (ICAF 2023; QuesTek ICMD page).
Shared_Capital_note: Machine capital and its sharing are plainly outside the documented scope of a fatigue-life prediction tool (ICAF 2023; QuesTek ICMD page).
Shared_Capacity_note: Print capacity is plainly outside the documented scope of a fatigue-life prediction and qualification tool (ICAF 2023; QuesTek ICMD page).
Speed_note: QuesTek claims AM qualification timelines fall 'from years to months', a claimed benefit, while the toolkit predicts fatigue life and does not compute part lead time or availability (QuesTek ICMD page; Metal AM, Mar 2025).

name: ORNL Peregrine AI layer-image in-situ monitoring software for powder bed AM
year: 2022 (FLC technology-transfer award, 10 licensees); 2025 (40+ licensees; AMMT nuclear qualification report)
developer: Oak Ridge National Laboratory, Manufacturing Demonstration Facility (Scime, Paquit et al.)
description: Segments each layer image of a powder bed build (visible and near-infrared cameras, with machine and melt-pool sensor data) with a deep convolutional network that classifies anomalies such as recoater hopping and streaking, spatter, swelling, superelevation and overheating, registered to CAD and scan paths at voxel resolution. It alerts operators mid-build, stores the data in each part's digital thread, and feeds a voxelized property prediction model that predicts local tensile properties and porosity hot spots for comparison with XCT and testing.
NRE_note: The report documents image registration, segmentation and per-machine network training on calibration builds, but no design-file, redesign or parameter-development cost enters Peregrine's output (ORNL/TM-2025/4056).
Production_note: Per-part production cost is outside the documented scope of a monitoring tool; ORNL claims lower cost and waste without figures (ORNL news, Apr 2025; ORNL/TM-2025/4056).
QA_Qual_note: Peregrine helped qualify TCR components and the report calls it the driver toward 'born-qualified' parts, but the tool outputs anomaly maps and voxel property predictions and sets no qualification gate, test set or accept/reject decision, and using it to cut fatigue and creep tests is listed as future work (ORNL/TM-2025/4056; Paquit and Scime, GAIN slides, May 2022).
QA_Insp_note: The tool's output is a layer-by-layer in-situ inspection that classifies anomalies pixel-wise, alerts operators and predicts porosity hot spots checked against XCT to triage flaws and show when targeted post-build inspection is needed, but no inspection cost or scope is computed (ORNL/TM-2025/4056; ORNL news, Apr 2025).
Storage_note: An in-process monitoring tool, so spare-part inventory is plainly outside its documented scope (ORNL/TM-2025/4056).
Shared_Capital_note: Peregrine runs on 20+ printer types with a desktop computer and an off-the-shelf camera, but machine capital and its sharing are outside its documented scope (ORNL news, Apr 2025; ORNL/TM-2025/4056).
Shared_Capacity_note: Cameras are deployed across several ORNL LPBF machines and ORNL and Argonne share an AM400 for comparison builds, but the software neither models nor allocates print capacity (ORNL/TM-2025/4056).
Speed_note: ORNL claims faster certification and less post-production analysis time without figures, while the tool does not compute part lead time or availability (ORNL news, Apr 2025).
